#10427. XREAL Aura is coming in November with a special $200-off launch discount

The first Android XR-powered smart glasses are almost here, and early adopters actually get a rare discount on the cutting-edge XREAL Aura hardware.

XREAL Aura is set to redefine what a “VR headset” can be by combining the form factor of XREAL display glasses with a small compute puck that clips to your waistband. XREAL and Google have teased Project Aura for months, announcing the official name and price last month, and now XREAL just unveiled the special launch price and release date on stage at Google’s Android Developer Summit.

The special glasses launch in mid-November, with preorders starting today, October 28, at Xreal.com and Best Buy. XREAL Aura will initially be available in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea (with a broader rollout in 2027) and is coming in two SKUs:

Both SKUs are available in standard and large sizes and come with an included carrying case that houses the glasses, compute puck, and cable. The cable is user-replaceable and uses a standard USB-C connection for longevity.

XREAL Aura will be launching alongside 150 made-for-XR experiences designed to showcase the power and capability of the new form factor. I got to use a near-final unit last month and was incredibly impressed with how XREAL and Google have been able to pull together the full Android XR experience on a pair of smart glasses, including full 6DoF spatial tracking and support for hand tracking and controllers.

XREAL Aura attaches via a USB-C cable to a compute puck, which is roughly the size of a phone. This has a generously sized trackpad on the front and a detachable belt clip on the back. The battery and Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset are inside the puck, taking the glasses’ weight down to just 95g (compared to ~500g for a VR headset).

XREAL and GameSir have partnered to deliver a new game controller built specifically for XREAL Aura (and Android XR). This one sports a prominent Gemini button that gives immediate access to Gemini’s helpful gaming capabilities (it’s actually more helpful than you might initially imagine). I also used this controller last month and found it to be wonderful. It feels similar to an Xbox Elite controller, but it is not spatially tracked.

A wireless portable keyboard is also on the way for productivity and multi-window workflows, but you can use any mouse and keyboard you’d like with Aura. XREAL Aura also supports wired mirroring, so you can plug your laptop or gaming console directly into the compute puck and add a spatially-tracked window to your view.

Preorders are open now and, of course, you’ll save $200 if you order XREAL Aura before the end of the year.

#10426. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10425. Outback Steakhouse store closures: See a list of doomed locations as franchisee files for bankruptcy

A number of Outback Steakhouse locations closed their doors last month in the lead-up to a bankruptcy petition by one of the casual dining chain’s largest franchisees, court documents reveal. The store closures span four states. Here’s what to know.

What’s happened?

Cerca Trova Restaurant Group Holdings, which operates as Out West Restaurant Group, one of Outback Steakhouse’s largest franchisees, sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on Monday.

The San Diego-based company, which currently employs around 3,669 workers, operates 61 Outback Steakhouse restaurants across Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, and New Mexico.

Outback Steakhouse, the dining chain known for its Australian theme, had more than 660 U.S. restaurants as of the end of last year, according to parent company Bloomin’ Brands.

Why did Cerca Trova file for bankruptcy?

Court records show the franchisee filed for bankruptcy to sell the majority of its assets.

However, that same day, Cerca Trova filed a motion to reject the leases on 10 restaurant locations that it had closed between October 11 and October 25.

According to court documents, the shuttered restaurants operated at a loss or at margins insufficient to cover their occupancy costs. These locations aren’t part of the proposed sale. 

Which Outback Steakhouse locations recently closed?

The following Outback Steakhouse locations closed in October.

Arizona

  • 4871 E. Grant Road, Tucson
  • 1860 E. McKellips Road, Mesa

California

  • 7575 Beach Blvd., Buena Park
  • 25261 N. The Old Road, Valencia
  • 26652 Portola Parkway, Foothill Ranch

Colorado

  • 7065 Commerce Center Drive, Colorado Springs
  • 15 W. Springer Drive, Highlands Ranch
  • 2066 S. Abilene St., Aurora
  • 8601 W. Cross Drive, Littleton

Nevada

  • 3645 S. Virginia St., Reno

The franchisee had previously closed three underperforming locations earlier this year, court documents show.

Growing financial pressure since 2018

In court documents, the company noted that it has faced growing financial challenges since 2018 due to declining traffic and rising labor costs.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, its revenue dropped around 35%. Cerca Trova has pursued a sale four times since 2018.

The company cited declining traffic and earnings—along with rising labor, food, and production costs—as the drivers of the mounting financial pressures that led to its recent bankruptcy filing.

On November 1, Bloomin’ Brands entered into a purchase agreement to acquire all of Cerca Trova’s assets for $26.3 million, subject to competing higher offers. The majority of Outback Steakhouse locations are already company-owned.

Fast Company reached out to Bloomin’ Brands to ask whether it plans to reopen any of the recently closed locations. We’ll update the story if we receive a reply.

#10423. Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform

Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.”

Existing third-party Connected Apps let you access Adobe, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Ticketmaster, and other services — now numbering over 50 — from the Gemini app. Google also announced a new Calm integration that will be available in the coming weeks. These @-integrations join first-party offerings like Google Workspace, Photos, and YouTube. To date, the creation process has required working closely with Google.

Google is now expanding availability on multiple fronts, starting with the Connected Apps Platform. It’s billed as a way to “build once and reach high-intent users.” Developers need to have a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their Connected Apps using the new Google Connected Console. This new website lets them track traffic, latency, and error rates, as well as control brand identity.

In addition to the Gemini app, Google will soon make existing Connected Apps available in Search. Developers can “choose whether [their app] will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both.” As part of the recent redesign, the Gemini app gained a new Customize page.

Developers can sign up for the preview at developers.google.com/connected-apps. Google is opening up access in phases over the coming months.

#10422. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi: Midterms sent a ‘very clear message’

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said this morning that Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory sent a “very clear message” about the damage inflation has done to American consumers.  

During an appearance on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Khosrowshahi said the problem stems from how the economy has evolved since the 2008 financial crisis, as wages have not kept pace with skyrocketing prices.

“When you look at capitalism, there’s capital investment and return on capital, and obviously there’s return on labor,” he said. “If you look over the past 20 years, return on capital has increased very, very significantly. You can’t say the same thing about return on labor.”

The rise of artificial intelligence is only adding to workers’ anxiety, he added.

“AI is an instantiation of capital where, to some extent, capital could replace labor as well, which is rightfully, in some cases, scaring people,” Khosrowshahi said. “But it’s also very, very powerful in its potential.”

Khosrowshahi said he was sharing his opinion and that he is “not a politician.”

When asked how politicians and business leaders should respond, Khosrowshahi pointed to the tax code.

“[The fact that] capital gains are taxed at a lower rate than regular income makes no sense to me,” Khosrowshahi said. “They should be balanced.”

“Whether you should raise one or lower the other one, that’s really up to the folks in power,” he added. “But it doesn’t seem right to me.”

Khosrowshahi has led Uber since 2017, when he replaced cofounder Travis Kalanick amid a series of scandals involving the company’s workplace culture and leadership. Khosrowshahi was previously the CEO of online travel company Expedia.

Uber employs millions of drivers and couriers who work as independent contractors.

Khosrowshahi’s comments came on the same day Uber reported $14.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 10% from a year earlier, and $1.4 billion in operating income, up 30%.

The company also said it expects to have about 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on its platform by year-end.

#10420. XREAL Aura debuts with 150 made-for-XR experiences, including Project Hail Mary, NBA, Fallout, and more

XREAL Aura already works with all your favorite Android apps thanks to Android XR, and that includes over 150 experiences that tap into the power of the XR glasses.

As I opened the NBA app on XREAL Aura and tapped the tabletop option, I watched the coffee table in front of me transform into a basketball court, complete with models of each player moving around the court in real-time. It was as if I were a giant looking in through the top of the arena. Not only could I get as close or as far away as I wanted, but all the game’s important stats were right there for me to peruse. The video below is taken from the Apple Vision Pro, but the experience is similar on XREAL Aura.

It was one of the most convincing reasons I’ve seen to own a pair of legit smart glasses, and the very reason XREAL chose to launch with Google’s Android XR at its core. All your favorite Android apps are here and work exactly as you hoped, and a curated selection of 150 now delivers a real sense of presence to the heart and soul of each app’s experience.

But it’s not just about compatibility or interoperability, either. The reach of Google’s Android platform means that big names like NBA, NASCAR, the San Francisco Ballet Company, Hulu, Netflix, Disney+, and so many more are playable in-glasses on day one, many with bespoke XR experiences.

Gamers will also be excited to know that Fallout is making a return in Fallout: Factions, a new strategy title for two players that brings classic units to a new tabletop experience. Then, there’s Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, an original mixed reality game with a story that takes place during the weeks Rocky and Ryland Grace spent trying to survive in space in the untold section of the novel (and movie) during the journey to Eridani.

Acclaimed actor and director Andy Serkis is even in on the mix with Nevatars, an Android XR exclusive that follows a character artist’s abandoned digital creations and will be free for the first 6 months. And then there’s Asteroid, a new type of immersive film from Doug Liman that takes the cinematic storytelling of a movie and meshes it with interactive gameplay via live conversational AI (Gemini). This one’s exclusive to Android XR and free for XREAL Aura owners.

Some of the most popular VR developers are also on board, including Resolution Games, who returns with a fresh port of the D&D-like strategy game, Demeo, plus the Android XR-exclusive Holochess (which is already on the Play Store). Holochess transforms the normally turn-based chess rules into a real-time strategy battle of Clankers vs. Xenoswarm, all on the table right in front of you. This 2-player game is free-to-play, and a third faction can be unlocked for $2.99.

There are also a ton of spatial games and experiences to play, as well as. Simply Piano XR merges physical instruments with virtual ones, giving you a real-time way to learn and improve your music skills while wearing your glasses. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg as developers continue to branch out with new, creative ways of using spatial computing devices like XREAL Aura.

#10419. Apple is restricting a fast-growing category of apps. Here’s what users need to know

Apple is about to put greater restrictions on dating apps and AI companions. 

Starting on November 16, the company will require developers to declare whether their apps use AI to facilitate romantic connections. The apps that do use artificial intelligence—whether it’s an AI companion or technology that assists humans in connecting with one another—will only be allowed for users older than 18. 

According to Apple’s November 2 announcement, apps will have to declare whether they offer real-world location sharing, as well as “features that enable dating or relationship connections between real people and/or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content.”

In addition, the announcement stated that app creators “must provide these declarations when submitting an app update or making changes to your age-rating questionnaire.” It noted that the declarations must be complete by January 12, and said that all apps using the technology must have a minimum age rating of 18-plus. 

In some places, location sharing won’t automatically impact minimum age restrictions, such as in Brazil, where regulations only require an above-16 rating. 

Dating apps have been widely adopting AI to assist romance-seekers in making connections. Apps like Hinge, Tinder, and Bumble use AI for tasks like helping with profile creation, choosing photos, suggesting matches, and more. And earlier this year, Bumble announced it’s introducing an AI matchmaker named “Bee” to the app.

Of course, the age-related changes may not be widely felt on dating apps themselves, given most dating platforms already have 18-plus age restrictions in place. Still, many AI companion companies have a large number of teen users. Some of the most popular apps teenagers are using to connect with nonhuman companions are Character.AI, Nomi, Replika, and ChatGPT. But while ChatGPT and Claude aren’t aimed at companionship, teens are using them that way in droves. 

According to a 2025 survey from Common Sense Media, 72% of teens ages 13 to 17 have used AI companions at least once. But a staggering 52% engage with them regularly. In maybe the survey’s most telling finding, 31% said these interactions are more satisfying than talking to humans. 

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that helps parents navigate tech and entertainment, has routinely recommended that AI companions should not be used by anyone younger than 18. In an April 2025 press release, James P. Steyer, the organization’s CEO, warned that AI companions are dangerous for minors for a host of reasons. “Social AI companions are not safe for kids. They are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency, which is particularly concerning for developing adolescent brains.”

Steyer continued: “Our testing showed these systems easily produce harmful responses, including sexual misconduct, stereotypes, and dangerous ‘advice’ that, if followed, could have life-threatening or deadly real-world impact for teens and other vulnerable people.” 

Fast Company reached out to Apple about the recent announcement but did not hear back by the time of publication.

#10416. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10415. Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million on the midterms. It bought him almost nothing

Elon Musk put about $474 million into the 2026 midterms, according to a New York Times tally. (That amount only tracks through October 14, when Federal Election Commission [FEC] and IRS filings stopped; the trillionaire may have given far more in dark money.) For comparison, the world’s richest man spent an estimated $250 million to get Donald Trump elected in 2024.

But this time, he has little to show for his efforts. Democrats wrested control of both the House of Representatives and Senate from Republicans Tuesday night. A Forbes analysis shows that 44 of Musk’s 106 candidates lost, including in the races that mattered most to him: Ken Paxton’s bid for a Texas Senate seat, Greg Abbott’s bid to remain Texas governor, and Vivek Ramaswamy’s bid for governor of Ohio. Eighteen Musk-backed candidates won, but all were in seats Republicans were expected to win anyway. Another 44 races remained uncalled Wednesday.

Musk’s money was funneled to Republican House and Senate candidates through his own super PAC, America PAC (about $216 million), the Senate Leadership Fund ($168 million), and the Congressional Leadership Fund for House races ($30 million).

The largest share of Musk’s midterm spending ($212 million) went toward helping Ken Paxton beat James Talarico for the Texas Senate seat formerly held by John Cornyn. Talarico walloped Paxton Tuesday night, winning by 12 points in the traditionally red state. In his victory speech, Talarico seemed to call out Musk, saying he had sent “a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor.”

Outside Texas, America PAC spent $22.7 million in six battleground states through October 20, filings show, including $8.9 million in Ohio and $7.2 million in Michigan. Democrat Sherrod Brown won the Senate seat in Ohio, while Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate seat in Michigan.

Congressional purse strings

Musk’s America PAC said its “only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington.” His businesses rely heavily on federal money: SpaceX booked $6.78 billion in federal contracts through October 1, compared with just $3.8 billion in all of 2024, per data from federal spending tracker FedScout. In May, the U.S. Space Force awarded it $4.16 billion for Golden Dome tracking satellites. The party that controls Congress controls the government’s purse strings. Musk’s gravy train may slow down or stop.

Republicans believed Democrats would have to take Texas to seize control of Congress.

In January, Democrats will chair the committees that fund and oversee SpaceX’s biggest customers. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME), whom America PAC backed, lost her seat—and with it, the Appropriations Committee chairmanship, which shapes NASA and Pentagon budgets.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has said he would investigate Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) if Democrats won. The Senate also confirms Federal Communications Commission (FCC) members, who control Starlink’s spectrum, and funds the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which licenses SpaceX launches. The new Congress can’t cancel contracts; the Pentagon and NASA award them.

With Paxton’s defeat, Musk also lost a reliable vote in the Senate—and gained a Texas senator in Talarico who identified him during the campaign as an out-of-touch trillionaire who personifies some of the country’s biggest problems.

Investigations

As Democrats clinched the House on Tuesday night, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who will chair the House Oversight Committee, posted two words on X: “LAWYER UP.” The warning was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and family, but Garcia’s office said he would also take on “corporate corruption,” and Musk may be at the top of that list. Democrats will run committees with subpoena power, allowing them to compel documents and testimony. In 2025, House Republicans blocked a Democratic motion to subpoena Musk. In January, Democrats will hold the gavels.

They’ve already named their targets. Committees are weighing probes of Musk’s time running DOGE, SpaceX’s and Tesla’s federal contracts, and his alleged role in restricting SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service to Ukraine’s military, Politico reports. (Musk says the U.S. military, not SpaceX, decides any limits on Starshield.)

Wall Street investors reacted quickly to Tuesday night’s election results. SpaceX shares fell 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% in premarket trading on Wednesday. Overnight, Musk posted on X: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

What Hinojosa’s win means in Texas

Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s surprise victory over Gov. Greg Abbott could put Musk’s plans to build data centers across Texas in jeopardy. Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers enact lasting safeguards. “Data centers are coming in and doing as they please—they are guzzling up all our water, guzzling up all our electricity—and the people have no say . . . that is the Wild West of data centers that Greg Abbott has created in Texas,” she said in July.

Hinojosa wants rules giving Texas residents more say over new developments, requiring companies to prove their projects won’t raise household water or electricity bills, and prohibiting nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark during the permitting process. She also wants to eliminate the government subsidies that have helped make Texas so attractive to developers.

Musk has major operations and investments in the state, including Tesla’s headquarters and largest U.S. plant, SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, and the planned Terafab semiconductor and AI chip plant. Musk gave an estimated $5.5 million to Abbott’s campaign.

Abbott’s administration gave Musk’s companies some major benefits. The governor’s office pushed broadband rules that favored Starlink, which then won about $110 million in state grants, triggering an audit. Terafab won about $1.7 billion in school tax breaks, and SpaceX more than $54 million in state grants, according to a lawsuit Hinojosa filed during the campaign.

That suit won Hinojosa access to more than 1,000 pages of Abbott-Musk communications that Abbott had called too “intimate and embarrassing” to release. In one message, Musk asked whether Abbott would “have his back,” to which Abbott replied, “100%.”

When she takes office in January, Hinojosa will control future incentive deals. She’ll also appoint the Texas Parks commissioners who would vote on any sale of Boca Chica State Park, which Musk wants to buy to expand SpaceX’s Starbase rocket facility in South Texas.

What the losses cost Musk

The $224 million Musk spent and lost in Texas isn’t likely to hurt his wallet much. He’s worth about $902 billion today, so he lost roughly one-fortieth of 1% of his wealth.

But the loss of a friendly Congress—and the diminished political clout of Musk’s friend Trump—could cost much more. About one-fifth of SpaceX’s $18.7 billion in 2025 revenue came from federal agencies, its initial public offering (IPO) filing says. That’s roughly $3.7 billion a year, or $7.5 billion over two years at 2025 levels. The Democratic Congress could decide to slow-walk new contracts, like May’s $4.16 billion Golden Dome award.

Musk now pitches SpaceX as a supplier of AI computing. Deals renting its Colossus data centers to Anthropic and Google could bring in $26 billion a year. The changing political tide could make getting permits for new data centers more difficult. In August, even the Musk-friendly Abbott paused new data center connections to the Texas grid.

The election results could also shake investors’ confidence in Musk and the companies he leads. SpaceX’s IPO filing calls the company “highly dependent” on Musk. When investors buy SpaceX or Tesla stock, they’re not just looking at the companies’ financials; they’re also buying into the “story” of Musk, who has fashioned an image of an unpredictable engineering genius with massive wealth and powerful friends. But his political connections look considerably less secure after Tuesday night. That could make investors less inclined to believe Musk’s claims that SpaceX will put data centers in space and become the largest AI company in the world.

On Tuesday morning, Musk tweeted “Vote red today!” But by Wednesday morning, the tweet had quietly disappeared.

#10412. Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape

The AI design giant Canva just announced the first-ever major round of layoffs in its 13-year history. As part of the restructuring, 1,271 people—around 22% of the company’s overall staff—will either be laid off, asked to change roles, or relocate to the company’s headquarters in Sydney, Australia. 

News of the layoffs was announced on November 3 (a perfect day to bury some bad news) in a press release from Canva cofounder and CEO Melanie Perkins. In the note, Perkins explains that the layoffs are part of a larger plan to make Canva’s teams more agile and less siloed, including by folding product, growth, and platform teams into one unit and reducing the number of “subspecialities” at the company.

“I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough,” Perkin’s letter reads. “To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.”

While Canva didn’t provide a broader business reason for the layoffs, the restructuring comes at a time when it’s working through some mounting growing pains and questions about the timing of a potential IPO. After spending the last several years going all-in on its AI-powered product suite, Canva is now facing the challenge of squaring its business model with an increasingly voracious user base.

Canva’s growth conundrum

In May, Fast Company wrote that design was entering its “frenemies” era. 

At the time, Anthropic had just launched Claude Design. The product seemingly came as a surprise to incumbent companies including Adobe and Figma, which had been operating under a multiyear collaboration with Anthropic to integrate Claude into their products, and didn’t expect the AI giant to debut its own design competitor. Meanwhile, Canva told Fast Company that it had actually helped Anthropic develop Claude Design, despite Canva’s own collaboration deal with the company. 

For Adobe, Figma, and Canva, working with frontier models offers the advantage of bringing new tools to market faster and benefiting from the sophistication of frontier models. The main downside is that using these frontier models also takes a lot of computing power, and that racks up major costs. As Canva has made a major push—by building its own models and acquiring AI companies—to become an “AI platform” over the last several years, those costs have become a significant problem.

In early August, Canva sent a note to its investors with an update: the company was downgrading its revenue growth forecast for 2026 from 30% to 20%. At the time, Perkins told shareholders that the “average cost of serving an AI task was too high” as the company relied heavily on its partnerships with frontier models to complete users’ requests. 

For context, by the end of 2025, Canva had more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users, meaning that some large portion of AI traffic on the site was likely generated by free users. In an August interview with Fortune, Perkins said that users’ demand for new AI features had “significantly exceeded” the company’s expectations, which came with both pros and cons. 

“This validated the demand, but also showed us we needed to reduce the cost of completing an AI task to support a broad rollout,” Perkins told the publication. “Rather than broadly rolling out a product before the underlying economics were ready, we decided to slow the rollout while we rebuilt the architecture, reduced unit costs and strengthened the business model.”

To reduce the intermediary costs that Canva incurs every time an AI task requires a frontier model, Canva has been working on developing first-party tools that can take up some of the work. For example, Perkins told Fortune that, since launching Canva 2.0 in April, the company’s cost-per-task has reduced by 90%. This October, Canva launched another product called Canva Brush, which it said reduced cost-per-task by 46% compared to the previous design agent. 

These new features have made improvements, but, based on its downgraded revenue forecast, Canva still has a ways to go before it fully irons out its economic model. The fact that user demand for Canva’s AI tools is outpacing its own capabilities seems to be a bullish sign for AI design at large. Now, Canva needs to figure out how to make the most of the surge—and the company’s first major layoffs could be part of its plan to get back on track.

#10409. Vibe Coding to Production: A Developer’s Checklist for Building Reliable Web Apps

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI coding tools can turn a plain-English description into a working web application in minutes. They can generate interfaces, connect APIs, create database schemas, and help developers move from an idea to a functional prototype faster than traditional workflows often allow.

But getting an application to run is not the same as making it production-ready.

The security gap is measurable. In its 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode found that 45% of AI-generated code samples failed security tests by introducing vulnerabilities associated with the OWASP Top 10. The research evaluated generated code samples, not complete applications or confirmed cyberattacks. Nevertheless, it highlights an important risk: code that works can still be insecure.

Real-world investigations have raised similar concerns. A May 2026 WIRED investigation into exposed data in vibe-coded applications reported security and data-exposure problems in applications built using popular AI coding tools. These findings concern the applications examined, rather than every application developed with AI.

The lesson is not that vibe coding is inherently unsafe. It is that generating software quickly does not eliminate the engineering work required to protect data, verify behavior, and maintain reliability.

AI can accelerate implementation, but production readiness still requires engineering discipline.

Whether you are a developer using an AI coding assistant, a founder building a minimum viable product (MVP), or a team experimenting with vibe coding, this checklist will help you evaluate your application before releasing it to real users.

Vibe coding is an AI-assisted software development approach in which developers describe requirements in natural language and use AI tools to generate, modify, and debug code. Rather than manually writing every component, developers guide implementation through prompts, feedback, and iterative refinement.

This approach can accelerate prototyping, interface development, and repetitive programming tasks. However, generated code must still meet the same quality standards as conventionally written software.

Consider a customer portal. An AI tool might generate a login page, a dashboard, and a database connection in a single session. The interface could look complete while the application still lacks proper authorization checks, reliable error handling, or protection against unauthorized data access.

These gaps become more consequential when an application stores personal information, processes payments, manages business records, or serves multiple customers.

Production readiness means an application has been tested and configured to operate reliably in its intended environment. It includes security, correctness, performance, maintainability, monitoring, and recovery.

Before deployment, evaluate the application across the following areas.

One common mistake in AI-assisted development is building features before defining what they should do.

A prompt such as "Build a project management dashboard" leaves important questions unanswered. Who can create projects? Can users access another person's tasks? What happens when a task is deleted? Which fields are mandatory? How should errors appear?

When these decisions are left to the AI, the implementation may reflect assumptions that do not match the product's requirements.

Before generating substantial amounts of code, document:

Core functionality: What must users be able to accomplish?

User roles: Who can view, create, edit, or delete information?

Data requirements: Which fields, relationships, and constraints are necessary?

Technical constraints: Which frameworks, databases, APIs, and hosting environments will be used?

Failure scenarios: What should happen when a request fails or data is invalid?

Acceptance criteria: What observable result proves that each feature works correctly?

For example, a task management application might have this requirement:

A user can view and modify only the tasks belonging to projects they are authorized to access. Unauthorized requests must be rejected without revealing protected data.

This is more useful than simply asking an AI tool to "add secure task management." It establishes a behavior that developers can implement and test.

Once the requirements are documented, ask the AI to implement one coherent feature at a time. Review the output before moving to the next feature.

This makes unexpected changes easier to identify and reduces the risk of introducing multiple interacting bugs through a single large generation.

Keep the requirements in a project document and update them whenever product decisions change. The specification should remain the reference point for both the developer and the AI coding assistant.

A functional interface can conceal serious implementation problems.

AI-generated code may contain duplicated logic, unnecessary dependencies, outdated API usage, incorrect assumptions about framework behavior, or abstractions that make future changes difficult. A successful build does not establish that the application behaves correctly.

Code review is therefore essential, even when an AI tool generates most of the implementation.

Start with the code responsible for important application behavior:

Check whether functions have clear responsibilities, whether data flows are understandable, and whether dependencies are actually needed.

For JavaScript and TypeScript projects, automated linting and type checking can catch many common mistakes. However, these tools cannot prove that business logic is correct or that permissions are enforced properly.

When reviewing a change, ask the AI to explain its implementation and identify its assumptions. Then verify those explanations against the actual code and relevant documentation.

If a function is difficult to understand, simplify it or request a clearer implementation. Code that nobody on the team can confidently maintain is a liability, regardless of how quickly it was generated.

Authentication answers the question, "Who is this user?" Authorization answers, "What is this user allowed to do?"

Both are necessary for applications that protect private information or restrict access to particular features.

An AI-generated application may implement a login screen and assume the security requirement is complete. In reality, hiding a dashboard element or redirecting an unauthenticated visitor does not prevent someone from calling a protected API directly.

Every sensitive operation should enforce the relevant permissions on the server or trusted backend.

For example, an application that allows users to view invoices should verify that the authenticated user is authorized to access the requested invoice. It should not rely solely on a user ID supplied by the browser.

Test both permitted and prohibited actions. A good security test confirms not only that the correct user can access a resource, but also that other users cannot.

For applications handling sensitive data, consider an independent security review before launch.

AI-generated applications often work well with expected inputs. Real users, however, submit incomplete forms, unexpected values, oversized files, malformed requests, and repeated actions.

Input validation and error handling help prevent these conditions from becoming application failures or security vulnerabilities.

Client-side validation improves the user experience, but it should not be the only line of defense. Requests can bypass browser validation entirely.

Validate incoming data on the server, using rules appropriate to each field and operation. Enforce database constraints where applicable, and use parameterized queries or safe ORM methods to prevent SQL injection.

For file uploads, validate file types, enforce size limits, and store files using a design that prevents unauthorized access. Do not assume a filename or content type supplied by the browser is trustworthy.

Users need understandable error messages. Developers need enough diagnostic information to investigate failures.

These requirements should be handled separately.

A user-facing response might say, "We couldn't save your changes. Please try again." An internal log can record a request identifier, the relevant operation, and a sanitized diagnostic message.

Avoid exposing stack traces, database credentials, internal configuration, access tokens, or sensitive records in production responses.

Also test what happens when external APIs time out, database connections fail, or required environment variables are missing.

A production-ready application should fail predictably, protect sensitive information, and provide a clear path to recovery.

Testing is particularly important in vibe coding because generated code can appear convincing even when it implements the wrong behavior.

Asking an AI tool to generate tests is useful, but those tests must be reviewed. A test suite can pass while validating incorrect assumptions or ignoring the application's most important failure cases.

Start with critical workflows rather than trying to test every minor interface detail.

For an e-commerce application, these workflows might include account creation, product selection, checkout, payment confirmation, and order retrieval. For a business dashboard, they might include importing records, updating a customer, assigning permissions, and generating a report.

Pay particular attention to boundary conditions.

What happens when a form is submitted twice? When an API returns an unexpected response? When a database operation fails halfway through a workflow? When two users update the same record simultaneously?

These scenarios often reveal problems that a successful demonstration will not.

For applications that process transactions, test idempotency where appropriate so that retries do not unintentionally create duplicate payments, orders, or records.

A web application can feel fast during development and become sluggish when it handles larger datasets, multiple concurrent users, or slower network connections.

AI-generated code should therefore be evaluated against realistic usage patterns.

Begin with the operations most likely to affect the user experience:

Use browser developer tools and server-side monitoring to identify actual bottlenecks before optimizing.

Database indexes can improve frequently used queries, while pagination can prevent interfaces from loading thousands of records at once. Caching can reduce repeated work when the data and consistency requirements allow it.

For public-facing websites, evaluate relevant Core Web Vitals and test performance on realistic devices and network conditions.

Avoid adding caching layers, complex abstractions, or performance libraries simply because an AI tool recommends them. Every additional component introduces maintenance costs and potential failure points.

Measure first, optimize the bottleneck, and measure again.

Generated applications frequently depend on third-party packages, API services, and environment-specific settings. Each dependency expands the application's maintenance and security responsibilities.

Before deployment, inspect the dependency manifest and lockfile. Remove unnecessary packages, verify that required packages exist, and review known vulnerabilities using appropriate dependency-scanning tools.

Keep frameworks and libraries updated according to a deliberate maintenance process rather than automatically accepting every suggested upgrade.

API keys, database passwords, signing secrets, and other credentials should not be embedded in client-side code or committed to a public repository.

Use environment variables or an appropriate secrets manager, depending on the deployment environment. Restrict credentials to the permissions they actually require, and rotate any secret that may have been exposed.

Remember that a variable included in a browser-delivered bundle is not secret simply because it was originally configured as an environment variable.

Also verify that development and production environments use the correct endpoints, database connections, authentication settings, and logging configuration.

A local application that works with unrestricted development credentials may behave very differently when deployed under production permissions.

Deployment should be a controlled process, not a final experiment performed after development is complete.

A repeatable deployment process reduces human error and helps teams identify which changes introduced a problem.

For projects that support it, establish a continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline with automated checks for:

Before launch, verify that you can restore the application to a known-good state.

This includes maintaining version control, documenting deployment steps, backing up important data, and testing restoration procedures. A backup is only useful if it can be restored successfully.

Database schema changes deserve particular attention. An incompatible migration can make an otherwise successful deployment unusable. For important applications, plan migrations so that application versions can coexist safely during rollout and rollback.

Also check how the application behaves when a deployment fails, a service becomes unavailable, or a configuration change introduces a regression.

A reliable release process should make failures easier to detect, contain, and recover from.

Testing happens before release and in controlled environments. Monitoring helps developers understand how the application behaves after real users begin using it.

Without monitoring, a deployment can appear successful while users encounter failed requests, slow pages, broken integrations, or database errors.

Set alerts for failures that require action. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal data in logs, and define retention and access policies appropriate to the application.

For AI-powered features, monitor additional factors such as model response failures, latency, token usage, and output quality. An application that depends on an external AI service must account for rate limits, changing model behavior, and provider outages.

Monitoring does not prevent every failure. It makes failures visible enough to investigate and resolve.

Before releasing an AI-generated web application, use the following checklist to assess whether the essentials are in place.

Requirements: Core features, user roles, constraints, and acceptance criteria are documented.

Code quality: Important code paths have been reviewed, and unnecessary dependencies have been removed.

Authentication: Identity and session handling are implemented appropriately.

Authorization: Protected resources and operations enforce server-side permissions.

Input validation: Requests, uploads, and database operations are protected by appropriate validation and constraints.

Error handling: Failures are handled predictably without exposing sensitive information.

Testing: Critical workflows, negative cases, and regression scenarios have been tested.

Security: Dependencies, secrets, configuration, and common vulnerability risks have been reviewed.

Performance: Important queries, endpoints, and user journeys have been evaluated under realistic conditions.

Deployment: Builds and releases follow a repeatable process with appropriate quality gates.

Recovery: Backups, restoration procedures, and rollback options have been considered and tested where applicable.

Monitoring: Errors, availability, and performance can be observed after release.

Not every application needs the same level of testing or operational complexity. A personal prototype has different requirements from a financial application or a multi-tenant SaaS product.

The important thing is to identify the risks associated with the intended use and address them before exposing real users or sensitive data.

A developer does not necessarily need an external review for every small experiment. However, an independent review becomes increasingly valuable when the application handles sensitive information, processes payments, supports multiple customer organizations, or implements complex permissions.

It is also worth considering when the original developer cannot explain important parts of the generated code or when repeated AI-generated changes have made the architecture difficult to understand.

A useful review should examine more than formatting and syntax. It should evaluate application behavior, data access, authentication, security controls, error handling, deployment configuration, and maintainability.

For teams using AI to accelerate development, the goal is not to eliminate AI-generated code. It is to make sure that the resulting software meets the quality standards expected of any application entering production.

Vibe coding changes how quickly developers can move from an idea to working software. It does not remove the need to understand requirements, validate behavior, protect data, test failure scenarios, and maintain the application after release.

The most reliable approach is to treat AI as a development accelerator within a disciplined engineering process. Define the requirements, review generated code, test critical workflows, enforce security controls, automate deployment checks, and monitor the application after launch.

Start with the checklist in this article and prioritize the controls that matter most to your application's risk profile. For a deeper look at the development process, read this guide to production-ready vibe coding.

The goal is not simply to build an application quickly. It is to build one that users can trust, developers can maintain, and businesses can depend on.

#10407. McDonald’s to add new value bundles next year

McDonald’s plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles early next year after a disappointing third quarter that saw lower traffic at U.S. restaurants.

McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday that the company recently began an eight-week test of mix-and-match and fixed-price bundles at 1,900 U.S. restaurants. Those bundles might feature a McChicken sandwich and small fries for $3.50, for example.

But around 4,000 franchisees have decided not to wait for the test results and have launched meal bundles of their own, he said.

“Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s, whether they’re looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal or a digital offer in the mobile app,” Kempczinski said during a conference call with investors.

U.S. same-store sales—or sales at locations open at least a year—fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald’s since early 2025.

McDonald’s restored some regional and national in-app deals and shifted some marketing spending to support value meals, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September and October. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies, which are losing customers as many Americans struggle with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living.

Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.

McDonald’s has been tweaking its U.S. value offerings for more than two years to try to lure back lower-income customers and better compete with rivals like Taco Bell, which offers a menu of 10 items that each cost $3 or less.

In June 2024, McDonald’s introduced a $5 Meal Deal. The next year, it debuted its McValue menu, and Extra Value Meals, which promise a 15% discount for a bundled meal compared to buying items individually. In April, it revamped the McValue menu, adding 10 items that cost $3 or less.

But not all of McDonald’s franchisees—who own 95% of the company’s U.S. restaurants—have been on board. Kempczinski said in August that only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering the revamped McValue menu. McDonald’s replaced its U.S. president that same month.

Kempczinski said the company’s previous efforts haven’t been enough because they didn’t offer compelling low-end deals.

“You need to have good entry-level value, particularly with the low-income consumer,” he said.

Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the third quarter. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September.

Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion.

Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit.

Shares rose more than 5% in morning trading Wednesday.

—By Dee-Ann Durbin, AP business writer

#10404. This map shows just how big Democrats won the midterms

The 2026 election was a total political reset from 2024, with many states that voted for President Donald Trump last time swinging to the left and giving Democrats control of the next Congress. A pair of maps shows through arrows just how dramatic the change in just two years really was.

To communicate the shift in vote margin from one party to another from the most two recent elections, The New York Times has used an election results map with arrows that show the shift in each individual county where most votes are now counted. Blue arrows to the left show a trend towards Democrats compared to the last election while red arrows to the right show a trend towards Republicans. The longer the arrow, the bigger the shift. Two years ago, that map was covered in red. It’s now filled by a sea of blue arrows.

The Times first use the arrows map 10 years ago to show the vote shift in 2016, and Times graphics editor Wilson Andrews told Fast Company in 2024 the style “adds another layer of storytelling.” While typical election map graphics show you the winner or vote share, this map conveys a sense of time, giving viewers a look at how much political attitudes changed from one Election Day to another.

Trump won the national popular vote in 2024 after making campaign promises to lower prices and avoid foreign wars, but in office he did the opposite, by illegally imposing tariffs and launching a war with Iran. These policy decisions raised costs, as did broad government corruption, pet construction projects that cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and his administration’s overly aggressive immigration enforcement tactics, which flipped many Latino voters he’d won in the previous election cycle.

In just two years, Trump’s positive approval rating dropped near its lowest ever—and is the lowest net approval rating for any incumbent president in a midterm since polling began. Tuesday’s results shows what that means from county to county in stark terms.

The Times shift map is an especially compelling piece of data visualization to depict upsets, because it subverts what we’re used to seeing from standard red-blue election results maps. Instead of just “red states” and “blue states,” that show you the winner, it shows where in the country the vote has most swung. The 2026 map shows tiny blue arrows in Democratic strongholds like Oregon, because the vote margin shift wasn’t that great, while in places we’re used to seeing always colored in red, like Texas or Kansas, the longest blue arrows blanket the state.

Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Tuesday a “change election,” and Democrats pulled off wins Tuesday in historically Republican places: Annie Andrews became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina since 1998, James Talarico became the first in Texas since 1988, and Adam Hamilton became the first in Kansas since 1932. Branding themselves as centrists, these Democrats ran in an especially unfavorable year for Republicans tied to an unpopular president that many of them didn’t even want to mention.

Showing election results through the shift in margin has become a popular form of data viz, and other outlets like The Economist and NBC News did their own versions of the map this year too. The story of U.S. midterms is one of buyers’ remorse, and long blue arrows in deep red states quickly show just how forcefully much of the American electorate wanted a refund.

#10401. How I Built a CRM with Vibe Coding Instead of Spending $1,000+ on App Builders

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

I have designed more than 100 websites and helped clients set up over 12 CRM and ERP systems. For years, my work revolved around WordPress, digital marketing, business automation, and helping companies choose the right technology.

But building a web application from scratch was a different challenge.

I wanted to move beyond configuring existing software and experience the entire product development process myself. I had an idea, a clear understanding of business workflows, and access to AI coding agents. What I did not want was another expensive subscription that would limit how I built, deployed, or maintained the application.

That decision led me to build a CRM using Claude, Next.js, Firebase Firestore, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, and Git.

The experience taught me something important: AI can reduce the cost of building software, but understanding what you are building still matters.

My background gave me a useful starting point. After working on more than 100 websites, I understood how users interact with interfaces, how businesses collect leads, and why a confusing workflow can make even good software difficult to use.

Setting up CRM and ERP systems for clients also helped me understand the operational side of software. I had seen how businesses manage contacts, sales pipelines, follow-ups, and reporting.

However, configuring an existing platform and building an application from scratch are two very different experiences.

When you configure a CRM, many architectural decisions have already been made. When you build one, you must think about the data model, authentication, permissions, integrations, deployment, and what happens when something fails.

I decided to use this project to learn those things through practical experience rather than limiting myself to website design.

My first instinct could have been to use a visual app builder such as Lovable or Bolt. These tools can be excellent for quickly generating prototypes and getting an idea off the ground.

But I wanted greater control over the codebase, architecture, and deployment process. I also wanted to avoid accumulating app-builder subscription costs during development.

Instead, I chose an AI-assisted coding workflow.

Claude acted as my coding partner. I described requirements, generated implementation drafts, reviewed the output, debugged problems, and refined features through repeated iterations.

This did not mean I could simply write a prompt and receive a finished application. I still had to make decisions, understand the generated code, test the results, and correct mistakes.

The financial advantage was meaningful. By avoiding paid app-builder subscriptions for this project, I saved more than $1,000 in potential tool costs and related expenses I would otherwise have budgeted for. That was my project-specific saving, not a claim that every custom application will be cheaper to build.

More importantly, I ended up with a codebase and development workflow I could control rather than depending entirely on a particular app-building interface.

I wanted a modern stack that supported fast iteration without sacrificing control over the application.

Claude helped me translate requirements into code, work through implementation problems, and iterate on features. I treated its output as a starting point, not something to trust without review.

Next.js provided the foundation for the web application. It gave me a structured way to build the interface and application logic while keeping the project organized as it grew.

Firestore handled the application's data storage. Its document-based model and integration with the Firebase ecosystem made it a practical choice for my development workflow.

Choosing a database is only part of the job, though. Data structure, access rules, query patterns, and the way records relate to users all require careful thought.

Tailwind CSS helped me build and refine the interface without maintaining a large collection of separate CSS rules. It also made iterative UI improvements easier.

Git gave me a history of code changes and a way to manage development safely. When an AI-generated change caused a problem, version control helped me inspect what had changed and recover when necessary.

Vercel provided the deployment environment for the application. Its integration with Git made it easier to move from code changes to deployed versions.

Together, these tools allowed me to build with AI assistance while retaining control over the underlying code and deployment process.

The biggest surprise was how quickly AI could produce a first version of a feature—and how much work could remain afterward.

A screen might look correct but behave incorrectly when connected to real data. An API integration could work in a simple test but fail when an external service returned an unexpected response. A feature could appear complete while overlooking permissions or edge cases.

Connecting different services required more than generating a request. I had to consider authentication, request and response formats, error handling, timeouts, and what the application should do when an external service became unavailable.

I learned to break integrations into smaller steps and verify each one before building additional functionality around it.

An application that stores customer information cannot rely on a good-looking login screen for security.

I had to pay attention to authentication, database access rules, permission boundaries, and the possibility of users accessing data they should not see. AI assistance made implementation faster, but security decisions still required careful review and testing.

A feature can technically work and still feel frustrating to use.

I learned to pay attention to loading states, error messages, navigation, responsiveness, and how many steps users needed to complete common tasks. I also had to think about how database queries and application behavior would change as the amount of data increased.

These were not problems that could be solved by writing a better prompt alone. They required observation, testing, and repeated refinement.

The most valuable lesson was that vibe coding is not the same as handing over software development to an AI model.

The developer's role changes. Instead of writing every line manually, more time goes into defining requirements, directing implementation, reviewing code, testing behavior, and deciding which trade-offs are acceptable.

My experience in WordPress and business systems helped me understand the workflows I wanted to support. AI coding tools helped me move from those requirements to a working implementation more quickly.

The combination was more valuable than either one on its own.

I also learned to avoid building too many features at once. Small, testable changes made debugging easier and helped me understand the application as it evolved.

Finally, I realized that shipping an application is not the end of the work. Maintenance, security updates, monitoring, and improvements based on actual usage remain important after launch.

Building this application expanded my skills beyond website design and configuring third-party software. I gained hands-on experience with application architecture, database integration, API workflows, version control, and deployment.

The project also became a meaningful addition to my personal portfolio. You can read the NeerSoft CRM project case study to see how I approached the build.

I am not suggesting that every business should build its own CRM or that app builders are the wrong choice. For some projects, a ready-made platform is the fastest and most economical option. For others, a visual app builder is an excellent way to validate an idea before investing in custom development.

The right approach depends on the requirements, budget, technical constraints, and long-term plans.

For me, building from scratch with AI coding assistance was the right learning experience. It helped me avoid more than $1,000 in potential app-builder costs while giving me greater control over the application and teaching me skills I could not have gained by configuring an existing platform alone.

My biggest takeaway is simple: AI makes building software more accessible, but the ability to define problems, make sound technical decisions, and verify the results is what turns generated code into a useful application.

About me: Ritesh Sharma is an SEO specialist, WordPress website designer, and vibe-coding practitioner with 11+ years of experience in digital marketing and web development. He specializes in technical SEO, AEO, GEO, website performance, and building user-focused digital experiences. He also explores AI-powered development, automation, and no-code technologies to help businesses build smarter, search-friendly websites and digital solutions.
