#10400. Red wasn’t always Republican. The surprising history behind America’s political color divide

“Better dead than red.”

Cold War conservatives used to say that, and they meant it: Better to suffer nuclear annihilation, they believed, than endure a “red” victory. And by “red” they meant anyone on the left of the political spectrum—from the Soviet communists to their “fellow travelers” in the U.S.

It’s strange, then, that America’s conservative party, the Republican Party, is now the red one. There’s no ideology behind the switch, no founding decision by either party to claim a color as its own. The whole red-state/blue-state vocabulary is much newer than most people assume. It dates almost exactly from the 2000 election.

And in many cases, it fails to capture the reality of politics in America.

When nobody could agree on a color scheme

Television networks needed to distinguish two candidates on a map, and for decades they just picked whatever looked good that year.

In 1976, NBC colored GOP presidential candidate Gerald Ford’s states blue and Democrat Jimmy Carter’s states red. Four years later, that same scheme meant Republican presidential candidate Ronald Reagan’s landslide victory painted the map almost entirely blue, which is a strange thing to picture now, given how thoroughly Reagan became the patron saint of the red party.

That wasn’t just a one-network quirk, either. The Washington Post was still assigning red to Democrats and blue to Republicans in graphics used during the 2000 campaign.

If you go looking for the decision that gave American politics its colors, you won’t find one. You’ll find almost a quarter-century in which nobody had settled on today’s version.

Bush v. Gore

That inconsistency ended in 2000 with the fight over Florida’s presidential votes, though nobody at any TV network decided it should.

The networks covering the presidential contest between Republican George W. Bush and Democrat—and sitting Vice President—Al Gore happened, that year, to converge on red for Bush and blue for Gore. NBC’s Tim Russert is often credited with popularizing the phrase “red states” during the campaign, though the exact origin is disputed.

Under normal circumstances, none of this would have mattered much. Four years later, some other combination might have taken hold, the way it always had before.

But 2000 wasn’t normal.

The election stayed unresolved for five weeks while Florida’s votes were counted, contested in court and counted again. Night after night, on every channel, Americans watched the same map, colored the same way.

By the time the U.S. Supreme Court ended it and Bush was certified the winner by 537 votes, the color scheme – red for Republican Bush and blue for Democrat Gore – had become familiar enough to stop looking like a choice at all. Nobody argued anyone into it; the map just stayed in front of the country long enough to seem inevitable.

The labels started doing more work

Once red and blue attached themselves to the parties, they didn’t stay confined to maps.

By the 2002 midterms, journalists were already writing about “two Americas: red and blue,” as though the country had sorted itself into two coherent cultures overnight.

By the 2004 campaign, the vocabulary was everywhere, carrying connotations that nobody had assigned it on purpose. Red became associated with rural America, religiosity, the South and the interior West; blue with cities, more secular electorates, the coasts and college towns.

There’s truth buried in that shorthand: American political geography really has sorted itself along those lines – more than it used to, at least.

But the language hardened fast, turning a graphics convention into shorthand for identities it was never built to describe. Within a couple of election cycles, pundits were talking about red America and blue America as though they were two different countries with two different sets of values, rather than two loose clusters of states that happen to vote differently.

The 2000 contested presidential election cemented the red-blue America convention.

What the map doesn’t show

I’m a political scientist, and here’s the problem I see with this crude way of presenting voter preferences. A state decided by 2 percentage points gets colored exactly the same solid shade as a state decided by 30. Pennsylvania in a close year and Wyoming in a landslide show up looking identical, even though one of them is split down the middle.

The map doesn’t lie about who won – it just can’t show you how close it was. The result, after 20-some years of maps built that way, is a picture of the country that looks more neatly sorted than the electorate actually is.

The red-blue convention didn’t invent regional political differences. Those are real, and they’ve been growing for decades.

What the convention does is magnify them. A standard election map colors each state by who carried it, not by the margin – a state won by 4 points gets the same solid shade as one won by 26. That’s not a limit of the medium; color could run on a gradient just as easily. It’s a choice, and one that tracks the actual mechanics of the election: The Electoral College is winner-take-all, so a map showing only the winner in each state is reproducing the same either/or logic that decides who gets the electoral votes.

A third color exists for exactly this problem. Princeton’s Robert Vanderbei built the first “Purple America” map after the 2000 election, shading each county somewhere between true blue and true red according to its vote split. Landslide counties are rare, so most of the map came out some shade of purple. The technique got wider attention after 2004 – Vanderbei’s map was Newsweek’s “click of the day” on its website, though it never ran in the magazine itself – and others built their own versions afterward.

But purple never became the convention. It turns up in academic work and the occasional data-journalism piece built to correct a flatter map – but rarely on the graphic behind a network anchor, and almost never in a candidate’s own description of the country.

By the time anyone offered the correction, red and blue were no longer just colors on a map. They were the language.

A reputation never quite earned

America’s conservative party ending up red is a decent trivia fact, the kind of thing that makes for good conversation at dinner. The real oddity runs deeper than that irony, though.

An arbitrary graphics convention, repeated for five weeks during a contested recount, hardened into a vocabulary that Americans now use to describe political geography, culture, and identity, as if the country had always divided itself this cleanly into two camps.

It never did.

Andrew Latham is a professor of political science at Macalester College.

#10398. AMVR’s new head strap is my favorite way to keep cool with a Meta Quest 3 or 3S

The upgraded AMVR BS1 head strap includes better ergonomics, a built-in fan, magnetic rechargeable batteries, and a new breathable mesh top support for ultimate comfort.

I don’t know how companies like AMVR and BoboVR keep doing it, but AMVR’s latest head strap is now the most comfortable cooling head strap I’ve ever used for the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S. If you’re still using the included cloth head strap or haven’t used a “cooling head strap” before, here’s how it works.

The AMVR BS1 uses a breathable forehead pad attached via magnets to the support bar. Inside that support bar is an adjustable-speed fan, which you can easily adjust using the recessed wheel on the right side of the head strap. This fan keeps sweat down and helps prevent lens fog, two problems that can be a constant annoyance.

The fan is powered by the magnetically detachable, rechargeable 8,800mAh battery pack that mounts on the back of the head strap, helping to even out the weight distribution across the headset. That battery pack will also charge your Quest while playing and adds around 4 hours of additional play time. You can always purchase more packs to keep things going for longer, if you need to.

Lots of padding can be found all around the headset, and the mesh support on top accepts any weight that remains. Every bit of padding is easily removable and washable, so you can keep things clean and tidy (especially if you share your headset with others). You can also get extra pads if you’d rather do it that way.

The back of the head strap cradles your skull with a mix of half supple padding and half grippy silicone. You’ll be double happy there, as the pad on the top part further cushions any headset weight, while the silicone keeps the headset from slipping forward and shifting weight onto your cheeks.

If you don’t need a fan, the BoboVR M3 Pro+ is currently $17 less than the AMVR BS1. I find the BoboVR M3 Pro+’s hybrid design to be slightly more comfortable, but the lack of a fan is a big negative for this particular BoboVR strap.

Once you’ve chosen a head strap, grab an AMVR FC4M face pad to add another layer of comfort to the headset. Like the AMVR BS1’s forehead pad, this face pad attaches to the Quest 3 (NOT the Quest 3S) via magnets and is made of breathable, easy-to-clean material. It’s perfect for staying cool year-round and makes the Quest so, so much more comfortable.

#10397. ‘I am standing on shoulders made of steel’: Keisha Lance Bottoms highlights Georgia’s fraught history in rousing victory speech

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected governor of Georgia, making her the first Black woman in the U.S. to hold the position. She also used her victory speech as a platform to highlight just how far the state has come.

In her speech on the night of November 3 in Atlanta, Bottoms opened up about her family’s past, referencing her family members Shephard and Betsy Peek, who were enslaved in Crawfordsville during the mid-1800s.

Bottoms shared how the day prior to the election, she visited the same town that her relatives once called home, with the trip becoming its own revelation for the Democrat.

“I visited the grave of Betsy Peak, my great-great grandmother, who was born in 1845, 30 years before emancipation,” she said. “In a cemetery field filled with unmarked graves, I found hers.”

She added, “I don’t know what dreams Betsy Peak had for her children or for her grandchildren or the generations that she would never meet, but I know I am standing on shoulders made of steel.”

But the same town—home to at least five generations of her family—was also home to a very different chapter of Georgia’s history.

“It was the town that was home to the former governor of Georgia and the vice president of the Confederate States of America, Alexander Stephens,” she said.

“Georgia is not defined by one moment in time”

The emotive speech and Bottoms’s historic win come more than 100 years after the Emancipation Proclamation and the Confederacy, with the governor-elect set to lead the state where her own family members were once enslaved.

She added, “yes, Crawfordsville produced the Confederacy’s vice president, but tonight it also produced your next governor.”

But the irony was not lost on her, turning the story into a lesson.

She added, “tonight should remind as that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person—it’s been defined by all of us.”

You can watch the full speech on C-SPAN.

#10394. Build a Reliable Analytics Pipeline Before Moving to a Data Warehouse

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Category: Databases / Back-End Development

Meta description: Build a reliable analytics pipeline with SQL. Learn to handle duplicate records, late updates, data quality tests, and reporting before warehouse migration.

A dashboard can load quickly and still report the wrong number. A retried import might count an order twice. An update might arrive after the daily report has run. A join might multiply rows without producing a database error.

For developers moving application data into analytics, these problems deserve attention before platform selection. A larger warehouse can process an incorrect query faster, but it cannot decide what your metrics should mean.

This tutorial walks through a small order-reporting pipeline. You will define the grain of a dataset, handle repeated deliveries, select the latest record version, and test the output before exposing it to a dashboard.

“Show daily sales” sounds specific until someone asks which date, currency, or order status counts.

What is the current total value of paid orders, grouped by order date?

Orders whose latest version has a paid status

Integer minor units; the sample uses USD cents

Later order versions can revise earlier dates

Current-state reporting, not an as-of ledger

That final distinction matters. If an order changes from paid to refunded, this report removes it from the paid-order total on its original order date. It does not record a refund event on the refund date.

An accounting-style report would need a different model, usually based on transactions or adjustments. A table of current order states cannot answer every historical question.

A useful pipeline has three responsibilities:

●     Raw storage preserves incoming records and ingestion metadata.

●     Staging models normalize types, identify duplicates, and apply source ordering rules.

●     Reporting models express business definitions at a documented grain.

Keep these responsibilities distinct even if they initially live in one database.

For example, raw data might contain five deliveries of an order update. Staging resolves those deliveries to one current order. Reporting then groups qualifying orders into daily totals.

This separation gives failures a location. If the raw layer is missing an update, changing the dashboard query will not fix the extraction process.

For a refresher on the statements used to create, populate, and query these layers, see SitePoint’s guide to SQL commands.

The following SQL uses PostgreSQL-compatible syntax and fictional records. Run it in a disposable development database.

The dataset contains three deliberate challenges:

●     Order 101 moves from pending to paid.

●     Its paid version is delivered twice.

●     Order 102 changes from paid to refunded.

A naive sum of every row marked paid returns 27,500 cents. Under our metric contract, the correct result is 12,500 cents: the latest paid versions of orders 101 and 103.

The difference comes from record semantics, not query performance.

Use a window function to select the newest version of each order:

The order of operations is essential. If you filter for paid records before ranking versions, order 102’s refunded version disappears before the query can consider it. The earlier paid version then looks current.

This example assumes the source supplies a monotonically increasing version per order. The ingestion identifier breaks ties between repeated deliveries; it does not establish which business update is newest.

If two deliveries share an order ID and source version but contain different values, treat that as a source-contract violation. A deterministic tie-breaker makes the result repeatable, but it cannot determine which conflicting payload is correct.

A successful SQL execution only proves that the database accepted the query. Add checks for the assumptions the report depends on.

For example, this query identifies conflicting payloads for the same source version:

When the project grows, dbt data tests provide a way to organize assertions about uniqueness, nulls, relationships, accepted values, and custom business rules. Custom tests can return the records that violate an assumption.

Tests should also cover behavior, not only table shape. Extend the fixture with a late-arriving older version and confirm that it does not replace the latest state. Add an exact repeated delivery and confirm that the totals remain unchanged.

The views above recompute their results from all available raw records. That makes the demonstration easy to understand, but repeatedly scanning the full history may become expensive.

An incremental pipeline needs additional rules:

●     Track which order IDs changed in the incoming batch.

●     Recompute current state for those IDs using their available history.

●     Replace or merge their modeled rows instead of blindly appending.

●     Rebuild the affected reporting groups.

If an update changes an order’s date or currency, both the old and new reporting groups need attention. Refreshing only the new group leaves a stale amount behind.

Do not assume that “yesterday’s partition” contains every record that changed yesterday. An update received today can affect an order created months ago.

Apache Airflow’s best-practice guidance discusses designing tasks for retries and repeatable inputs. Regardless of scheduler, make the batch boundary explicit and advance checkpoints only after the required output has been committed successfully.

Hard deletes need their own policy too. If a source silently removes a record, a pipeline that only imports changed rows will not discover the deletion. Use deletion events, tombstones, or periodic reconciliation according to the source’s capabilities.

You do not need an orchestration platform, transformation framework, and new warehouse to validate one metric.

Prototype schemas, transformations, and reporting queries

When a separate development or analytics database is sufficient

Organize SQL models, dependencies, documentation, and tests

When transformations become a maintained project

Schedule dependent jobs and manage retries

When several pipeline steps require coordinated execution

Lint SQL using the project’s configured dialect

When shared SQL needs consistent review standards

Choose storage separately from orchestration. A scheduler does not decide how facts should be modeled, and a transformation framework does not guarantee source completeness.

Before adopting a warehouse, measure query duration, concurrency, freshness requirements, and interference with application traffic. For some workloads, precomputed results are enough to improve reporting responsiveness; SitePoint’s materialized-view tutorial explains that approach in PostgreSQL. Refresh behavior and acceptable staleness still need an explicit policy.

A migration becomes easier to evaluate when the team can show a small working pipeline, documented metrics, representative queries, and known failure cases.

For teams evaluating data warehouse consulting services, those artifacts make a useful review brief. Ask for concrete decisions about source ordering, historical changes, reconciliation, access controls, and recovery procedures, together with the assumptions behind any cost estimate.

Keep the review focused on observable outcomes. For example:

●     Can a failed batch be replayed without changing correct totals?

●     How are conflicting source versions detected?

●     Which reports change when an old order is updated?

●     Can a dashboard total be traced back to source records?

●     Who owns freshness alerts and recovery?

These questions also help an internal team review its own design. The important deliverable is a system whose behavior can be explained and tested.

A dashboard total needs context about when its underlying data became usable.

Track the latest successful ingestion, transformation, and validation separately. A recent extraction timestamp does not prove that downstream models finished building.

Likewise, a quiet source can make an event timestamp look old even when ingestion is healthy. Combine source activity with pipeline execution metadata before deciding that the data is stale.

Define the serving behavior when checks fail. You might keep the last validated result available with a visible freshness warning rather than replace it with an unverified total. Store the successful version if that is the policy: a live view over changing raw data does not preserve a previous validated snapshot.

A trustworthy analytics pipeline begins with a precise question and a testable data model.

Define the reporting grain, preserve incoming records, resolve source versions before filtering, and verify that retries do not alter correct results. Then measure whether the workload needs a different storage platform.

Those foundations make a future warehouse migration easier to reason about and make the dashboard useful before that migration begins.

#10392. Gen Z is discovering what millennials felt in 2008, and the internet is losing it

The votes are in and millennial optimism is back with all its props: avocado toast, BuzzFeed quizzes, a stomp-clap-hey playlist, and, of course, a Coexist sticker.

A blue tsunami swept the 2026 midterm elections. The Democrats won their first senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and flipped the notoriously red state of Texas blue, taking the governorship and a senate seat, and won control over both chambers of congress, sparking widespread celebration.

The blue festivities continued beyond the late-night victory parties, flooding social media platforms with thousands of posts where users reclaimed the bygone era of optimism and the collective feeling of hope and possibility. 

“This is what millennial optimism felt like,” one user said on X, with another adding, “as an elder millennial, I’ve forgotten how to handle optimism.”

For most, translating the feeling into a post is easiest done by referencing iconic pieces of media at the time, from the websites one visited to the songs that filled their playlists.

“Millennial optimism is back baby. I’m blasting Florence and the Machine bass boosted the dog days ARE over,” one user said in a post with over 18,000 likes.

 A user added, “they’re gonna bring buzzfeed back.” Another replied, “resistance is back so hard, this app is about to be renamed twitter.” 

Others have taken to sharing how the excitement is felt on the streets as well, with one user sharing a video from a club in Austin, with partygoers singing along to fun.’s We Are Young while election coverage filled the screens.

But for most, the return of optimism comes along with a series of cultural moments this year that have teased “woke is back.”

“Woke being back means that it’s actually the perfect time for a glee reboot you guys didn’t have your third eye open,” one user said, referencing a forthcoming reboot of the popular 2010s show Glee. Others also referenced the reboot of Lena Dunham’s millennial-focused show Girls, with one user adding, “Girls and Glee returning was the sign. We just were too scared to see it.

The next generation of hopecore

The optimism is not just for the actual millennials who experienced the Obama days as young adults—Gen Z is joining in on the hopecore as well.

“I finally understand how this feels,” a user said on X, alongside a video of Lin Manuel Miranda’s Hamilton, a 2016 Tony Awards performance of The Battle of Yorktown. 

A user replied, “everybody shut up its gen z’s turn for millennial optimism.”

But Gen Z—who romanticized millennial optimism earlier this year through old Instagram filters, twee outfits, and edits with 2010s songs—are jumping in on a trend with their own style, with humor driven by irreverent sarcasm and hyperbole.

Oftentimes, the Gen Z flip direct Republican talking points—like a pushback on pronouns and diversity—and satirically turn them into celebratory posts.

“We are going to have pronouns you xeople won’t believe,” one user shared in a post with 69,000 likes. 

Another added, “blue wave so strong, they’re already saying if you don’t have your pronouns back in your email signature by noon tomorrow, Cory Booker will show up at your parents house and make your mom do the Nae Nae.”

Others simply relied on old memes, and a change to reclaim the term “lib.”

“Feel like i just fell out of a fucking coconut tree,”a user said on X, referencing Kamala Harris’ viral 2024 meme.

Another added, “I’ve libbed out before but i don’t think i’ve ever libbed out quite like this before.”

#10391. ‘I don’t feel like libbing out’: LGBTQ+ rights took blows in these states despite midterm election blue wave

For Democrats, this week’s midterm elections went nearly as well as they could have hoped. The party has gained at least seven seats in the Senate and 29 in the House of Representatives, securing full Congressional control for Democrats. Some conservative strongholds even flipped blue, including Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina.

The election also marked a number of groundbreaking firsts for the country, including the first Black woman to serve as governor, the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, and the first Muslim elected to the Senate. 

But the so-called “blue tsunami” doesn’t mean liberal policies won out everywhere, even in places where Democrats gained or maintained control. Four states passed or are close to passing ballot initiatives to restrict the rights of transgender children, including three that voted blue in this election.

States’ anti-trans initiatives

So far, two ballot initiatives restricting the rights of trans student athletes have already passed. That includes Nebraska’s Initiative 442, which amends the state’s constitution to require that schools designate sports teams as male, female, or coeducational based on “biological sex,” also banning “students of the male sex” from playing on girls’ teams. The measure passed with 68% approval.

Also already passed is Arizona’s Proposition 318, which similarly requires schools to designate teams by gender and prohibit any students assigned male at birth from playing on girls’ teams. Unlike Nebraska, Arizona was solidly blue in this election, with Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs winning reelection.

The other states with initiatives about trans athletes on their ballots include Colorado and Washington, both of which have Democratic governors and two Democratic senators.

In Colorado, two ballot initiatives centered on trans children. Proposition 134 would follow Arizona and Nebraska’s lead in requiring athletes to play on teams matching their sex assigned at birth, while Proposition 135 would prohibit gender-affirming surgery for minors.

Washington’s Initiative 638 is perhaps the most controversial of all these measures. Beyond banning students from playing on sports teams not matching their sex assigned at birth, the initiative would also require that all players on girls’ teams provide a statement from a medical provider verifying their sex, potentially through genital exams.

Colorado and Washington’s measures are still too close to call, but reports show they are currently on track for approval.

LGBTQ+ social media reacts

Amid online celebration in the wake of the blue tsunami, the success of these anti-trans measures has spoiled for some what would otherwise be a resounding political victory.

“I don’t feel like ‘libbing out,’” reads one viral post sharing a graphic of the initiatives’ early results. It’s garnered more than 243,000 views on X.

“Yes, there is a blue wave. but the amount of transphobic initiatives are passing, even in deep blue states, is very very concerning,” wrote another user.

Others agreed that the measures’ success in Democratic strongholds was especially troublesome: “‘Blue wave’ but trans people aren’t even safe in Denver, Colorado,” reads one response to the news.

“Blue wave is great but please don’t leave trans women and girls behind while you celebrate,” asked a fourth user. “Trans girl’s rights were successfully taken away yesterday in several states, they’re still here and deserve to be fought for.”

#10387. Canva just laid off 1,200 people. But its severance package is earning praise

Design tech company Canva is doing some major restructuring: The move will impact about 1,200 employees, or roughly 22% of its staff. But the company’s also getting attention for how it’s treating the newly terminated employees. 

On Tuesday, CEO Melanie Perkins announced the news in a post on LinkedIn. She also shared a letter that laid out a generous severance package that’s being fawned over on social media.

The letter explained that all terminated employees would receive six months of salary,  regardless of location. The Sydney-based company also said it will remove the one-year vesting cliff for those who joined the company within the last year, which means even those who recently joined can walk away with shares in the company. 

They will also continue to receive healthcare, plus dedicated career support, resume help, coaching and interview preparation, plus one year of LinkedIn Premium. The company also launched a fund to provide $10,000 grants to those looking to start a company or project or their own. “Whether it’s starting a business or doing something meaningful for their local community, the fund is designed to help get those ideas off the ground,” Canva explained in the letter. 

The company is even allowing all terminated employees to keep their MacBook laptops.

“We’re making significant changes to how we’re organised, which sadly means saying goodbye to many exceptionally talented people who have helped build Canva into what it is today,” Perkins wrote in her LinkedIn post.

Perkins added that the company put in the time and effort to create “an opt-in alumni directory” for those who are being forced to leave the company, where former employees can learn about work opportunities. Perkins also included her email address and asked leaders with any work opportunities to reach out to her directly.

The CEO didn’t specify a reason for the layoffs in the note. But the news comes at a time in which the company is gearing up for a potential IPO following several years of spending on its suite of AI-powered products.

The CEO continued: “This is the hardest decision we’ve made in Canva’s history, and we know it will deeply impact many people and their loved ones. While we believe these changes are critical to help set Canva up for the future, Canva would not be the company it is today without their hard work, and we want to do everything we can to help set them up well for their next chapter.”

More often than not, when companies go through massive, major overhauls (like laying off nearly a quarter of their employees), the news is about how those employees may struggle to find employment, or how the company failed to support them. 

But Canva has seemed to take a more humane approach than we’re used to. In today’s era of forever layoffs, companies drop staff with decades of loyalty abruptly over a group Zoom call, and that’s it.

Commenters on the CEO’s post were quick to weigh in on how the company is showing other leaders how to gracefully handle layoffs. 

“Really impressive, empathetic, transparent, and generous way to communicate what was undoubtedly a very hard decision,” one LinkedIn commenter replied. “Especially with what this industry has seen over the past year, this is an example for other organizations on how to do a hard thing right.”

Another added, “Plenty of companies will do layoffs this year. Few will do them like this.” 

That’s likely the case, but with all of the positive attention surrounding Canva’s restructuring layoffs, it’s hard to imagine that it won’t inspire at least a few leaders to take note. Or at least, inspire more workers elsewhere to push for this in the future after being shown the door.

#10386. Google had a very good, very bad Q3

Good morning! Today I’m reading about the death of the internet, deciding whether to buy a PROLED or many pro LEDs, building all my IKEA furniture with this step-by-step 3D app, trying desperately to get into the Readwise Books early access, and playing an “Enhanced 3D” Command & Conquer: Red Alert on my PC.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings were interesting. Despite a 25% rise in revenue and a healthy net income of $26 billion, analysts were disappointed with the company’s results, sending the stock down as much as 11% in after-hours trading.

On the plus side, the company’s cloud business is booming, doubling year-over-year revenue to $30 billion as it attracts frontier labs to its data centers. But advertising revenue didn’t meet expectations, and investors appear to be worried that its search advertising business, one of the most efficient sources of recurring revenue in history, is not keeping up with changing user behavior.

As Anthropic gets ready to soar into its IPO later this year, mature businesses like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon are racing to adapt to a market where demand for AI infrastructure is outpacing compute supply. But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

So it’s no surprise that it’s expanding ads in AI Mode to 10 new markets this week, with more to come by the end of the year. While the post was only a few paragraphs long, expanding its AI ad business may end up being one of the company’s most consequential announcements of 2026.

I didn’t get to see either of the first Dune movies on IMAX, but you can bet your ass I’ve already secured opening-day tickets for the third one. Dune: Part Three debuts in December, and we now have the final trailer that showcases the impending showdown between Muad’Dib and Chani as the former realizes the consequences of his galactic war.

On the gadgety side, there’s another impending showdown brewing between XREAL’s Android XR-powered Aura glasses and Meta’s upcoming VR Glasses.

I liked Jasmine Uniza’s video below comparing the two because, until I watched it, I didn’t realize the extent of the diverging approaches to reality they’re each taking. The Aura glasses are more traditionally translucent and somewhat awkwardly project two OLED screens on top of the dimmed lenses, allowing the outside world to filter through. Meta’s VR Glasses eschew the traditional headset shape and weight of the Quest but block out far more of the outside world and use external cameras, like their predecessors, to pipe in mixed-reality footage.

Finally, some personal news of a sort: I am now a permanent host of The Sideload. If you know me at all, you know I love a podcast, and Will Sattelberg was my co-host at the Android Police podcast for three years before he left for 9to5 last year. I’m so excited to be doing this again every week with him, and I hope you’ll tune in to our most recent episode about the death of the web browser and other good news.

When Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations of the Mac Studio in August, it said a configuration with 512GB of RAM would be available in October. Today, the company officially revealed the pricing of that option.

If you head to the Mac Studio configurator on Apple’s website, you’ll see the new 512GB upgrade option. As previously announced, the 512GB option is only available with the top-tier M5 Ultra chip that has a 36-core CPU and 80‑core GPU.

#10385. Working With a Marketing Agency: A Technical Guide for Developers and Designers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sooner or later, most teams that build websites end up working alongside a digital marketing agency. The agency asks for CMS access, wants tracking scripts added, suggests URL changes, and sets targets for page speed. If nobody on the product side understands what is being asked and why, the result is broken analytics, accidental noindex tags, and migrations that quietly erase years of search visibility.

This guide is for developers, designers, and technical founders. It covers the engineering side of that collaboration: environments and access, analytics implementation, redirects, structured data, performance budgets, and crawler access, with code you can adapt and a checklist you can hand to whoever you are working with.

Marketing briefs rarely say it, but most outcomes are decided in the codebase and the design system:

That is why healthy collaborations look like a shared engineering effort with a reviewable change process, not a monthly PDF report.

Almost every painful marketing-and-engineering story falls into one of the patterns below. Each has a cause you can see in the code and a fix that takes minutes, if you catch it before launch.

Give the agency a staging environment and least-privilege access rather than production admin rights. Keep staging out of search results so test pages are never indexed. At the web-server level that can be a single header:

The risk is the other direction: that header reaching production. Add a post-deploy check to your pipeline so a launch fails loudly instead of silently:

Reports are only as good as the data behind them. Agree on a naming convention for UTM parameters before the first campaign, and document it:

For conversions, prefer explicit events pushed to a data layer over fragile click-based triggers. Developers implement them once, and every tool downstream can reuse them:

Test each event in your tag manager's preview mode on staging, and treat event names and parameters as part of your API: changing them is a breaking change that should be announced.

Changing URLs without redirects discards accumulated search visibility. Before launch, export every indexable URL, map each to its new location, and implement permanent redirects:

Do not rely on spot checks. This script reads a two-column CSV of old and new paths and verifies that each old URL returns a single 301 to a destination that returns 200:

Run it against staging before launch and against production right after. Redirect chains (A to B to C) and redirects that land on a 404 are the two failures it catches most often.

Structured data helps search engines and AI systems understand who you are. Generate it from the same data that renders the page, so it never drifts from the visible content, and escape it properly when you embed it:

Validate the output with Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator as part of review, not after launch. If you would rather not hand-write the JSON-LD for every page type, free Schema Markup Generator can produce a starting point, which you should still validate with the tools above.

Ask for Core Web Vitals targets, and make sure marketing scripts do not break them. Google's published "good" thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of real-user visits, are:

A budget nobody checks is a wish. Lighthouse CI can fail a build when a page exceeds one, which turns "please keep it fast" into a rule that applies equally to your code and to any tag the agency adds:

Sizes are in kilobytes and timings in milliseconds. Route every new tracking or advertising tag through code review and measure its cost before it ships.

AI-generated answers favor content that is clearly structured, factual, and easy to attribute. In practice that means descriptive headings, concise answers near the top of a page, accurate structured data, server-rendered content, and a deliberate decision about which crawlers may access your site. That decision lives in robots.txt, and it is an engineering and business call, not a default:

Check the documentation of each crawler you care about for its current user-agent name, since these change. If a vendor promises AI search visibility, ask exactly what they will change on the site and how they will measure the result. The field is young and claims are easy to make.

The following scenario is illustrative, not a real client story, but it combines problems that appear again and again. A team redesigns its site and changes URLs from /services/seo-audit to /solutions/audit. The redirect map covers the top 50 pages, so the launch looks fine. Three weeks later, organic traffic is down by a third. The cause is a long tail of 800 blog and resource URLs with no redirects, plus a CDN rule that rewrites trailing slashes and turns every single redirect into a chain of two hops.

Both problems would have been caught by the checks above: exporting every indexable URL from the sitemap and server logs rather than only the top pages, and running the redirect verification script against staging. The lesson is that migration work is mostly verification, and verification can be automated.

The best collaboration is the one that fits your stack and your team's way of working. Put the agreements above in writing, automate the checks that can be automated, and treat marketing changes like any other change to the product: reviewed, tested in staging, and measured after release. When engineering and marketing share the same process, the results tend to follow.

#10380. Check if eMudhra CA Is Still Trusted in Your Runtime

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Eight eMudhra intermediate Certificate Authority private keys are trivially recoverable from their public certificates. Any attacker can mint trusted TLS certificates for arbitrary domains. Browsers have already blocked these compromised intermediates through revocation mechanisms, but most non-browser runtimes — curl, Python, Node.js, Go, and Rust — still silently trust them. This affects any team operating server-side infrastructure, CI pipelines, or CLI tooling that makes outbound TLS connections. If your stack trusts the eMudhra chain, an attacker can forge certificates your code will accept without complaint.

This guide provides a diagnostic sequence: test every runtime in the stack against the compromised certificates, remediate by updating trust stores, and verify the fix sticks. The primary source for this disclosure is Scott Helme's detailed writeup.

In RSA key generation, you derive the private exponent d via the modular inverse of the public exponent e modulo λ(n) (the Carmichael totient of the modulus), where λ(n) depends on the prime factors of n. RSA's security depends entirely on d being large — typically hundreds of digits — making it computationally infeasible to derive from the public key alone.

eMudhra generated eight intermediate CA certificates with single-byte d values. Specific recovered values include d=4, d=56, and d=115, as documented in Scott Helme's disclosure post. These are not large numbers. They are recoverable from the public certificate in milliseconds. Anyone with access to the public certificate (which is, by definition, public) can reconstruct the private key and sign certificates that chain up to eMudhra's trusted root. That means arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain, indistinguishable from legitimate ones to any client that trusts the eMudhra chain.

An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

The practical consequence is total impersonation capability. An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

Major browsers have deployed mitigations through their respective revocation infrastructure. The compromise was reported to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and eMudhra on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Chrome pushed a CRLSet update blocking the intermediates the same evening, Mozilla blocked them in Firefox via OneCRL within hours, Apple applied its platform block on October 19, and Microsoft rolled out a disallowed-certificate CTL update. Current browser versions already reject the compromised intermediates.

The problem lies everywhere else. Non-browser TLS clients skip revocation checks by default. curl does not check CRLs or OCSP unless explicitly configured to do so. Python's requests and urllib3 libraries rely on the certifi bundle and perform no revocation checking. Python's standard library urllib.request module uses the system SSL store, not certifi. Node.js's https module uses either a compiled-in root store or the system store depending on build configuration, with no active revocation. Go's crypto/tls loads system roots but does not perform revocation checks. Rust's rustls paired with webpki-roots uses a bundled Mozilla root set, while native-tls defers to the system store; neither checks revocation by default.

This creates a trust store gap. The system CA bundle on a Linux server, the certifi bundle shipped with Python, and the compiled-in roots in Node.js might all still contain the eMudhra intermediates or trust the root that chains to them. Without manual intervention, these runtimes remain vulnerable.

The incident's official test infrastructure, documented on the status page at emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com, provides twelve TLS endpoints: one for each of the six compromised TLS intermediates, served twice - once chaining to eMudhra’s emSign ECC root and once chaining to Sectigo’s cross-signing AAA Certificate Services root. Host names follow the pattern dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (eMudhra chain) and dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (Sectigo cross-signed chain), with dv/ov/ev and g3b/g3c variants covering all six TLS intermediates. The diagnostic logic is straightforward: if a runtime connects successfully, it still trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. If the TLS handshake fails with a certificate verification error, the runtime correctly distrusts the intermediate. The bare domain emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com serves only the status page itself over an ordinary Let’s Encrypt certificate, so connecting to it proves nothing - always test the per-intermediate subdomains. Test at least one -emudhra host and its -aaa-emudhra counterpart: a store can distrust one root path while still trusting the other.

Important: A network or DNS error will also produce a connection failure. Before concluding SAFE, confirm the endpoint is reachable by running curl -v --insecure https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ and verify that any TLS error is certificate-related (e.g., "certificate verify failed"), not a network connectivity error.

Run curl with verbose output against the test endpoint:

If the connection succeeds and returns an HTTP response, the system's CA bundle still trusts the compromised intermediate. Look for SSL certificate verify ok in the verbose output. If instead curl reports an error such as SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate or certificate verify failed, the intermediate is distrusted and the runtime is safe.

For a more granular view, use OpenSSL's s_client directly:

A Verify return code: 0 (ok) means the chain is trusted and the system is vulnerable. Any non-zero return code, such as Verify return code: 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate), indicates the intermediate is not trusted.

Each runtime below connects to the same test endpoint. A successful HTTP response means the runtime trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. A certificate verification error means the runtime correctly rejects it.

This tests the system SSL store only; urllib.request uses the system SSL context, not the certifi bundle. An ssl.SSLCertVerificationError confirms the intermediate is distrusted. Check the error message to confirm it references a certificate verification failure rather than a configuration or network problem.

A successful response here means the certifi bundle specifically trusts the compromised chain, independent of the system store.

If Node.js prints a status code, it trusts the compromised intermediate. A certificate-related error in the output means it does not. Whether Node.js uses its compiled-in roots or the system store depends on build configuration, so this test reflects whichever store your build uses.

Initialize a module first, then save the following as check.go:

Run with go run check.go. Go loads system roots via crypto/x509, so the result reflects whether the OS trust store has been updated.

Run with cargo run. With rustls + webpki-roots, the result depends on whether the bundled root set has been updated. With native-tls, the result reflects the system store.

Offline verification needs PEM chains for the eight compromised intermediates. The research disclosure site linked in Scott Helme's post at https://scotthelme.co.uk/eight-bits-of-trust-emudhras-ca-keys-cracked-in-milliseconds/ is the canonical starting point for the incident's test material. Use only chains you have verified come from that source, save them as individual .pem files in a local emudhra-chains/ directory, and check their integrity against any checksum the researchers publish. Do not use copies from unverified mirrors.

The directory should contain one PEM file per compromised intermediate chain before you continue.

Use a shell loop to test each chain individually against the system CA bundle. The glob form (openssl verify ... *.pem) is unreliable across OpenSSL versions — multi-file positional arguments require OpenSSL ≥ 3.0 and can silently skip files on older versions. Use the loop instead:

On Debian/Ubuntu systems, the bundle is typically at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. On RHEL/Fedora/CentOS, look for /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt. On macOS, the system bundle is at /etc/ssl/cert.pem, though Homebrew-installed OpenSSL uses its own path.

If any chain returns OK, the system store still trusts that compromised intermediate and is vulnerable. A verification failure means it is distrusted.

Python's certifi bundle location can be found with:

Node.js behavior varies: some builds use a compiled-in root store derived from Mozilla's NSS roots, while others defer to the system store. The --use-openssl-ca flag forces Node.js to use the system's OpenSSL CA store instead of its compiled-in bundle. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store. Verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca; if no output appears, the flag has no effect on that build.

Go's crypto/x509 package loads system roots at runtime, so Go programs inherit the system trust store. There is no separate bundle to verify.

Run a shell loop to verify all eight chains against the certifi bundle:

Any OK result means the certifi bundle is still vulnerable.

The following commands apply to specific distributions. Run openssl version first to confirm your baseline.

If the distribution has not yet issued a patch removing the eMudhra intermediates, you must manually distrust the certificates. The correct mechanism is distribution-specific:

After any manual changes, regenerate the consolidated bundle by running the appropriate update command for your distribution and re-verify with the shell loop above.

Important: Homebrew's CA bundle only affects Homebrew-linked binaries (e.g., Homebrew-installed curl, python3). System tools (/usr/bin/curl, Safari, system Python) use the macOS Keychain and require a macOS security update via System Settings → Software Update. You can verify which curl you are using with which curl.

macOS caveat: Apple’s October 19 platform block covers Safari and Keychain-based clients, but the built-in curl, git, python3, perl, and ruby verify against /etc/ssl/cert.pem without checking revocation, and that file has not been updated at time of writing. The incident status page publishes an official workaround that strips the two affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, plus a PIP_CERT fix for the built-in pip. Homebrew’s ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 is patched.

For the system Keychain, open Keychain Access and search for eMudhra intermediates. Apple's platform-level block propagates through macOS security updates, though exact timelines for older macOS versions differ. Older macOS versions that no longer receive security updates will never receive the distrust entry.

Verify the new version by checking pip show certifi and comparing against upstream release notes. Applications that pin an older certifi version in their dependency files remain vulnerable until that pin is updated.

For Node.js, upgrading to a patched release that includes updated compiled-in roots is the primary path. Alternatively, launching Node.js with --use-openssl-ca defers trust decisions to the system store, which you might have already patched. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store; verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca. Pre-built binaries from nodejs.org might not honor this flag. Different LTS lines will receive the updated root store at different times.

Go relies entirely on the system store, so confirming the system CA update has been applied is sufficient.

For Rust projects using rustls with webpki-roots, run cargo update to pull the latest version of the webpki-roots crate, which derives its root set from Mozilla's NSS. Projects using native-tls defer to the system store.

Rebuild container images with updated CA certificates. Pinned base images are a particular risk — they can lag behind security patches indefinitely.

CI pipelines using cached or pinned base images should pull fresh images or explicitly upgrade ca-certificates as a build step.

Electron's trust store source depends on version and platform. Consult the Electron documentation on certificate verification to determine whether your version uses Node.js's compiled-in root store or the OS certificate store — the boundary has shifted across major releases, and no single version threshold applies cleanly. Upgrading the Electron version or overriding certificate verification via the session.setCertificateVerifyProc() method are the available remediation paths. Verify the specific behavior against the Electron version in use.

Distrust at the intermediate level stops the current attack, but it is fragile: new intermediates cross-signed under the same root would be trusted by default. Mozilla has therefore gone further and removed the eMudhra root entirely in NSS 3.131.1, and Chrome has confirmed it is removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3, the root that signed the compromised intermediates, from the Chrome Root Store, with the change reaching devices from October 27. Note also that the compromised intermediates were cross-signed by Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services root, so a chain can build through either root - blocking only the eMudhra root path does not close the Sectigo one, which is why the incident’s official Linux workaround distrusts both roots.

The following shell script runs openssl verify against all eight chains and exits non-zero if any chain is still trusted. Drop this into a CI step or run it as a cron job.

Monitor the following sources for updates on CA trust store changes:

Browsers auto-protect through active revocation infrastructure. Everything else — server-side HTTP clients, CLI tools, containerized services — requires manual verification and remediation.

Browsers auto-protect through active revocation infrastructure. Everything else — server-side HTTP clients, CLI tools, containerized services — requires manual verification and remediation. The action sequence is: (1) test against the online diagnostic endpoints, (2) verify offline against local trust stores, (3) update all system and language-level CA bundles, and (4) automate the check in CI so regressions from image rebuilds or dependency changes are caught immediately.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.

Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”

Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:

We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.

Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.

We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.

We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.

Bethesda is officially confirming today that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. The confirmation came in a less than 10-minute video celebrating 40 years of Bethesda game studios.

It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series, and studio chief Todd Howard made the announcement today and called it the “perfect time” to fully name the game.

Bethesda isn’t sharing any more details on The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel today, though. The Xbox Wire press release on the name is literally just a picture of the logo.

I reported in Notepad last week that Bethesda was planning to name the game in November, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online. Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.

#10373. Prompt Caching API Example: Cut Token Costs in Node.js

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. For Node.js developers making repeated API calls with stable system instructions, few-shot examples, or long reference documents, prompt caching can deliver up to 90% cost reduction on cached tokens.

The problem is that three major providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — each implement prompt caching differently. Opt-in mechanisms, minimum token thresholds, TTL behavior, cache-hit indicators, and discount rates all vary. Developers must piece together incompatible documentation.

The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js. The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, TypeScript 5+, an API key for at least one of the three providers, and familiarity with async/await and REST API consumption.

All three providers cache from the beginning of the prompt forward — only the prefix qualifies. A "stable prefix" is any content that does not change between requests: system instructions, few-shot examples, long reference documents, or boilerplate context. Keep the prefix byte-identical across calls. Any mutation, even a whitespace change, invalidates the cache and forces a full re-processing pass.

Prompt design matters. Front-load all static content and append variable content (the user's actual question, dynamic context) at the end.

The following table captures the critical differences across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini:

For explicit caching, Gemini requires the largest minimum prefix at 32,768 tokens, making it suitable only for very large context windows. Gemini 2.5 and newer also enable implicit caching by default, which works more like OpenAI’s automatic approach. Anthropic offers the steepest read-token discount at 90%, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. OpenAI is zero-config but offers the smallest discount at 50%.

Update tsconfig.json with these essentials:

The CacheAwareRequest holds the provider-agnostic input shape. The CacheUsageReport normalizes the output so that calling code never needs to know which provider-specific field indicates a cache hit. The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate on cached tokens, while estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates actual savings relative to total tokens.

OpenAI caches automatically. There is no flag to set, no resource to create. The only requirement is that the prompt prefix must be at least 1,024 tokens long. The system message is the natural place for the stable prefix.

The systemPrompt string should contain the full stable prefix. As long as it exceeds 1,024 tokens and remains identical across calls, OpenAI will cache it automatically within its TTL window.

Anthropic requires explicit opt-in via a cache_control breakpoint. The breakpoint is placed on the last content block of the stable prefix. Everything before (and including) that block is cached; everything after is processed fresh.

The cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } annotation marks the boundary. On the first call, Anthropic reports cache_creation_input_tokens. On subsequent calls within the 5-minute TTL, it reports cache_read_input_tokens instead.

Gemini uses a two-step process. First, create a cachedContent resource via a separate API call, specifying the content and an explicit TTL. Then reference that resource in subsequent generateContent calls. The minimum prefix is 32,768 tokens.

Note: The GoogleAICacheManager class may be exported from @google/generative-ai/server rather than the top-level @google/generative-ai depending on your installed SDK version. If the import below fails, try import { GoogleAICacheManager } from "@google/generative-ai/server". Verify with: node -e "const m = require('@google/generative-ai'); console.log(typeof m.GoogleAICacheManager)" — if it prints undefined, use the /server subpath.

The cached content object must be stored and reused. If the TTL expires, the resource must be recreated. In production, persist the cached content name to a database or cache store to survive process restarts; the in-memory Map used in the factory below is lost on every cold start, causing redundant cachedContent creation and additional billing.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

The Gemini path stores cached content objects in a Map keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the full system prompt, avoiding both redundant cache creation on repeated calls and cache key collisions that could occur with prefix-based keys. A secondary inflight Map ensures that concurrent requests with the same prompt do not trigger duplicate cache creation calls.

OpenAI exposes cache data at response.usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. When this value exceeds zero, the request hit the cache.

Anthropic splits caching into two fields: response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (populated on the first request when the provider writes the cache) and response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens (populated on subsequent requests that read from it). Check whether cache_read_input_tokens > 0 to confirm a hit.

Check response.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount. If it exceeds zero, the cached content resource was used for that request.

The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate applied to cached tokens specifically. The estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates the actual savings relative to total tokens in the request — for example, if only 100 of 10,000 tokens were cached at Anthropic's 90% rate, the estimated savings would be ~0.9%, not 90%. The hash comparison across requests reveals whether the prefix changed. The token estimate uses a 1.3x multiplier on word count as a rough approximation (+-30% error); production systems should use provider-specific tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI) for precision.

Cache misses happen for several concrete reasons. You changed the prefix between requests (even whitespace or trailing newline differences count). Your prefix falls below the provider's minimum token threshold. The TTL expired — Anthropic's 5-minute default is particularly aggressive. You switched the model parameter between requests. Or, in Gemini's case, you did not pass the cachedContent name to the generation call.

Run with npx tsc && node dist/demo.js openai. Swap the argument to anthropic or gemini to test other providers. The first request populates the cache; the second reads from it.

Realistic savings depend on reuse frequency within the TTL window. OpenAI provides a 50% discount on cached input tokens. Anthropic provides 90% on cached read tokens, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. Gemini provides 75% for Gemini 1.5 Pro (the Flash rate is not confirmed at time of writing). Anthropic reports reduced latency on cache hits, but none of the three providers publish fixed latency benchmarks for caching; consult each provider's official prompt caching documentation for current figures.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

Start by adding streaming response support to the request-builder, since cached prefixes work with streaming on all three providers. From there, implement persistent TTL management for Gemini's cachedContent resources (which otherwise require manual recreation after expiry), and wire the cache usage logger into an observability pipeline like OpenTelemetry spans for production cost monitoring.

For full details on each provider's caching behavior, consult the official documentation: OpenAI Prompt Caching, Anthropic Prompt Caching, and Gemini Context Caching.

#10371. Samsung’s advanced sleep apnea detection is coming to these Galaxy wearables

Samsung announced a new, advanced version of its AI-powered sleep apnea detection, and which devices it will appear on in November.

Sleep apnea detection was first introduced to Galaxy devices in 2024, after Samsung gained approval from the FDA in the US. The tool was offered as a baseline detection feature, so users who might be suffering from frequent breathing interruptions during sleep would be aware and seek further medical help.

Samsung says its new and improved version uses an AI algorithm to analyze breathing disturbances per hour (via GSMArena). It goes beyond detection and breaks those disturbances down into more granular detail – closer to something a dedicated sleep study would be equipped to do.

Users will need to record at least five hours of sleep twice within 10 days for the sleep apnea detection tool to properly get results on their Galaxy Watch or Ring.

Samsung is still adamant that this tool does not replace professional diagnosis; it’s simply better at making the user aware of their sleep habits.

Selling the exact same model worldwide at the same price while disabling features under the guise of country restriction is unfair. For example, keeping health features inactive in certain regions under the name of FDA approval. If Samsung wanted to, they could easily enable features like blood pressure and ECG for non-medical use for Bangladesh—or at least in countries where these features aren't legally prohibited—for health awareness. Not doing so feels like a form of deception toward customers.

Samsung says the new sleep apnea detection feature will roll out in November, starting in Korea, after the tool was approved by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. It’s FDA-approved in the US, as well, so it should follow shortly.

So far, Samsung has detailed these wearables:

After the initial rollout, the Galaxy Watch 7 and Watch 8 will get an update as long as they’re running Wear OS 7.0 or later.

There are no plans to dismantle the current sleep apnea detection tool available on the Galaxy Watch 4 and later.

#10366. Xbox’s smallest-ever controller is surprisingly comfortable

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Nano controller is designed for young people, anyone with smaller hands, and gaming on the go.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Even though I knew Microsoft’s new Xbox Nano controller was tiny, I still gasped when I unboxed it a few days ago. The compact controller is small enough to slip into a pocket unnoticed, and it has been designed specifically for younger people, or for anyone with smaller hands.

I’m not young, but I do have small hands, and I’ve been surprised at how comfortable the Nano is during gaming sessions. At just over 5 inches long, almost everything on this controller has been shrunk down somehow. The ABXY buttons are ever so slightly smaller than a regular Xbox controller, and the thumbsticks feel like miniature versions. Microsoft hasn’t changed the D-pad, though, or the size of the glowing Xbox button at the center of the controller.

The big difference I noticed with the Nano over a regular Xbox controller was the size of the triggers. While they are fully analog and pressure sensitive, they have more of a click when you bottom them out compared with the thud on a bigger Xbox controller. They’re noticeably smaller, as you’d expect, and the bumper buttons above the triggers feel less clicky than the regular ones.

I thought the Nano controller would feel awkward after a few hours of gaming, but the grips really help with comfort levels — a lot of smaller controllers sacrifice grips to keep the controller thin and lightweight. It does mean the Nano doesn’t sit flush on a table, but at 101 grams (0.22 pounds) it’s still really lightweight.

I can’t speak for those with bigger hands, but I’d expect the Nano controller won’t be well-suited to everyone. The size makes it ideal for young children, though. I tried to get my 1-year-old son to try the Nano, and he responded with a smile, so I guess he likes it.

I haven’t had enough time to get a full idea of battery life yet, but it seems to drain around 10 percent in around 30 to 40 minutes. That suggests a lot less battery life than the 30 hours you’d get on a rechargeable pack for the larger Xbox wireless controller. Thankfully, the Nano charges quickly, and I found I could get from 30 percent to 60 percent charge in less than 10 minutes. You can plug in a USB-C charger to top up the battery and carry on playing while you charge.

The only thing missing on the Nano controller that I would have loved is vibration support. I assume it’s not there because of an impact on battery life, because even the smaller Nintendo Joy-Con controllers have rumble support.

The Xbox Nano controller will be available on November 4th, priced at $49.99.

#10364. Google Photos update fixes the bug that hid edited pictures

A bug in Google Photos has left edited pictures invisible to other Android apps, but Google has now rolled out a fix.

Since roughly July/August of this year, editing a picture in Google Photos has left Android users with the bizarre side effect of making that image unavailable to other apps. After saving the edit, the picture would vanish from the image picker in apps like Telegram, WhatsApp, and more. A workaround to this was to save the image as a copy rather than the original, but it’s frustrating nonetheless.

Google has thankfully, finally fixed this issue.

The fix is apparently in Google Photos v7.97, Artem Russakovskii (owner of APKMirror) mentions, and we’ve been able to confirm the hidden image behavior no longer occurs on v7.98 either. The company acknowledged the problem last month and confirmed a fix would be coming.

The exact cause remains unclear at this point, but that doesn’t matter now seeing as the problem is fixed. If you’re still seeing the bug, let us know in the comments below.

#10363. CORS Error Fix: Diagnose Console Errors and Configure Headers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.
