Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every frontend developer will eventually stare at a CORS error in the browser console, watching an API call fail for reasons that seem opaque. A CORS error fix requires understanding what the browser is actually telling you, matching that specific message to its root cause, and applying a targeted, security-conscious server configuration.

The scheme, host, and port together define an "origin." https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins (different schemes), as are https://example.com and https://api.example.com (different hosts). https://example.com and https://example.com:443 are the same origin because port 443 is the default for HTTPS, and browsers omit it in origin comparisons. The browser enforces the same-origin policy on client-side JavaScript reading responses, not on sending requests. This distinction trips up many developers: the server may still receive and fully process the request; the browser simply refuses to expose the response to the calling code. The request lands, the database row gets written, and the browser throws an error anyway. The policy exists to prevent a malicious page from silently reading sensitive data from another origin using the user's ambient credentials.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a controlled opt-in mechanism via HTTP response headers. The server signals to the browser that a specific foreign origin is permitted to read its responses. Four headers control the mechanism: Access-Control-Allow-Origin specifies which origin is allowed, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods declares which HTTP methods are permitted. Access-Control-Allow-Headers lists which custom or non-simple headers the client may send, while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials indicates whether the browser should expose the response to credentialed requests.

The browser does not treat all cross-origin requests equally. "Simple" requests use GET, HEAD, or POST with a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain, and no custom headers. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a simple request and triggers a preflight.

Simple requests go directly to the server, and the browser evaluates the CORS headers on the response. Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends automatically before the actual request, asking the server whether the real request would be acceptable. If the OPTIONS response lacks the proper CORS headers, the browser never sends the real request at all.

A typical Chrome DevTools error reads: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Two origins appear in this message. The URL after "fetch at" is the target server, the resource the code tried to reach. The value after "from origin" is the page's own origin, the one making the request. Chrome is stating that the target server's response did not include an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the requesting origin, so the browser blocked the response from reaching JavaScript.

The most common variant is the missing header: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The server simply did not include the header at all.

When the console says Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check, the server either did not respond to the OPTIONS request correctly or returned a non-2xx status code for it.

Redirect variant: Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. Developers commonly misdiagnose this one. It occurs when the URL triggers a redirect before reaching the application handler. Typical culprits include HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades, trailing-slash normalization (e.g., /api/data redirecting to /api/data/), or a load balancer rewriting URLs. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request follows the redirect, and the Fetch specification (§4.8) forbids following redirects on preflight requests, so the entire flow fails. Fix the URL so no redirect occurs.

Credential variant: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. When fetch is called with credentials: 'include' or XMLHttpRequest sets withCredentials = true, the server must respond with the exact requesting origin, not *. The browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials.

Entry point: What does the console error say?

Each branch leads to a specific fix section in this article. Bookmark this decision tree and start here every time a CORS error surfaces.

Before modifying any server code, verify what the server actually returns by simulating a preflight request from the command line:

The -i flag prints response headers. -X OPTIONS sets the HTTP method to OPTIONS, mimicking the browser's preflight. The Origin header declares the requesting origin. Access-Control-Request-Method tells the server which method the real request would use. Access-Control-Request-Headers lists the custom headers the real request would include.

If these are absent, the server is not configured for CORS. If the response is a 301 or 302 redirect, the redirect variant is the culprit.

During local development, the least-configuration way to eliminate cross-origin issues is to proxy API requests through the dev server so the browser sees all traffic as same-origin.

With this configuration, a fetch('/api/users') call from the frontend at http://localhost:5173 is forwarded to http://localhost:3001/users. The browser never sees a cross-origin request. Without changeOrigin: true, the Host header sent upstream retains the dev server's hostname, which may cause backend rejections if the target validates the Host header. This is strictly a development-only solution. Production builds served from a static host will not have this proxy, so proper server-side CORS headers remain necessary.

Tested with: cors@2.8.5, express@4.18, Node.js 20 LTS. The cors package API surface has been stable since 2.x; check the changelog if you are on an earlier major version.

The simplest fix to unblock development uses the cors npm package with its defaults:

This applies Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every response. It unblocks any requesting origin, but it cannot be used with credentialed requests, and it exposes every endpoint to every origin on the internet. Any page an attacker controls can issue authenticated requests to your API and read the responses if the user is logged in. Move past it quickly.

For production, validate the incoming Origin header against an allowlist and reflect only permitted origins:

The origin function receives the Origin header value and calls callback(null, true) to allow the request. When true is passed, the cors package automatically reflects the incoming Origin header in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Vary: Origin. This satisfies the credential requirement and prevents open CORS misconfiguration. Setting credentials: true in the options causes the middleware to include the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response header. The cors middleware automatically handles OPTIONS preflight responses when applied at the app level.

Tested with: Next.js 14.x App Router, Node.js 20 LTS. The OPTIONS handler behavior and middleware matcher syntax changed between Next.js 13 and 15; exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach.

The cors npm package does not plug directly into the Next.js App Router (as of Next.js 13+). Instead, set headers manually in a route handler:

The OPTIONS export explicitly handles preflight requests and returns a 204 No Content with the required CORS headers. Without this, Next.js returns a 405 Method Not Allowed for OPTIONS in some versions (the exact behavior changed between 13 and 14), triggering the preflight failure variant. Exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach. The getCorsHeaders function returns an empty object for disallowed or absent origins, ensuring that server capabilities (supported methods and headers) are not disclosed to untrusted origins.

For projects with many API routes, centralizing CORS logic in middleware avoids repetition:

The matcher restricts this middleware to API routes only. Access-Control-Max-Age instructs browsers to cache preflight results. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400. The Vary: Origin header is only set when a cross-origin request is detected (the Origin header is present and allowed), avoiding unnecessary CDN cache fragmentation on same-origin or server-to-server requests. CORS headers including Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are only sent to allowed origins, preventing server capability disclosure to untrusted origins.

Tested with: Nginx 1.24+. The map directive behavior is stable across modern Nginx versions.

When Nginx sits in front of a backend, it is often the right place to manage CORS centrally. Important: Do not use if with add_header inside a location block -- Nginx's if block causes all parent-scope add_header directives to be silently ignored, breaking CORS headers on actual (non-OPTIONS) API responses.

The map directive builds an allowlist: if $http_origin matches a listed value, $cors_origin is set to that value; otherwise it remains empty. The always parameter ensures headers are added even on error responses (4xx, 5xx), which is critical because Nginx's add_header without always silently drops headers on non-2xx responses.

Nginx's if directive creates a new configuration context. Any add_header inside an if block discards all add_header directives from the enclosing scope.

Why the if block contains all headers and return 204: By placing return 204 inside the if block, the OPTIONS request is fully handled there and never reaches the outer add_header directives or proxy_pass. Non-OPTIONS requests skip the if block entirely and the outer scope's add_header directives and proxy_pass handle them. This separation avoids the inheritance pitfall: each request path (OPTIONS vs. non-OPTIONS) has its own complete, self-contained set of headers.

Note on empty $cors_origin: When the allowlist excludes the origin, $cors_origin resolves to an empty string, and Nginx emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: (a blank header). Browsers will reject CORS for the request, which is the correct security outcome. However, emitting a blank header is technically non-conformant with RFC 6454. The most robust production solution is to handle CORS in the application layer (Express/Next.js) and have Nginx proxy transparently, or to use OpenResty/Lua for conditional header suppression.

After deploying, verify that both curl -X OPTIONS and curl -X GET against the same URL return the expected CORS headers.

A frequent source of the redirect CORS variant is a proxy_pass trailing-slash mismatch. If the location block is location /api but proxy_pass is http://127.0.0.1:3001 (no trailing slash), Nginx may issue a redirect for /api/ normalization before the request reaches the handler. Similarly, a return 301 https://... rule placed before the CORS location block can redirect the OPTIONS preflight. The fix is straightforward: ensure trailing slashes match between location and proxy_pass, and place any redirect rules after or outside the API location block so they do not intercept OPTIONS requests.

Use an explicit origin allowlist. Avoid * when credentials are involved; the browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials: 'include'.

Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Methods to only the methods the API actually uses. Listing every HTTP method widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

Set Access-Control-Max-Age to cache preflight responses. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400 (24 hours). Use 7200 as a safe cross-browser default, or 86400 if your users are primarily on Firefox and you want fewer preflight round-trips.

Include Vary: Origin on every response where Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set conditionally. Without it, CDN or proxy caches may serve a CORS response cached for one origin to a different origin, causing intermittent failures.

Never mirror the request Origin header back without validating it against an allowlist. This is an open CORS misconfiguration that effectively disables the same-origin policy for any attacker-controlled origin.

Do not install browser extensions that disable CORS either -- they mask the problem during development and expose you to real cross-origin attacks on every other site you visit.

Avoid adding CORS headers in both the application framework and Nginx simultaneously. Duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers cause the browser's CORS origin comparison to fail; the browser receives the response but blocks JavaScript from reading it, producing the same CORS error the fix was meant to resolve.

Read the console error, match it against the decision tree, apply the targeted fix, and verify with the curl preflight command. Use the decision tree above as a reference for every future CORS error.

Microsoft is about to launch its new Xbox Nano controller tomorrow, and the tiny device has a little secret. The Nano can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi to improve latency. It’s a feature Microsoft hasn’t officially announced yet, but one I’ve been anticipating since the Xbox Nano leaked earlier this year.

The Nano will be able to connect directly to Microsoft’s cloud servers to reduce latency, much like how Google’s Stadia controllers used to work. This new cloud connect feature for the Nano is being privately tested on the new Xbox Cloud Gaming website, and it will require you to pair the controller over Wi-Fi to Microsoft’s Xbox Cloud Gaming servers using the Xbox mobile app.

I’m expecting Microsoft to announce this as a preview for the new Xbox Nano controller soon, before it’s fully supported across Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and on smart TVs. I first started reporting that Microsoft was planning a new controller with Wi-Fi connectivity to reduce Xbox Cloud Gaming latency earlier this year. I’d expect the upcoming Xbox Elite 3 controller will also have the same functionality.

Microsoft had also planned to introduce a direct-to-cloud feature on a new Xbox controller, codenamed Sebile, as part of an Xbox Series X refresh console in 2024. The refresh console was canceled, and it’s not clear when we’ll eventually see a new Xbox wireless controller with direct cloud functionality.

Samsung has big plans for its foldable lineup in 2027, but also one more release for 2026. The Galaxy W27 just went official as the company’s latest foldable, but you probably wouldn’t want to buy this one even if you could.

The Galaxy W27 continues Samsung’s pattern of releasing a China-exclusive variant of its flagship, book-style foldable. This year, it’s based on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and includes all of the same specs – 8-inch inner display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 200MP main camera, and everything else.

It mostly comes down to the fit and finish. Samsung has given the Galaxy W27 some slick golden accents and two striking color variants. One is a dark red, the other a dark blue. This model also comes with 16GB of RAM as standard, regardless of if you pick the 512GB or 1TB storage options. It’s also optimized for Tiantong satellite comms, SamMobile points out.

But this special edition comes at a cost. It starts at CNY 18,999, around $2,800 USD. The 1TB upgrade lands at CNY 21,999, around $3,300 USD. Rosstat acknowledged suffering cyberattacks but denied leaked data claims.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) admitted that its servers were hit by coordinated cyberattacks between October 29 and 31. However, it denied claims that tens of terabytes of data had been leaked, as asserted by hack groups like the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow. Rosstat stopped publishing annual cause-of-death statistics in 2024, but the hackers say that the huge new 23TB data haul includes data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only,” reports The Moscow Times. A new chart shared by the hack groups using the data suggests that as many as 50,000 Russian soldiers are killed every month.

Rosstat is very much like the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States, or the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the UK. It isn’t a big juicy military infrastructure target, but if accurate war casualty figures can come from the claimed exfiltrated data haul, then it would be a considerable win for Ukraine and its supporters.

Today @cpartisans and SilentCrow took down Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the nerve center behind every socioeconomic number this regime produces. Full breakdown below 👇 https://t.co/wUKfyUi6y6November 1, 2026

As we mentioned in the intro, both the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow claim to have snagged lots of sensitive data from the Russian government thanks to this breach. The former’s tweet includes evidence and a breakdown. “Entire IT infrastructure wiped: Domain controllers, databases, servers, virtualization, document workflow, workstations, admin consoles, VPN,” notes a follow-up post about the Rosstat hack attack. “Systems destroyed: STATEK, CSOD, Demography, SED, ESSO, OFSN, internal employee surveillance, StatRegister, websites and more.”

This is a developing story with the Belarusian CyberPartisans promising to share more sensitive information from Rosstat after they have picked through it. The Rosstat website was reportedly defaced with hacker messages and logos. Rosstat remains inaccessible at the time of writing.

We spotted an interesting graphic shared by the Belarusian CyberPartisans, which included the Silent Crow logo. A chart indicates that over the last two years, between 25,000 and 50,000 Russian soldiers were killed every month. The October 2026 figure is just a smidgen under 50,000, if this data leak news is genuine.

These same hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the likes of the disruptive Aeroflot IT systems hack, and a state real estate company hack with two billion records, both in 2025. “Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia,” notes the report.

#10355. Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.

One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.

For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”

In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.

Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”

However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.

Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.

In a new post from Valve published after we first ran this story, the company acknowledged that following a “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months,” it’s “running a little behind right now” and taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews, saying that much of the delay is “having to re-review games.” It has updated its release checklist for developers, including requiring them to run a game through Steam for at least five minutes. Valve also says that further improvements are on the way for the build review process.

Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

Update, November 3rd: Added new post from Valve.

#10354. Building Accessible Navigation Menus with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Navigation is one of the most important components of a website. It helps visitors discover content, move between pages, and understand how a site is organized. However, a navigation menu that works well with a mouse may create problems for keyboard users, people who rely on screen readers, or visitors using small mobile screens.

Building an accessible navigation menu involves more than adding a few ARIA attributes or increasing the size of clickable elements. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, keyboard interaction, visible focus indicators, responsive layouts, and predictable behavior.

In this tutorial, we will build a responsive navigation menu using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We will also examine common accessibility mistakes and explain how to test the finished component.

HTML provides several native elements that communicate the purpose and structure of a navigation interface.

A website's primary navigation should generally use a

element containing a list of links. This structure helps browsers and assistive technologies identify the navigation region and understand the available destinations.

The aria-label gives the navigation landmark a descriptive name. This becomes particularly useful when a page contains multiple navigation regions, such as a primary menu and a footer menu.

Using a list also communicates that the links form a related group. Each link has a meaningful destination, making it possible for visitors to navigate the site without relying on visual positioning alone.

A common mistake is using clickable

elements instead of links. Although JavaScript can make a div respond to clicks, it does not automatically provide the same keyboard behavior and navigation semantics as an anchor element.

For navigation to another page, use an anchor. For an action that changes the interface, use a button.

A navigation menu should adapt to the available screen width without hiding important links or creating horizontal scrolling.

The following CSS creates a flexible desktop navigation layout:

Flexbox aligns the logo and navigation horizontally while allowing the link list to wrap when necessary.

The gap property controls the spacing between links without requiring individual margins. Removing the list markers also produces a cleaner navigation layout while preserving the underlying list semantics.

Notice that the hover style includes an underline as well as a color change. This provides an additional visual cue instead of relying exclusively on color.

However, hover effects alone are insufficient because touchscreens do not have conventional hover behavior, and keyboard users do not navigate with a mouse.

Many visitors use the Tab key to move between interactive elements. A navigation menu should make the currently focused link easy to identify.

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display a focus indicator when it is appropriate, particularly during keyboard navigation.

Avoid removing the browser's default outline unless you replace it with a clearly visible alternative.

Keyboard accessibility also depends on the HTML structure. Standard anchor elements already support keyboard focus and activation, so the basic navigation above does not need custom JavaScript keyboard handlers.

That is an important design principle: use native browser behavior wherever possible rather than recreating it unnecessarily.

On smaller screens, a horizontal navigation menu may occupy too much space. A toggle button can provide a compact alternative while preserving access to the links.

The menu button is hidden on larger screens and displayed on smaller ones. On mobile, the navigation links are initially hidden until JavaScript adds the is-open class.

The aria-expanded attribute communicates whether the menu is currently expanded, while aria-controls identifies the element controlled by the button.

These attributes must reflect the actual interface state. Adding them without updating their values when the menu opens and closes can confuse assistive technology users.

The JavaScript should update both the visual state and the accessibility information when the user activates the button.

When the button is clicked, the code reads the current state, reverses it, updates aria-expanded, and toggles the CSS class.

Because the button is a native HTML button, it already supports keyboard activation. There is no need to add separate Enter or Space key handlers.

For a production implementation, you should also consider what happens when the viewport changes from mobile to desktop. For example, if the menu is open on mobile and the visitor resizes the browser, the desktop layout should not remain in an inconsistent state.

A more complete implementation can synchronize the menu state with the responsive breakpoint, close the menu when a navigation link is selected, and ensure that hidden links cannot be reached through keyboard navigation.

A navigation menu may look correct and still be difficult to use. Testing should cover both automated checks and real interactions.

Start with keyboard testing. Use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through the logo, menu button, and navigation links. Check that focus indicators are visible and that the order follows the visual and logical structure.

The menu button appears at the intended breakpoint.

Activating the button opens and closes the navigation.

The aria-expanded value matches the visible state.

Hidden links are not available for keyboard interaction while the menu is closed.

Selecting a link takes the visitor to the correct destination.

You can also use accessibility inspection tools to identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, and other common problems.

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot establish that every interaction is understandable. Manual testing with a keyboard and, where possible, a screen reader remains important.

For larger websites, reusable navigation components and automated browser tests can help prevent accessibility regressions when styles or interaction logic change.

Accessible navigation starts with semantic HTML and builds on that foundation through responsive CSS, visible focus indicators, and carefully implemented JavaScript.

Native links and buttons provide much of the expected keyboard behavior automatically. Responsive styles make the menu usable across screen sizes, while accurate ARIA state helps communicate whether a collapsible menu is open or closed.

The most reliable approach is to keep the implementation as simple as possible, use browser features instead of recreating them, and test the actual experience rather than relying only on how the interface looks.

When accessibility is considered from the beginning, navigation becomes easier to maintain and more usable for a wider range of visitors.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a new post today, Valve acknowledged that it’s seen “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months” and says it’s “running a little behind” by taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews instead of the typical 3-5 days.

Indie developers have recently expressed frustrations over lengthy approval times for Steam games, even causing some games to miss planned launch dates. Valve says that “much” of the delay is having to re-review games, so it’s making some changes to the release checklist for developers to hopefully “cut down on re-reviews for basic functional issues.”

The changes include requiring developers to run games through Steam for at least five minutes. “Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam,” Valve says. “This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam.”

Other requirements include making sure that achievements are ready and confirming any required common redistributables, like DirectX or Visual C++, that Steam may need to install.

Valve also says more improvements are in the works for the build review process.

#10347. What “Clear Form” Should Really Do: Managing Draft Data in JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A user fills out a form, requests a preview, and then changes their mind. They click “Clear,” the inputs become empty, and the interface appears ready for someone else.

A moment later, the previous preview returns.

The application cleared the fields, but an asynchronous request still held the old values and updated the screen when it finished. Similar problems occur when drafts remain in browser storage, validation messages retain personal details, or a component’s internal state survives a visual reset.

For developers building onboarding, expense, application, and document workflows, clearing a form is a state-management operation. It deserves the same attention as submission.

This article explains how to define that operation, prevent stale results, and inspect the outcome using practical browser and testing tools.

Start by listing the places where a draft exists. The visible inputs are only one location.

When reviewing a financial-data interface, a useful design exercise is to map which information belongs to the current draft and what should happen when the user starts again. The same exercise applies to expense submissions and customer onboarding; the implementation must be assessed separately from the visible interface.

Name actions according to their actual scope. “Clear this form” should not imply that previously submitted records have been deleted. If a draft has been saved remotely, distinguish clearing the current screen from deleting the saved draft.

For a broader introduction to form structure and validation, SitePoint’s guide to modern HTML forms provides useful background.

Autosave is convenient, but persisting the entire form after every keystroke is an architectural decision, not a harmless UI enhancement.

For a short workflow, keeping the draft in memory may be sufficient. For a longer workflow, decide which fields may be retained, how the user understands that behavior, and when the retained copy is removed.

Browser storage options have different lifetimes. According to MDN’s sessionStorage documentation, session storage is associated with a page session and survives reloads. It should not be treated as equivalent to an ordinary variable that disappears when the page reloads.

Nor does shorter retention make storage a security boundary. The OWASP HTML5 security guidance cautions against storing sensitive information in local storage because JavaScript running in the origin can access it.

This reduces unnecessary copies. It does not provide secure memory erasure or protect a page from every script that can access its data.

The native form.reset() method restores controls to their default values. It does not necessarily make every field empty.

For example, an input rendered with a default value can return to that value after a reset. The method also does not clear a separate preview element, invalidate a network response, or update every framework-managed state variable.

Use a small HTML form with empty defaults for the following example:

The clear control uses type="button" so the application can coordinate the complete operation.

In a React or Vue implementation, apply the same policy to the state that controls the inputs. Clearing the DOM while leaving the component state intact can cause the old values to reappear.

Cancellation helps reduce unnecessary work, but request identity is what protects the interface from a stale result.

Assign each request a generation number. Whenever the draft changes or is cleared, advance that number. A response may update the UI only if its number still matches the current generation.

The following JavaScript works with the HTML above. It assumes a same-origin POST /api/preview endpoint that accepts JSON and returns {"summary":"plain text"}. That endpoint is an integration requirement; it is not implemented here.

Editing a field also invalidates the preview. Otherwise, users could mistake a result based on earlier values for a result based on their current input.

The code writes server-provided text with textContent rather than interpreting it as HTML. It also displays a fixed failure message instead of echoing request values into an error.

AbortController allows the client to abort fetch-related work. Aborting a browser request does not guarantee that server processing stopped or that data already received by the server was deleted.

The generation check enforces the narrower promise: obsolete work must not update this interface. SitePoint’s introduction to the Fetch API explains the request and response mechanics behind the example.

The example intentionally does not save drafts. If your application does, add cleanup to the clear operation rather than assuming that resetting the form handles it.

Remove the application’s specific draft entry. Avoid localStorage.clear() as a general cleanup shortcut, since it also removes unrelated keys for that origin.

Keep the UI honest if storage cleanup fails. Do not announce that every saved copy is gone when the application has only emptied the visible controls.

An object URL should be revoked when it is no longer needed, but revoking it does not delete a file the user already downloaded.

For programmatic changes, call the same invalidation function used by input events. Assigning an input’s value in JavaScript does not automatically trigger the user-input event handler.

You do not need a large dependency stack to verify a clear operation. Each of these tools answers a different question.

Chrome’s local-storage inspection guide explains how to inspect stored entries. Check session storage and IndexedDB too if the application uses them; an empty local-storage table is not proof that no browser persistence exists.

Mock Service Worker is useful for creating reproducible response conditions during development. Use fictional fixtures so debugging sessions do not depend on real personal records.

With Playwright network interception, hold a preview response until the test explicitly releases it. Fill the form, request a preview, clear the draft, and only then release the response. Assert that the input remains empty and the preview never returns.

A controlled release is more reliable than hoping a fixed delay creates the right race. Also test two requests completing in reverse order.

A useful review checks the operation at several points:

Supplement automated accessibility checks with keyboard and screen-reader testing. The Playwright accessibility guide explains that automated checks detect only some accessibility problems.

Verify backend behavior separately. Server validation, authorization, retention, and deletion require their own implementation and tests. A clean browser interface cannot demonstrate those guarantees.

A reliable clear operation has a defined scope. It invalidates pending work, resets the application’s draft state, removes derived output, and handles persistence according to the product’s stated behavior.

The implementation can remain small. What matters is that the team knows where draft data lives and tests what happens when events arrive in an inconvenient order.

When developers make those boundaries explicit, “Clear form” becomes a predictable action rather than a visual reset that leaves the previous workflow running.

#10345. The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’

Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The PC gaming mods repository Nexus Mods is making disclosures about AI mandatory for uploads of new mods, meaning that mod authors will have to declare “whether AI has been used in their work,” the site announced today as part of a big post about AI-generated content on the platform.

“One of the most consistent concerns we’ve heard is that it’s not clearly disclosed when AI has been used to create a mod,” according to the post from site owner Victor “Foledinho” Folmann. “We already have tags for AI-generated and AI-assisted mods, but we recognise that there’s a lot more we can do to make that information more accessible and clear for you all.” Any mods tagged as “AI-assisted” will also be required to include “a public explanation of how and where AI was used.” AI tags will also be “more prominent” on mod pages.

Folmann says Nexus Mods is “pro-human creativity” but “won’t introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods.” As for why that is:

The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We’d prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

Folmann notes that Nexus Mods won’t use mods to train AI and “will not sell or license them to anyone doing so.” However, the site is working on “clearer control” over how mods can be reused on others and strengthening attribution for when “a mod uses another Mod Author’s mod with the appropriate permissions.”

Nexus Mods is also making changes to the Recently Added section of the site to address a problem of mod authors uploading many mods at once, which makes other mods fall down down the page. “This is less of an issue related to AI, but it’s becoming much more prevalent as mod production is speeding up,” Folmann says. The changes include trying limits on how many mods from one author are shown at a time and “tighter restrictions” on uploads from new accounts. The platform is also launching controls to hide AI-generated content in game pages and on the homepage, and “next up,” in search.

Nexus Mods’ full AI policy is here, and mod authors have 60 days to update their existing mods to meet the requirements. The 60-day grace period ends on January 2nd, and after that time, the site will begin enforcing the rules.

Google secures approval for its Minnesota data center despite local protests, lawsuits, and power supply concerns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google has secured approval for a proposed data center in Hermantown, Minnesota, following a unanimous vote by the city council, MPR News reports. The decision, reached on Friday, October 30, clears a major hurdle for the company following at least two postponed meetings and hours of public opposition, though the project still faces lawsuits and a separate inquiry into its electricity supply. The proposed development could cover just over 200 acres in a rural residential area outside Duluth with three data center buildings spanning approximately 1.66 million square feet.

The council approved a development agreement, a special use permit, and provisions for decommissioning the site if construction is abandoned or the facility eventually closes. The meeting, which was capped at 85 people and offered a livestream, ended shortly before midnight, with some criticizing the attendance restriction. Council member John Geisler, however, clarified the move, noting that the decision concerned local land use application rather than the wide debate over artificial intelligence or big technology companies.

“What we've done tonight is not about AI. It's not about big tech. It's not about software. It's about a project here in Hermantown, a land use application, and agreements that are associated with that,” Geissler said.

The approval comes at a hefty price for Google, with the company being forced to make several changes during the approval process. The company changed its initial plan of putting up four buildings to three, capped their height at 33 feet, and agreed to monitor nearby private wells —but each building would still be larger than six football fields. Google also agreed to withdraw an earlier request for up to $80 million in property tax breaks. The revised arrangement is now expected to generate about $3 million in annual property tax for the city, with a separate decommissioning agreement valued at $210 million in place.

Supporters point to those provisions as evidence that Google had responded to local concerns. Opponents, however, argue that the changes did not address the important questions of whether such a colossal development belongs in the area. The dispute echoes other data center battles within local communities, with Alabama residents being unable to halt a 50MW Bitcoin mining facility in August, despite local moratoriums, exposing gaps in the state's zoning rules. In September, a proposal for a 1,300-acre data center in Pennsylvania by NorthPoint Development also faced resistance despite its developer offering $10,000 to thousands of nearby households. Key issues raised mostly by residents in both cases have been about noise and water consumption by such facilities and property values.

It’s important to note, however, that Hermantown’s vote does not mean Google can immediately begin construction. Three lawsuits filed by The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center challenge the city’s zoning process and ownership of the land, and are also demanding the project’s environmental review. The project’s environmental needs are also another pain point, given it requires about 500 megawatts, comparable to the combined demands of homes in Minneapolis, St. Paul, Duluth, and Rochester, as per the Citizens Utility Board of Minnesota. Google still needs approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission on power consumption, despite its agreement with Minnesota Power.

The scale of demand is a recurring point of friction in data center proposals. Last year, the OpenAI Stargate facility in Michigan received approval for a 1.4-gigawatt power supply — construction, however, started in June 2026 despite objections from local residents. Google is also pursuing a separate data center project near Pine Island, close to Rochester. That proposal is now subject to a more extensive environmental review following a legal settlement.

#10341. Google stock drops amid AI fears; AI Mode has ‘lower monetization,’ getting more ads

Google is bringing ads to AI Mode globally as it admits that the new take on Search brings “lower monetization,” all while $GOOG stock is seeing a fairly major drop.

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call yesterday saw Google’s Philipp Schindler acknowledging that AI Mode, the company’s Gemini-powered new take on Search, has “lower monetization” compared to traditional Search. So the “strong growth” of AI Mode didn’t have as much of a positive impact on Google’s bottom line simply because the mode doesn’t generate as much revenue.

…It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we’re seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we’re now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries…

In a blog post the same day, Google announced that AI Mode would be getting ads in global markets. US users will also start to see “multiturn ads” in follow-up queries.

Our research shows that people are comfortable with ads in AI Mode and find them highly relevant. In fact, click-through rates are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.

Now we’re scaling ads in AI Mode in Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Singapore. In Q4 2026, we plan to expand to additional locales, including Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, $GOOG stock dipped by 27 points around the time of the earnings call and has continued to drop on October 29. It currently sits around $280, just a few points higher than a March 30 low of $273.14. The 12% drop reduces Google’s market cap by over $500 billion. NBC News points out that it is the second-biggest drop behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025.

The drop is not directly due to AI Mode itself, but is attributed to weaker-than-expected earnings in Q3. Ad revenue from Search still makes up roughly half of Google’s overall revenue.

Our Daniel Bader expands on this in the latest issue of Inbox, our twice-weekly free newsletter:

…But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

#10340. All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake

Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is scheduled to release on November 5th. You can follow along with all of our coverage of the game right here.

Nintendo revealed yesterday that it held blind voice auditions for the Ocarina of Time remake and ended up casting an actor for the same role they had in the original. That actor was apparently Kaori Mizuhashi, who played Navi in the original and is listed as Navi’s Japanese voice in a leaked credits sequence for the remake, Eurogamer reports.

Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom. As a result, Zelda has never been bigger, and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past. Or so it seemed.

For one of the biggest Switch 2 exclusives so far, Nintendo has gone back to Ocarina of Time, which originally launched on the N64 in 1998. It’s one of the most influential and revered games in the long-running franchise, a game that showed that the classic Zelda formula — one that used a large world to connect a handful of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons, creating a grand adventure — could work in three dimensions. Now Ocarina has been remade for the Switch 2 in a way that accomplishes exactly what a good remake is designed to do: preserve the core of the original experience while making it more accessible for modern audiences. And it shows there’s still some life left in the traditional Zelda formula.

For the Ocarina of Time remake, Nintendo developers said in a new interview that they wanted to “preserve the experience of spamming the Roll Attack to forward roll your way across Hyrule Field.” I have very fond memories of rolling around the world in the original.

In the remake, you can still spam Roll Attack, but you can also dash.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches later this week, and in the lead-up Nintendo has put out the first half of a lengthy developer Q&A, covering everything from what changed gameplay-wise, to the new visual style, which was inspired by puppet shows. As art director Aya Shida explains:

Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds. We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game.

The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.

The long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 launches next Thursday, November 5th. In other words, you have a week remaining to secure your physical edition with a $10 discount at Amazon and Walmart. Once the game launches, the physical version will almost certainly go from $59.99 to $69.99 while the digital version will stay at $59.99.

Nintendo had the unenviable task of reimagining its Nintendo 64-era masterpiece for the Switch 2, and based on our hands-on time with some sections of the game, it’s a lot of fun to play. The graphics and art style are fantastic, and the controls have been modernized to be simpler to pick up for those who are already experienced with third-person action games, including other modern Zelda titles.

I’ve really warmed up to the game’s art style, especially in this new trailer. And after reading my colleague Cameron Faulkner’s hands-on preview, I’m looking forward to returning to Hyrule even more. The game launches on Switch 2 on November 5th.

With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original.

More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button.

It was briefly shown during Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct today, but Hori’s website now has a listing for its $49.99 electronic ocarina. You can play your own songs by pushing buttons, play one of 12 pre-programmed songs from the games, use it with the Ocarina of Time remake’s sound recognition feature, or connect headphones for a private jam session.

Link’s next adventure now has a release date. During a Legend of Zelda stream for the franchise’s 40th anniversary, Nintendo announced that the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 is launching on November 5th. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI.

Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.”

Tuesday’s Nintendo Direct showcase felt like an important moment for the company. With the Switch 2 heading into its second holiday season, one in which the hardware will be even more expensive thanks to a price hike, it was a chance for Nintendo to really sell new audiences on its latest console — but that’s not exactly what happened. While there were some impressive-looking titles, there wasn’t much that felt truly new. Instead, the two major Switch 2 exclusives that will round out the 2026 calendar are both remakes from the Nintendo 64 era.

If you missed it, the final reveal of the Direct was a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2. We don’t know when, exactly, it’s launching, but Nintendo says it’ll be out this year. The brief teaser didn’t reveal much of what the game will look like, nor how it might differ from the N64 original, so chances are you can expect an Ocarina-focused Direct in the coming months that will detail more. Whenever it comes out, the Ocarina remake will follow the Star Fox remake, which is launching later this month in an attempt to revitalize Nintendo’s long-dormant sci-fi series for modern audiences.

Nintendo announced a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time during its Nintendo Direct presentation on Tuesday. It will launch sometime in 2026 on Nintendo Switch 2. More details will be announced “in the future.”

This new title is the first major release in the franchise since 2024’s Echoes of Wisdom, which starred Princess Zelda herself. Echoes followed 2023’s Tears of the Kingdom, a direct sequel to Breath of the Wild — both of which got upgraded Switch 2 versions alongside the launch of the new console last year. In November, Nintendo also launched the hack-and-slash title Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment.

#10339. Best AI Brand Mention Tracking Tools for Enterprises in 2026: 6 Tools Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

At a large company, the hard part of buying an AI brand mention tracking tool is procurement. IT asks about single sign-on, legal asks where the data sits, and the marketing team that wanted the tool waits weeks to log in. A pilot on one brand in one market looks cheap, then the other markets, the other teams and SSO arrive and the quote looks nothing like the trial.

That is why a generic "best tools" list helps enterprise buyers less than it should. All the tools below track how often ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI answers name your brand. What separates them at enterprise size is everything around the tracking: how many people can log in, how logins are controlled, whether the data can leave the tool and whether it copes with ten markets instead of one.

This guide compares six tools on those points. Peec AI ranks first because it combines unlimited users, enforceable SSO, source-level analysis and a published price ladder. The other five suit different buying situations.

AI brand mention tracking measures how often, where and how favourably AI engines name your brand when buyers ask category questions. A tool runs a fixed prompt set daily across engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot, then reports mention rate (visibility), position inside the answer, sentiment, share of voice against competitors and the sources each answer cited.

For an enterprise, the answers differ by engine, country and product line, and a single visibility number hides most of that. Similarweb's May 2026 figures put ChatGPT at 53.9% of AI chatbot web visits, Gemini at 27.9% and Claude at 9.2%, against roughly 76% for ChatGPT in June 2025. The question "what does AI say about us?" is now spread over at least three engines.

Access and identity. Ask how many users each plan allows, whether SSO is available and on which plan, and whether you can enforce it. Most tools put SSO on their top tier or a custom plan, so budget for an enterprise contract early.

Markets and brands. Check whether the price grows per country, language or brand. Ten markets multiply a prompt set quickly.

Data access. The data has to reach the reporting leadership already reads: CSV export, an API, a BI connector or an MCP server.

Source analysis. A mention rate shows where you stand. Source data shows why, by listing the pages each engine read. Without it you cannot tell whether you are missing because nobody writes about you or because your own pages are not picked up.

Prompt volume and engines. A hundred to a hundred and fifty prompts per brand and market is a realistic start. Check which engines each plan includes and which sit behind add-ons.

Cost at your real workload. Price the tool for the users, markets and prompts you will have in a year, not for the pilot.

Enterprise teams rarely run on the entry tier, so the tables below price two realistic workloads: about 150 prompts, and about 350 prompts on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode with 15 users, both tracked daily on three engines. Price per prompt is the monthly price divided by the prompts the plan includes. Rankscale and AthenaHQ price by answers or credits instead, so Rankscale's rows use the answer volume the workload needs: 150 prompts on three engines over 30 days is 13,500 answers a month, and 350 prompts is 31,500. Profound does not publish prices and is left out of the tables. Treat every figure as directional: enterprise contracts are custom and billed annually, so published self-serve prices show where a negotiation starts, not what you will pay.

Peec AI has the lowest price per prompt in the first table and the lowest monthly price in the second. Scrunch AI's Core plan costs $2.00 per prompt at 125 prompts and five users, and its larger plans are quote-only. Against Rankscale, the only other tool here with a published enterprise price, Peec AI costs 36% less at 150 prompts ($245 against $385) and 37% less at 350 prompts ($495 against $780). Rankscale does include more engines in its price, which Peec AI reserves for Enterprise. On ChatGPT plus both Google surfaces with 15 people logging in, Peec AI is the cheapest of the tools priced in these tables: $495 against $638 for Otterly.AI once Google AI Mode is added, and $780 for Rankscale. Otterly.AI and Rankscale include more engines in their price.

One thing changes these tables: single sign-on. Peec AI, Profound, AthenaHQ, Scrunch AI and Otterly.AI put SSO on Enterprise, and Rankscale puts it on a custom plan. If IT requires SSO, every tool here becomes a quote, and the published prices only show where the negotiation starts. Annual billing takes 15% to 17% off most of these.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform with a New York office. It tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice, breaks every answer into the sources the engine read and turns the gaps it finds into prioritised actions. At enterprise scale its pricing is the main difference: users are unlimited on every plan, and Peec does not charge per country or language, with multi-country tracking from the Advanced plan.

Best for: Enterprise teams that want one tool for every market and every team, and need to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Profound suits purchases that have to clear an information security review before anything else. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise, and it raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026, which settles the vendor-risk question quickly.

Best for: Companies where compliance and vendor risk decide the purchase.

AthenaHQ was built by two former Google Search and DeepMind engineers. Its Enterprise plan has the longest feature list of the quote-based tools: SAML and OIDC single sign-on, audit logs, a 2-hour SLA, a dedicated Slack channel and executive dashboards that feed Tableau, Power BI and Looker. An optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page actions, which suits large companies that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Enterprises short on people to act on the data, who want BI dashboards and audit logs.

Scrunch AI publishes one self-serve plan and sells everything else through a quote. Core costs $250 a month and includes 125 prompts, 5,000 responses a month, five user licences and Google single sign-on, which is enough for a pilot with a small team.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price and five users, with nine engines available on Enterprise.

Rankscale is the only tool here where the enterprise price is on the website. Enterprise is $780 a month for 12,000 credits, up to 48,000 answers, with REST API access and a dedicated partner. Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral are on every paid plan.

Best for: Teams that need a published enterprise price and the widest engine list.

Otterly.AI has the lowest entry price here, with unlimited team members on every plan and unlimited workspaces from the Standard plan, which helps when several business units want their own view. It is a lighter product than the five above, and SSO sits on its Enterprise plan, which starts from 1,000 prompts.

Best for: Business units that want their own workspace at a low price.

The most common mistake is buying for the pilot. A team runs a trial on one brand and one market, picks the tool with the friendliest entry price and finds out in month four that adding other markets, other teams and SSO moves them onto a quote that looks nothing like the trial.

Before you start a trial, write down three numbers: how many people will need to log in within a year, how many markets you sell in, and whether IT will require SSO. Then ask every vendor to price that.

Enterprise AI brand mention tracking is mostly a question of fit with how a large company buys. Peec AI is the strongest overall choice because users and markets do not drive its price, SSO can be enforced, and its source analysis shows what to fix instead of only how you rank.

Profound is the better route when a compliance review decides everything, AthenaHQ when you want BI dashboards and drafted work, Scrunch AI when you want a published entry price with five users, and Rankscale when you need a published enterprise price.

Whichever you pick, price your real workload, ask about SSO first and remember that the tool measures: what moves the number is being on the pages the engines read. The best AI brand mention tracking tools for enterprises are the ones that show you which pages those are.

What does an enterprise AI brand mention tracking tool cost?

Directionally, between $245 and $780 a month on published plans for 150 to 350 daily prompts: Peec AI Pro at $245 and Advanced at $495, Scrunch AI Core at $250 for 125 prompts, Otterly.AI Premium at $489 and Rankscale at $385 to $780. On Peec AI that is $1.41 to $1.63 per prompt with unlimited users. Once SSO is required, every tool here is a custom quote. The spread is driven by users and markets more than by features.

If more than a handful of people will log in, IT will usually ask for it. Every tool here puts SSO on Enterprise or a custom plan, so plan the budget for that contract instead of the self-serve tier.

How many prompts does an enterprise need?

A hundred to a hundred and fifty per brand and market. Start with the questions your sales team hears, then the comparisons buyers make between you and named competitors. More markets multiply the set. More product pages usually should not.

SEO usually owns the measurement. What breaks is the fix, because much of it means getting mentioned on sites you do not control, which sits with PR or communications. Agree that split before you buy.

The second October Gemini for Home update was released by Google today. It bundles a few fixes with a lengthy section in the changelog dedicated to the Google Home app.

Project takes a stock Qwen 3.5 4B and compiles a RISC-V CPU into its weights.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI engineer Divyansh Agrawal has revealed the Qwenputer. Described in its most basic terms, Qwenputer is an experimental blend of the stock Qwen 3.5 4B AI LLM with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU compiled and inserted directly into its weights. In use, Qwenputer can run processor arithmetic operations – or even run C and MicroPython code on its built-in CPU, eschewing any external runtime or tool use. Moreover, it can run Doom, albeit very slowly. You can see the Qwenputer running Doom on its RISC-V CPU by expanding the tweet below.

QWenputer by @divagr1925 is so cool! but... can it run DOOM? Ofc yes! E1M1 on the RISC-V CPU compiled into Qwen3.5-4B weights. will opensource too https://t.co/hEa46rD6CJOctober 29, 2026

The implementation of Qwenputer raises some interesting concepts and solutions. For example, the developer used Qwen’s Gated DeltaNet (GND) state as RAM, which Agrawal reckons is “a pretty neat trick.” They admit that using these ‘fast weights’ as RAM isn’t an original concept, but modifying Qwen 3.5 this way does seem to be a first.

Unlike traditional LLM creation, adding a ‘CPU’ doesn’t involve training. This RISC-V CPU implementation “is 11 transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, and none of their weights are learned: a compiler computes every one,” it is explained. Agrawal boasts that Qwenputer’s built-in CPU “passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.”

The developer stresses that Qwen makes use of this ‘CPU’ to send instructions and read them back with no external tool or runtime calls. In practice, it works as intended. Use of the CPU inside Qwenputer provides exact calculations, overcoming the arithmetic weaknesses of many LLMs. Moreover, users can run code on the CPU inside the LLM, with C and MicroPython compatibility.

Not content with wedging a CPU into an LLM, Agrawal decided to also give it a filesystem. They describe this extension of the model as relatively trivial, since RAM is already in place. Indeed, the filesystem storage also uses the DeltaNet state. There are 1,024 slots holding up to 512 files. Moreover, this storage is persistent if you save the state at the end of a conversation with the LLM.

Due to its expanded resource use, Qwenputer has basically doubled the size of the underlying Qwen 3.5 4B LLM to almost 19GB. Thus, Agrawal recommends a workstation with 24GB of VRAM or more for testing Qwenputer in its current version. Efforts are being made to streamline coding in Qwenputer, as well as make it run faster.

The project is experimental. One gets the impression that Agrawal built Qwenputer primarily as an experiment to explore what is possible, rather than to solve a specific problem. Nevertheless, the creation of this custom LLM raises some interesting concepts and makes the mind wander regarding potential practical applications.

In addition to the above-linked blog, you can learn more about Qwenputer from its MIT-licensed code on GitHub. If you want to jump straight in and tinker with this fascinating project, you can now grab this LLM from Hugging Face.

#10335. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time never gets old

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The franchise has evolved since 1998, but the first 3D Zelda stands up incredibly well in its Switch 2 remake.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom. As a result, Zelda has never been bigger, and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past. Or so it seemed.

For one of the biggest Switch 2 exclusives so far, Nintendo has gone back to Ocarina of Time, which originally launched on the N64 in 1998. It’s one of the most influential and revered games in the long-running franchise, a game that showed that the classic Zelda formula — one that used a large world to connect a handful of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons, creating a grand adventure — could work in three dimensions. Now Ocarina has been remade for the Switch 2 in a way that accomplishes exactly what a good remake is designed to do: preserve the core of the original experience while making it more accessible for modern audiences. And it shows there’s still some life left in the traditional Zelda formula.

The story remains unchanged from the original. It’s a third-person action-adventure game where you play as a little forest dweller named Link who gets pulled into an adventure to save the fantasy realm of Hyrule from a villain named Ganondorf. That’s true of basically every Zelda title, and here the twist comes from a musical instrument (the titular flute-like ocarina) imbued with magical powers. Over the course of the game you learn songs that can change the weather, warp you across the landscape, mess with the flow of time, and more.

The original Ocarina was renowned both for its large 3D world and for the intricacy of its dungeons, which required using the ocarina, along with various other items, to solve puzzles in clever ways. At a certain point you’re even jumping back and forth in time, navigating spaces as both tiny Link and his adult version. The challenge steadily grows in complexity right up until you face Ganondorf in his castle, forcing you to use a huge range of items at your disposal.

The most notable difference in the remake is how it looks. Gone are the blocky, fuzzy N64-era graphics, which have been replaced with something that blurs the line between fantasy art and realism. While it’s not a fully open world like Breath of the Wild, this version of Hyrule, which has a large open field that connects a series of dungeons and villages, is still incredibly lifelike; everything from rushing water in a lake to the swaying grass outside of a ranch looks and moves in realistic ways. The flip side is that, while the characters are more detailed than before, they’ve been rendered with a style inspired by puppets and stage shows. It’s a tricky balancing act that the game mostly nails. The characters look like exaggerated caricatures, but at the same time they’re imbued with such a level of detail that they don’t feel out of place against the more realistic backdrops. Link is the best example; while his face almost looks like a porcelain figure, his outfit is like something a real adventurer would wear, made by weaving together grasses found in Kokiri Forest, where he lives.

It looks great in practice — although Ocarina does suffer from some frustratingly dark areas, like in most modern games — and it also sets the remake apart from the rest of modern Zelda adventures. The Breath of the Wild line has a fantastical, Studio Ghibli-inspired look, while the top-down spinoffs have cutesy, toylike graphics. Ocarina splits the difference and comes out looking like something distinct, yet unmistakably Zelda. The Switch 2 graphics also do a great job of heightening the emotion. There’s an incredible sense of grandeur when you first walk into the stark Temple of Time, with a single ray of light illuminating the dark interior. Iconic moments like wandering blindly through the desert take on a new sense of tension and terror because of how the game looks as sand whips around you, obscuring your view of the harsh landscape. Fighting Dark Link on a foggy, desolate beach was enough to get my heart racing.

Perhaps more important than the visual update is a number of smart gameplay changes. Early 3D games can be awkward to play now because designers were still working out how best to navigate 3D spaces. The Ocarina remake fixes this in a few ways. For one thing, you now have free camera control, making it possible to look anywhere by moving the right stick, just like in any modern game. This makes it easier to keep your eye on enemies around you or spot important details for solving a puzzle. The game now also lets you jump whenever you want — in the original Link could only jump at designated points — which makes moving around in spaces feel less restrictive. Other modern touches include being able to equip items quickly with the D-pad instead of having to go to the pause menu, and the “threads of time,” which is a fancy name for a tool that tracks your quests so you can more easily figure out what to do next.

As an example of how much these tweaks can impact the experience, let’s revisit the infamous Water Temple. Over the years since Ocarina of Time first launched, this dungeon has become known primarily for being extremely difficult. It involves constantly playing a song to make the water rise and fall so you can access different levels, while also frequently equipping iron boots that cause Link to sink to the bottom when necessary. With the original controls this was tedious and frustrating. But I didn’t find it difficult at all in the remake; I could quickly equip the boots whenever I needed to, and the camera allowed me to clearly see what I needed to do. The Water Temple was always a well-designed dungeon hindered by the technology of the time. In the remake, I could fully appreciate what the developers were going for.

There are a handful of other changes — expanded dialogue, the ability to hum songs into the Switch 2’s microphone, the fairy Navi thankfully toning down her annoying hints — and they all build toward the same goal: enhancing the original without changing its essence. Unlike a lot of classic games, the original Ocarina of Time is still relatively easy to play; it’s available through a Switch Online subscription, and the 3DS version from 2011 remains a great port. But the remake does enough to make it the ideal way to play, particularly for that big new audience of Zelda fans that started with Breath of the Wild. More importantly, it’s proof that Zelda can be many things simultaneously. And that’s an exciting prospect for Hyrule’s future.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on the Switch 2 on November 5th.
