Creality’s K3 is a solid entry into the swelling tool changer market, but without the lid and TPU Kit ready at launch, we’re left wondering what else this machine is capable of doing. The overly large spool holders impose a frustrating limit on the brands of filament you can use. Still, this is a good printer for fans of the Creality lineup who only need PLA or PETG.

Top hat and TPU printing kit not available at launch

Spool holders are too large for many 3rd party spools

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Creality has finally caught up with the tool changer fad, presenting us with a speedy, four-nozzle system named “KliTek” mounted on a Creality K3. Tool changers are the way to go, since they do not compromise speed for color and eliminate the need to waste your filament in the form of “printer poop.” The K3 is still programmed to create a purge tower on multicolor prints, but this is a small fraction of the filament wasted using any type of AMS-style color system.

The new KliTek nozzle system supports printing with different-sized nozzles in the same print, which sounds more useful than I actually found practical. Users will also be able to blend colors in Creality Print, a trick picked up from Snapmaker’s open-source Full Spectrum. This method creates the optical illusion of new colors by stacking very thin layers of filament.

The tool-changing system works very well and never dropped or misplaced a tool during the review. Creality has tucked 37 sensors inside the printer, with 12 dedicated to the nozzle swapping process alone. No, I’m not going to name all of them, but they do work. I didn’t get a single bad print during the review, even when running at higher speeds.

However, the K3 looks suspiciously like a Snapmaker U1 clone, departing from the black and grey aesthetic of the K1 and K2 3D printers. It has conveniently placed, side-mounted spool holders that are a tad too large for many 3rd party brands of filament. We’re not sure if they’re trying to herd us towards a walled garden of Creality plastics, or if they simply didn’t check out all the options.

Unfortunately, the Creality K3 needs a lid for printing high-temperature filaments, and this “tophat” was not ready at the time of the review. Creality says the top hat will be packaged with a TPU Kit to enable the printing of super soft materials.

The K3 is currently on preorder with a price tag of $849. The competition for affordable tool changers is pretty stiff, and Creality hasn’t brought anything new to the table, which is keeping the K3 off our list of the very best 3D printers you can buy. But if you’re a fan of the Creality ecosystem, it’s a welcome addition to the fleet.

260 x 260 x 260 mm (10.23 x 10.23 x 10.23 in)

PLA/PETG/PCTG/TPU/CF and GF filled (up to 300 °C)

Double-sided Textured PEI steel flex plate (up to 100 °C)

482 x 420 x 536 mm (18.97 x 16.53 x 21.10 in)

The Creality K3 comes with everything you need to assemble and maintain your printer. The included tool kit has hex keys, side cutters, grease, and a nice nozzle cleaner. There is also a paper copy of the quick installation guide and a 200g spool of white Creality filament.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Creality K3 has four tools, each with a built-in ceramic heater, nozzle with a hardened steel insert, and filament path. The KliTek system supports printing with different nozzle sizes and different materials in the same print. Like the Prusa/Bondtech INDX, the extruder and cooling fan are mounted on a single toolhead.

The rest of the Creality K3 shares its design with the K2. The printer has a solid metal frame clad in white plastic and a glass door with dampened hinges. The motion system is Core XY, with a linear rail for the X axis and linear rods for the Y axis. The bed rides on four linear rods driven by 2 lead screws belted to a single stepper motor on the bottom of the printer. Parts cooling is provided by a blower fan in the toolhead and a large side-mounted blower fan mounted on the left side of the case. The stock Creality K3 comes with an open top, so chamber cooling is not an issue. Unfortunately, this makes the printer rather loud.

The Creality K3 has a 720p camera located at the top right of the printer, which does a great job providing print monitoring from the device tab in the slicer and the Creality Cloud app. There is also an AI camera that monitors for build plate detection, foreign object detection, and spaghetti detection. There were no false positives during the test.

We did not get to review the special TPU kit, which will allow the machine to run super soft TPU, which is becoming quite trendy for those interested in printing shoes. The kit will replace the CFS Nano material handler with a CFS Flex and add dry boxes for the filament and a special high-flow nozzle. The kit will be bundled with a lid/ tophat with ventilation and air filtration.

The Creality K3 arrives with some assembly required. After removing the packing material, you need to remove the four screws securing the bed for shipping, and there is a nice reminder to do this when first firing up the printer.

The spool holders twist into the printer’s side panels and are numbered to match the filament slots. Two PTFE guide brackets, also numbered, need to be secured to the rear of the printer with M4x6 screws, as does the bracket for the CFS Nano. There is a communication cable that runs from the rear of the printer to the CFS Nano as well.

The tool cables attach to the top of the printer with 2 M4x12 screws each, with the PTFE tubes running to the CFS Nano. The toolhead communication cable is attached with M3x5 screws on the toolhead and M4x8 screws on the right side of the printer. Attaching PTFE guide tubes from the side brackets up to the CFS Nano completes the assembly.

The Creality K3 does an excellent job calibrating and bed leveling as part of its initial self-check. Bed leveling can be repeated at the start of each print.

Loading filament into the Creality K3 is pretty simple. Filament is inserted into a port on the side bracket, which guides it up to the CFS Nano, which does the rest. The filament waits in the tube until called for by a print job. It is then loaded into the tool.

To unload, the tool is selected from the printer’s screen. The printer then cuts the filament and retracts it out of the tool, and it can be manually pulled out of the CFS Nano the rest of the way.

All four filament slots can read RFID tags in the spools to load information for Creality-branded filament. For other filament brands, the printer will beep to remind you to manually enter the filament type and color.

The latest version of Creality Print 7.3 is available from Creality.com. It is based on the Orca Slicer and Ultimaker Cura Engine. The default settings worked well, and there is a new AI assistant mode, which is still labeled as beta. At the time of the review, the only thing missing for the K3 was a button to map the filaments into the slicer. The button is still there for the earlier K-series printers in the slicer. The slicer does have filament mixing for more color combinations.

A link at the top of the page will take you to Creality’s AI Creation tools and Creality Cloud, Creality’s online file-sharing service. If you don’t like the Cloud, you can export files from the slicer and either move them to the printer with a USB stick or move them over your home network by accessing the printer’s FLUIDD interface. To access FLUIDD, you need to find the IP address of your printer and type that into a browser window, followed by:4408 with no spaces.

The Creality K3 comes with a 200g spool of white Hyper PLA. If you want more colors and materials, you should check out our guide to the best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions.

For the first print, I was going to run a pumpkin fidget toy, so I grabbed a spool of Prusa orange and was really quite cross when it didn’t fit on the preposterously large spool holders. I decided right then to mod the spool holder with the Creality Pika scanner. I took the scan into Tinkercad and reduced the diameter of the spool holder, then ran the new spool holders in Inland basic white using a .2 layer height and an average print speed of 170mm/s. The print took 8 hours and 34 minutes to complete. I do not usually mod printers while reviewing them, but Prusa Orange is perfect for pumpkins.

Below is the original spool holder (left) and the modded version (right).

For my second print, I did a pumpkin fidget toy I found on MakerWorld using Prusa orange PLA, Elegoo green PLA Pro, and Polymaker black HT-PLA Pro. I used a .2 mm layer height and printed with an average speed of 160mm/s; the print took a little over six hours. It came out nice without a hint of overextrusion. I liked it so much I decided to print it again scaled up to 200%. Using the same settings, the larger print took 16 hours and 28 minutes and is also very nice with a good fidget action.

For PETG, I printed a plate of 3 flexy geckos I found on Creality Cloud using Prusa Carmine Red, Prusa Sky Blue, and Bambu Lab basic white PETG. Using a .2mm layer height and running at 180mm/s, the print took 5 hours 45 minutes to complete. The geckos are smooth and clean, plus all of the links work perfectly with no stringing or overextrusion present.

The Creality K3 did not have its special “flex” CFS at the time of review, but I decided to try TPU anyway. I printed some omni wheels for a Death Racer we’re working on in both hard TPU for MFS from Inland and some 95A Inland rainbow TPU. The stock CFS Nano had no trouble pushing these, and the toolhead extruder had no problem with it. It did well. Trouble came when I tried some 90A TPU from Bambu Lab. I’d stick to the harder stuff until the TPU kit is ready.

I did get good prints with the black TPU for AMS and the rainbow 95A filaments. The prints are omni-wheel rollers from the Deathracer project of Michael Baddeley. Both sets of eight rollers were printed at a .2mm layer height at an average speed of 50mm/s and each took a little over 4 hours to print. There was a tiny bit of stringing, but otherwise the rollers are perfect.

The Creality K3 is a terrific printer that should become more capable with accessories like the tophat and TPU kit in the future. The oversized spools are a little annoying, but easily fixed. The only thing I worry about is Creality’s track record of releasing a printer, then introducing a better “pro” or “max” model within four months. I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a six- or eight-color K3 variant before next spring.

At its prelaunch price of $849, it’s $100 more than a similarly equipped, slightly larger Snapmaker U1, which is a tough place to be. It is also the same price as the fully enclosed Flashforge Creator 5 Pro, which we didn’t review, but we did check out the budget model Flashforge Creator 5, which is currently available for $699.

#10300. Top 5 3D Animation Software in 2026

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Choosing the best 3D animation software depends on your experience, budget, and creative goals. Some tools offer complete 3D modeling and animation workflows, while others specialize in professional character animation, visual effects, or AI-powered video creation. This guide compares five options and notes how each fits into web and game projects, so designers and developers can see which one suits their pipeline.

Blender is one of the strongest free options for anyone looking for comprehensive 3D animation software. This open-source application combines modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, rendering, simulation, and compositing in one package.

Blender provides a broad production workflow without requiring users to pay for a standard commercial license. Its active community, learning resources, and add-on ecosystem make it accessible to independent creators. It is suitable for everything from simple animated scenes to complex short films and game assets.

For web and game developers: Blender ships with a glTF 2.0 importer and exporter, and glTF is the format libraries such as three.js load for 3D on the web. See the Blender manual’s glTF page for export options.

Its extensive interface and feature set can feel overwhelming to new users. Learning advanced rigging, lighting, materials, and rendering takes time, and some established studios may have specialized pipelines built around other applications.

Beginners, freelancers, indie game developers, students, and professionals who need a powerful 3D animation tool without a software subscription.

Autodesk Maya is a professional 3D application widely associated with character animation, rigging, film production, and game development. It offers detailed control over character movement and complex animation workflows, making it a strong choice for artists working in established production environments.

Maya provides sophisticated tools for animating characters and managing complex scenes. Its established role in many professional workflows makes it a valuable skill for artists pursuing careers in film, television, and game development. It also offers detailed control over animation timing, character motion, and rig behavior.

Maya generally requires a paid subscription, which can be expensive for hobbyists and independent creators. Its advanced interface also takes time to learn, particularly for users who have never worked with professional 3D software.

Professional animators, film and television artists, game studios, and users who need advanced character animation and rigging capabilities.

Cinema 4D is a 3D modeling, animation, and rendering application known for its motion graphics workflow. It is widely used for commercial visuals, broadcast graphics, product animations, and creative work that combines 3D elements with graphic design.

Cinema 4D is a strong option for designers who want to create polished motion graphics and branded animation. Its MoGraph workflow can make repetitive or complex movements easier to manage, and its integration with common design workflows is helpful for agencies and creative teams.

For web and product designers: Cinema 4D includes a glTF exporter, which helps when a designer needs to hand a 3D model to a developer for the web. Maxon documents the options on its glTF export settings page.

Cinema 4D is a commercial product, so ongoing licensing costs may be a concern. Although it can handle a wide range of 3D work, users focused on highly specialized character animation or procedural visual effects may prefer tools designed around those workflows.

Motion designers, advertising agencies, broadcast artists, product visualization specialists, and creators who regularly produce animated graphics.

Houdini, developed by SideFX, is a 3D software package known for procedural workflows and advanced visual effects. Rather than relying entirely on manually created steps, artists can build systems that generate and modify complex scenes, simulations, and effects.

Houdini offers exceptional flexibility for technical artists and visual-effects specialists. Procedural workflows make it possible to create reusable systems and adjust complex effects efficiently. Its capabilities are particularly valuable when a project needs detailed simulations or large numbers of interconnected elements.

For game developers: SideFX offers Houdini Engine plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine, which let procedural Houdini assets be used inside those engines. SideFX explains the plugins in its Houdini Engine FAQ.

Houdini has a steep learning curve, especially for beginners who are unfamiliar with node-based workflows. Building effective procedural systems requires patience and technical understanding. While free learning options are available, some commercial uses and advanced workflows require an appropriate paid license.

Visual-effects artists, technical directors, simulation specialists, and experienced 3D creators working on demanding film, television, or game projects.

MagicLight.AI is different from the four tools above. It is an AI-powered video creation platform rather than a traditional 3D application, so it produces finished animated videos, not editable 3D scenes, rigs, or game assets. It is included here for readers who want animated storytelling without building a 3D pipeline. It supports AI-generated characters, scene creation, storyboarding, and voice features.

MagicLight.AI can reduce the time and technical effort needed to create animated videos. It is particularly useful for content creators, educators, marketers, and storytellers who want to focus on the script and final message rather than mastering a complex 3D production pipeline.

MagicLight.AI is not a replacement for dedicated 3D software when you need precise control over mesh topology, character rigs, keyframes, physics, or custom 3D scenes. Creators who need editable 3D assets for games or studio production will need a conventional 3D application such as the ones above.

Content creators, educators, and marketers who want to produce animated videos efficiently without learning a traditional 3D animation workflow.

The right software is the one that supports your actual production needs. Before choosing a tool, consider the following factors.

If you want to model objects, build character rigs, and control animation precisely, start with a dedicated 3D application such as Blender or Maya. If your goal is to create animated storytelling videos from scripts or ideas with less manual production work, an AI video tool such as MagicLight.AI may be a more convenient option.

Blender is an excellent starting point if you need a complete 3D toolset without a standard license fee. Houdini also has a free Apprentice edition with restrictions. Maya and Cinema 4D are commercial applications, so compare their current plans against your expected usage before committing.

Different applications suit different workflows. Blender is versatile, Maya excels at character animation, Cinema 4D is well suited to motion graphics, and Houdini is especially powerful for procedural effects. MagicLight.AI is better suited to AI-assisted video production than to detailed, manually controlled 3D scene creation.

Beginners may find Blender’s extensive learning resources helpful, although its broad feature set takes time to master. Maya and Houdini demand more specialized skills for advanced work, while Cinema 4D is often considered by motion designers seeking a more direct design-oriented workflow. AI video tools can reduce the amount of technical setup required, but still require creative direction and review.

Think about where the finished animation will be used. A web project may need a lightweight glTF model. A game project may require exportable 3D assets, rig compatibility, and a game-engine workflow. A commercial motion graphic may depend on rendering and compositing integration. A social video or animated explainer may prioritize turnaround time, narration, subtitles, and scene continuity.

The best 3D animation software in 2026 depends on your budget, experience, and intended output. Blender is the strongest starting point for many users who want a comprehensive free 3D workflow. Autodesk Maya is a compelling option for professional character animation, Cinema 4D suits motion graphics and commercial visuals, and Houdini stands out for procedural effects and complex simulations. MagicLight.AI offers a different approach: it helps creators generate animated videos with AI rather than manually building a traditional 3D production pipeline.

Blender is one of the best free options because it includes modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and other production tools in a single open-source application. It is suitable for beginners as well as experienced artists.

Yes. Free software can support professional-quality work when used effectively. Blender, for example, provides a comprehensive toolset for animation and rendering. The final result depends on the artist’s skills, project requirements, hardware, and production workflow.

Blender is a strong choice for beginners who want to learn traditional 3D modeling and animation without paying for a standard software license. Those who mainly want to create animated videos from stories or scripts may prefer exploring an AI video creation platform such as MagicLight.AI.

Blender and Cinema 4D can both export glTF, a format widely used for 3D on the web. Blender is free, so it is the easiest place to start.

Data centers not owned by the Russian state will have 24 hours to provide access to 10% of their capacity if they are called upon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Owners of non-state data centers in Russia have been told to hold back 10% of their capacity, ready to aid the country's state-owned IT infrastructure should the need arise. That's the message from President Vladimir Putin, with the aim of quickly unlocking additional data center compute capacity in the future if it becomes needed by the state, reports Reuters.

This comes as Russian data centers have become targets for Ukrainian drone attacks in recent weeks, causing huge amounts of damage and affecting state-owned internet services. In early October, drones struck Russia's largest data center in what was the second such attack in as many days. The huge 63-megawatt facility was so badly damaged that multiple modules had to be removed from service completely. At the time, users reported problems with Yandex Mail, Disk, Documents, Pay, and Market despite Yandex claiming that key services remained up and running. Two weeks later, Russia's finance ministry's data center was damaged after Ukrainian drones targeted the facility. It was reportedly home to Russia's tax databases as well as other state registry data.

Now, Putin has told the Digital Development Ministry to inventory all available data center capacity and floor space at privately owned facilities throughout the country. A new government commission will be given the power to order the release of reserved data center capacity. Once ordered to do so, third-party data center owners will have 24 hours to comply. The temporary use of data centers located outside Russia has also been mooted, pending the approval of Russia's Federal Security Service. (FSB)

It isn't just drones that have been targeting Russian data centers. On the same day that news broke of the country's plan to siphon data center capacity from third parties, the Russian Federal State Statistics Service admitted that its servers were hit by cyberattacks that saw 23TB of data stolen. It's reported that the haul includes new data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only.”

Data centers have become a target for Russia, too. It bombed Ukrainian facilities in September of this year, resulting in the loss of internet connectivity for 100,000 households. At the time, a government official noted that Ukraine's internet network is highly decentralized before admitting that users should expect local disruptions to service.

Google has updated its Android distribution numbers with the latest update showing that Android 17 is on just 1% of devices, while Android 16 now makes up the biggest slice of the pie.

Updated as of October 19, Google’s latest Android distribution numbers offer a peek into the rollout speed of Android 17. Having released to Pixel phones in June, the update has been available for roughly four months.

At this point, though, Android 17 makes up just 1% of active Android devices, Google’s data shows.

That’s compared to over 25% for Android 16, which released last year. Android 16 was on 7.5% of devices in Google’s last update in December 2025/January 2026, which landed several months after Google released the update. The timing here requires context, as major players like Samsung have only started widely rolling out their Android 17 updates in the past few weeks and are very unlikely to be included in this 1%.

Fragmentation issues still plague Google's ability to control it's experiences. Seemingly no plans to address.

The growth of Android 16 is pretty impressive, too, as older versions tend to be still be more widely in use at this point in the schedule, but Android 16 has managed to consolidate quite a bit.

Google dropped Android 5 (Lollipop) from its data with this update, with Android 5.1 making up just 0.2% of active devices. Android 11, for reasons unclear, still holds over 10%, while Android 12 has dropped to 9.6%. Android 11 has had a higher share in the past few updates.

Update 11/2/2026 3:00 PM ET: As it turns out, the ultimate parent company and holder of all Tachyum intellectual property is Cayman Islands-based Tachyum Ltd., which controls U.S.-based Tachyum Inc., which in turn controls Slovakia-based Tachyum s.r.o. that is responsible for the lion’s share of Tachyum’s development of the Prodigy universal processor. This means that while Tachyum Inc. and Tachyum s.r.o. can be declared insolvent and liquidated, Tachyum Ltd. can continue operations, establish new entities and continue developing Prodigy.However, the Cayman Islands company holding Prodigy-related patents is itself the target of liquidation proceedings. Therefore, the Slovak subsidiary’s bankruptcy cannot necessarily protect Prodigy’s intellectual property from creditors. If Tachyum Ltd. is liquidated, the control over the Prodigy patents could pass to court-appointed liquidators, who could sell them to repay creditors. While the current Tachyum management could buy Prodigy’s patents back cheaply, they would have to compete with other interested buyers and satisfy the applicable sale requirements. In any case, this could be the end of the road for Tachyum.

Tachyum, the company behind the overpromised and overhyped universal Prodigy processor, has filed for bankruptcy in Bratislava, Slovakia, reports Forbes (as observed by @System360Cheese). The filing follows a court order initiating bankruptcy proceeding after the company repeatedly missed its development and production milestones — but there are still theoretical chances that development of the processor will continue.

Despite eight years of development and numerous promises, Tachyum has yet to demonstrate working Prodigy silicon. Tachyum introduced Prodigy in 2018, targeting a 2019 tape-out and 2020 commercial availability. But the company repeatedly postponed the processor's launch, first to 2021, then to 2022, 2023, 2024, and eventually 2025.

Meanwhile, Prodigy's specifications changed considerably along the line: The original 64-core design evolved into a 128-core processor manufactured on a 5nm-class process technology, then a 192-core chip with 16 DDR5 memory channels. In late 2025, Tachyum announced yet another radical redesign: a chiplet-based architecture with 1,024 cores, 24 DDR5 memory channels, and TDP of 1,600W manufactured using TSMC's 2nm-class node. The redesign would require substantial additional development work and would have delayed commercial availability until 2030 or beyond.

According to court documents cited by Forbes, Tachyum Slovakia itself filed for bankruptcy on October 22, 2026, without waiting for a petition from creditors seeking to recover unpaid debts. The Bratislava III Municipal Court subsequently initiated bankruptcy proceedings after determining that the company's petition met the legal requirements. Under Slovak law, a company that voluntarily files for bankruptcy is presumed insolvent, according to Forbes, so technically Tachyum Slovakia is bankrupt.

If the court formally declares Tachyum bankrupt, a court-appointed trustee will take control of the company's assets, which could then be sold to repay creditors. We do not know at this point what these assets are, but theoretically they may include intellectual property related to its Prodigy processor, patents, and other technologies in addition to hardware used for development. Unless Tachyum secures additional financing or finds a buyer that can fund further development, work on Prodigy could effectively end.

Bankruptcy proceedings against Tachyum's Slovak entity do not necessarily mean that its affiliated companies elsewhere will also cease operations. Furthermore, the company's IP could survive under new ownership (if the company finds a buyer, or transfers IP ownership to another entity), which could theoretically let Prodigy development to continue. Nevertheless, the bankruptcy filing casts serious doubt on Tachyum's ability or intention to bring its long-delayed processor to market.

Theoretically, Tachyum's owners could potentially use bankruptcy proceedings to shed the company's debts, acquire its intellectual property through another legal entity, and resume Prodigy development. There are other options too.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Although most of Tachyum development activities are concentrated in Slovakia, Tachyum Slovakia is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based Tachyum Inc. according to Dennik N. If the American parent company owns the Prodigy IP, while the Slovak subsidiary employs engineers, conducts development, and accumulates debts, bankruptcy could enable the group to eliminate a substantial portion of those liabilities without losing its most valuable technological assets. In short, Tachyum's Slovak subsidiary could disappear along with much of its unpaid debt, while the American parent retains Prodigy IP and attempts to commercialize it somehow in the future. If the Slovak subsidiary owns the IP, the American parent could theoretically buy it from the bankruptcy estate and attempt to commercialize it eventually. Meanwhile, there is another complication: The American parent has reportedly faced pressure from its own creditors, some of whom have requested its liquidation, according to Dennik N. In this case, the destiny of the Prodigy IP is completely unclear.

For now, the future of Prodigy may depend on who actually owns Prodigy's intellectual property — Tachyum Inc. in the U.S. or Tachyum Slovakia — and whether the American subsidiary continues to exist or gets liquidated. The answer could determine whether this bankruptcy represents the end of Prodigy or a restructuring of the Tachyum group with the aim to continue development.

#10291. How to Test Location-Aware APIs with FastAPI and PostGIS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Catch coordinate-order bugs, distance mistakes, boundary cases, and bad spatial assumptions before they reach production.

A location endpoint can return HTTP 200 and still be wrong by kilometers. That is the uncomfortable part of testing geospatial APIs: ordinary API checks tell you whether the request worked, not whether the geography is correct.

Spatial bugs can look harmless in code review. Latitude and longitude get reversed. A radius value is treated as degrees instead of meters. A query works near one city but behaves differently elsewhere because the geometry column uses the wrong type. The JSON is valid, the tests are green, and the map is still wrong.

In this tutorial, you will build a small FastAPI endpoint backed by PostGIS and then test the spatial behavior directly. The examples use deterministic fixtures positioned at known distances, so the tests verify geography rather than only response structure.

The API exposes one endpoint: GET /places/nearby. A client sends longitude, latitude, and a radius in meters. The service returns nearby places as GeoJSON features, ordered by distance.

The useful part is not the endpoint itself. The useful part is the test strategy. We will check coordinate validation, exact distance boundaries, GeoJSON coordinate order, and the database query that turns a radius into a spatial filter.

Use a geography column when the API is answering human-scale distance questions in meters. PostGIS can then calculate on the ellipsoid instead of treating longitude and latitude as flat Cartesian coordinates.

The endpoint below validates longitude, latitude, and radius with Pydantic, then sends a parameterized query to PostgreSQL. The SQL uses ST_DWithin to filter candidates and ST_Distance to return the measured distance.

The API accepts lon and lat as separate named parameters. That removes ambiguity at the HTTP boundary. GeoJSON still uses [longitude, latitude] when the response is created.

Hard-coding two real businesses and hoping their distance is approximately right makes a fragile test. A better approach is to create test points at exact distances from a fixed origin.

PostGIS can generate those fixtures with ST_Project. In the test database, create one point 500 meters away, one 950 meters away, and one 1,500 meters away. Now a 1,000-meter query has an unambiguous expected result: the first two belong in the response and the third does not.

This is the first test that actually proves something spatial. It is not checking that the endpoint returns a list. It is checking that the 1-kilometer contract means what the API says it means.

GeoJSON coordinates are longitude first, latitude second. Many developers naturally think latitude first because that is how coordinates are commonly spoken. A validation layer can catch the most obvious reversal before the database ever sees it.

Longitude must be between -180 and 180. Latitude must be between -90 and 90. That will not catch every reversal, because both numbers may sometimes fall inside both ranges, but it catches a large class of failures and gives clients a useful error instead of a misleading map.

A response can be syntactically valid JSON and still violate the GeoJSON contract. Assert the geometry type and the coordinate order. For a known query point, longitude should appear in element zero and latitude in element one.

Spatial boundaries deserve their own tests. A place at 999 meters should be included in a 1,000-meter search. A place at 1,001 meters should not. A place exactly at the boundary should behave consistently with the predicate you chose.

ST_DWithin includes features whose distance is less than or equal to the supplied threshold, so document that behavior and test it explicitly.

Unit tests are useful for request validation, but mocking the repository layer removes the most important part of this API: PostGIS itself. Keep a small integration-test database and run at least a few tests against the real extension.

That catches mistakes that mocks cannot: geography versus geometry behavior, SRID mismatches, spatial indexes, units, and changes to SQL functions. A location API is one of the cases where a cheap database integration test buys a lot of confidence.

Correctness is only half the story. A radius endpoint that scans every feature will work in development and become painful at production scale. Add a GiST index and inspect the query plan.

The exact plan depends on your data and PostgreSQL version, but you should see the spatial index participating in candidate filtering. Treat an accidental sequential scan on a large production table as a regression worth investigating.

For a real project, I would split the tests into two groups. Fast validation tests run on every commit. PostGIS integration tests run in CI with a temporary PostgreSQL/PostGIS service.

The CI gate should cover invalid coordinates, zero or negative radius values, known-distance fixtures, boundary behavior, GeoJSON output, and at least one query-plan or performance sanity check for larger datasets.

This is more work than asserting status_code == 200, but it tests the thing users actually care about: whether the API's answer is geographically true.

Location APIs fail in ways ordinary web tests are not designed to notice. The response can have the right schema, the database call can succeed, and every field can look reasonable while the location itself is wrong.

The fix is not a giant testing framework. Start with a few spatial invariants you can prove: known distances, valid coordinate ranges, correct GeoJSON order, deterministic boundary behavior, and real PostGIS integration tests. Those checks turn geography from an assumption into something your CI pipeline can verify.

OpenAI plans community agreements and infrastructure commitments as it prepares to rebrand data centers amid growing public opposition

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI is reportedly preparing a major public relations campaign to influence how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as “AI Compute Campuses,” Axios reports. The initiative comes ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and forms a broader effort to influence the debate around AI before the 2028 presidential race. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, noted that the midterms would be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” He expects AI to be a major issue for presidential candidates as the technology raises concerns over its impact on jobs, the economy, and the environment.

The proposed terminology change by OpenAI has been ongoing since August as the company focuses on promoting safeguards for the powerful technology, which Lehane described as “speed limits.” The proposed AI compute campuses is particularly interesting as it comes as opposition to large data centers accelerates across the U.S. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. OpenAI hopes to address these concerns through community agreements and a different way of presenting the infrastructure. “Compute campuses better describe the role of the infrastructure we are rebuilding for AI," a company spokesperson separately stated. He added that these projects represent long term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs.

The latest proposal follows similar efforts by other technology companies to improve their relationship with communities hosting their infrastructure. In January, Microsoft announced a community-first approach, promising to cover electricity cost increases associated with its data centers, and invest in local infrastructure and jobs. However, while changing the name may be easier, changing public opinion may bring some headaches. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed are opposed to having a new data center built in their community. Another report in August detailed how negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently take place behind non-disclosure agreements, leaving residents without access to important project information.

The resistance has also affected actual construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have already moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle’s $16 billion Stargate project went ahead with their project in Sanile township despite local opposition. Meanwhile, Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback.

OpenAI is not alone in trying to reshape the language surrounding AI. President Donald Trump has previously pushed for terminology change, directing Federal agencies and urging AI companies to replace artificial intelligence with ‘super intelligence.’ Trump announced the change in late September arguing that the word "artificial" made the technology sound "fake." His administration subsequently instructed state department employees to use super intelligence or SI in official directives, websites, reports and policy documents.

Some technology executives have also embraced the terminology. Nvidia CEO Huang has previously referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories" while Elon musk announced plans to rename his AI company SpaceXAI to SpacexSI last month. Meta, meanwhile, established Meta superintelligence labs in 2025, and Microsoft has also assembled a team focused on developing superintelligence. OpenAI’s proposed terminology will now face a more difficult test than simply finding a name as communities will still want answers about the raised issues. Lehane, however, acknowledged that public scrutiny is part of the process saying, “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects.”

#10286. Nothing OS 5.0 (Android 17) is now rolling out to Nothing 4a and 3a series phones

Nothing Phone 3a, 3a Pro, 4a, and 4a Pro owners are in for a treat with the Nothing OS 5.0 update, now rolling out to all four phone models globally.

The Nothing OS 5.0 update began rolling out to Nothing Phone (3) owners just a few weeks ago, and now the stable build is ready for Nothing’s more budget-minded phones. The Nothing Phone (3a), Nothing Phone (3a) Pro, Nothing Phone (4a), and Nothing Phone (4a) Pro are now in line to get the big update, which includes a slew of new features alongside all the goodies that come with Android 17.

As is the case with all firmware updates, the Nothing OS 5.0 update is rolling out in batches to owners of the aforementioned four Nothing Phone models, so if you don’t see the update right away, just keep an eye out for the notification over the next few days.

Alternatively, you can navigate to system settings, scroll down to system, tap system updates, and then hit the check for updates button. My Nothing Phone (4a) Pro doesn’t have the Nothing OS 5.0 update yet, so be aware that yours might not either.

The Nothing OS 5.0 update includes a new Glyph app, which offloads the Glyph Interface features to a dedicated app with a tweaked UI. Quick Settings now supports split mode, so if you like the iOS-style split notification and Quick Settings concept, you can use that here. The home screen is now easier to arrange and organize with bulk icon management, and three new widgets (Collector, Away Time, and Glyph Timer) can now be used.

You’ll find a new Translucent theme selectable system-wide, as well as new lock screen customization options to play with. The camera UI has been refreshed once again, and a new Dual-view Video mode lets you record with the front and rear cameras simultaneously. There’s even a new yellow AI Processing status indicator that alerts you when your phone is processing potentially sensitive AI data.

See the full Nothing OS 5.0 update changelog here: Nothing Phone (3a) series, Nothing Phone (4a), Nothing Phone (4a) Pro.

Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.

Update: Amazon just closed my account.Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist. Be careful!November 1, 2026

Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.

The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.

Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”

He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”

Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.

With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.

Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.

Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.

Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

#10283. 7 Checks Developers Should Make So AI Search Can Read Their Site

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Search results now include AI-written answers that cite pages, and people increasingly ask chat tools for recommendations instead of scrolling a list of links. For developers, this does not mean learning a new discipline. It means making sure the basics are in place so that crawlers and answer engines can reach, read and quote your pages.

Most problems are plain engineering mistakes: a blocked crawler, a page that renders nothing without JavaScript, or markup that disagrees with the visible text. This article covers seven checks, including one script you can run against your own robots.txt.

AI features in search do not need a special file or a special format. Google's documentation on AI features and your website states that a page needs to be indexed and eligible to appear in Search with a snippet, and that there are no additional technical requirements. It also says there is no need for new AI-specific files or special schema.org markup.

So start with the fundamentals. Check for accidental noindex tags after a deploy, confirm important pages return a 200 status, and make sure staging settings never reach production.

Answer engines read text. If your key information lives in images, canvas elements or content that only appears after a client-side script runs, a crawler may never see it. View the page source and the rendered HTML, and compare them. Product names, prices, definitions and steps should be present as real text.

Structured data helps systems understand a page, but only if it agrees with what visitors see. SitePoint's guide to JSON-LD for developers shows how to build markup that search and AI systems can parse. Generate it from the same data that renders the page, and validate it after every template change. Markup that contradicts the visible text is worse than no markup.

Your robots.txt decides which crawlers may fetch your pages. Some sites block AI crawlers deliberately, and others block them by accident through a broad rule. SitePoint's technical guide to working with a marketing agency lists robots.txt decisions about which crawlers may access the site among the checks developers should own.

This small function reads a robots.txt string and reports which common AI-related crawlers are blocked from the whole site:

Run it against your live robots.txt. If a crawler appears in the list and you did not intend that, fix the rule. Note that blocking a crawler is a legitimate choice. The goal is that it is a decision and not an accident.

Developers can check access and markup, but judging how a brand shows up in AI answers often needs someone who tracks that area full time. An AI search consultant such as Austin Heaton works on answer engine optimization.

Traffic from AI features in Google Search is included in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Set up that report, tag your own campaigns with consistent UTM parameters, and watch referral traffic from chat tools in your analytics. You cannot control the answers, but you can see whether clicks arrive.

Most visibility problems appear after a deployment: a template change drops the structured data, a new rule blocks a crawler, or a redesign hides text behind a script. Add a small post-deploy test for the checks above. A failing robots.txt check or a missing JSON-LD block should stop the release before a crawler finds the problem.

Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup for AI search? Google's documentation says no new AI-specific files or special structured data are needed for its AI features. Standard indexing and crawling requirements apply.

Should I block AI crawlers? That depends on your goals. Blocking is a legitimate choice, but make it deliberately and review it regularly.

Where do I see AI search traffic? For Google, AI feature traffic is counted in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Other tools show up as referrals in your analytics.

Making a site readable to AI search is mostly ordinary engineering: keep pages indexable, put key content in text, keep structured data consistent, decide crawler access on purpose, measure what you can and retest after every release. The robots.txt check above is small, but it catches one of the most common accidental blocks before it costs you visibility.

#10282. What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar Justice" to Staples' gift card bonanza.

The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

#10279. Stop Overpaying for App Builders: How to Build Premium Websites and Web Apps with AI

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a professional website or web application no longer requires a large development budget. AI coding agents have changed how developers approach design, development, and deployment. Yet many founders and freelancers still assume they need to pay for a dedicated AI app builder before they can create something polished.

Visual app builders such as Lovable and Bolt can help users turn ideas into working prototypes quickly. Their convenience is valuable, especially for beginners. However, subscriptions, usage limits, and additional services can increase the cost of building and maintaining a project.

There is another approach: use AI coding agents with a development stack you control.

I discovered this firsthand when I moved beyond WordPress development and built a CRM from scratch.

Instead of relying on a dedicated app builder, I used Claude, Next.js, Firebase Firestore, Tailwind CSS, Git, and Vercel.

The experience changed how I think about the cost of building software.

App builders reduce the technical barriers to software development. You describe what you want, and the platform generates interfaces, application logic, and sometimes database integrations.

The problem is not the tools themselves. It is assuming that a paid app builder is the only practical way to build a professional product.

Consider what happens when a project grows. You may need more iterations, additional integrations, more control over the generated code, or a different deployment setup. Depending on the platform and plan, these requirements can introduce additional costs or constraints.

There is also a difference between creating a prototype and building a maintainable application. Generating a dashboard is relatively straightforward. Ensuring that its permissions, database operations, error handling, and security work correctly requires additional engineering.

Paying for an app builder does not automatically solve these problems.

Before subscribing to another platform, ask a more useful question: Am I paying for a capability I genuinely need, or am I paying for a workflow I could manage directly?

I have designed more than 100 websites and helped clients implement over 12 CRM and ERP systems. My experience gave me a strong understanding of website design, business workflows, and the practical problems software needs to solve.

However, configuring existing platforms is different from developing an application from scratch.

When I decided to build a CRM, I wanted to learn the entire process, from writing code to managing data and deploying the application. I also wanted to avoid spending money on a dedicated app-builder subscription when I could use AI coding tools with a more flexible development environment.

I chose Claude as my AI coding agent and used a stack built around Next.js, Firebase Firestore, Tailwind CSS, Git, and Vercel.

This approach helped me move from requirements to implementation without depending on a single visual app-building platform. I also saved more than $1,000 in potential app-builder costs and related expenses compared with the approach I had considered.

That figure reflects my own project and spending decisions. It is not a guarantee that every developer will save the same amount.

More importantly, I gained practical experience with API integrations, application security, performance, and user experience. Those lessons became part of my technical portfolio.

You do not need to reproduce my exact stack for every project. The important idea is to choose tools that work together and give you an appropriate level of control.

An AI coding agent can help generate components, implement features, explain unfamiliar code, and investigate errors.

I used Claude to accelerate implementation and work through development challenges. Instead of asking it to build the entire application in one prompt, I worked through smaller tasks, reviewed the output, and refined the results.

The developer still needs to understand the requirements and verify the generated code. AI can accelerate development, but it cannot guarantee correctness.

Next.js provided the framework for building the web application. It supports structured development, routing, and different approaches to rendering and application logic.

For developers who want more control than a visual builder provides, working directly with a framework also makes it easier to understand how the application is organized.

Firestore provided the database layer for my project. Its document-based data model and integration with the Firebase ecosystem made it a practical choice for the application.

However, using a managed database does not eliminate the need to design data structures carefully, configure access rules, and evaluate query performance as usage grows.

A premium-looking interface depends on more than colors and typography. Spacing, consistency, responsiveness, accessibility, and clear user flows all influence the result.

Tailwind CSS helped me build and refine the interface using utility classes, making iterative design changes easier to manage.

Git allowed me to track changes, review revisions, and recover from problematic updates. Vercel provided the deployment environment and a convenient workflow for connecting releases to the codebase.

Together, these tools supported a development process that was not tied to a dedicated app-builder subscription.

A low-cost stack is only useful if the development process is disciplined.

Start by defining the application's purpose, primary users, and essential features. Then create a simple design system covering typography, spacing, colors, buttons, forms, and navigation.

Build one feature at a time. Ask the AI agent to explain its implementation, review important changes, and test each feature before expanding the application.

For a website, pay attention to responsive layouts, accessibility, loading speed, and search engine requirements. For a web application, also test authentication, permissions, database operations, and error handling.

Finally, deploy early enough to test the application in a realistic environment. Keep the code in version control and make sure you understand how to update, maintain, and recover the application.

These steps matter more than choosing whichever AI tool is currently receiving the most attention.

No. App builders can be excellent choices when speed, simplicity, and minimal setup matter most.

A founder validating an idea may benefit from launching a prototype quickly. A nontechnical user may prefer a managed platform over maintaining a codebase. A team may also find that a paid subscription costs less than the time required to manage its own development environment.

The right decision depends on the project.

If you need extensive customization, want direct control over your code, or expect to develop the application further, an AI coding agent combined with a conventional development stack may offer greater flexibility.

Compare the total cost of ownership rather than the subscription price alone. Include development time, hosting, database usage, API costs, security, maintenance, and the effort required to change platforms later.

AI has made software development more accessible, but accessibility does not mean every project needs another subscription.

My experience building a CRM taught me that a coding agent, a well-chosen technology stack, and a structured development process can be a practical alternative to a dedicated app builder.

The goal should not be to avoid spending money at all costs. It should be to spend where the investment creates genuine value.

Before paying for another tool, explore what you can accomplish with AI-assisted coding and tools you control. You may discover that the biggest limitation is not your budget, but your willingness to learn a different way of building.

Build with the tools that fit your project—not simply the tools that make the first demo easiest.

#10276. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform rated 4.8/5 on G2 and used by 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users. It covers candidate sourcing, outreach, interview scheduling and a recruiting CRM in one workspace, for solo recruiters through multi-recruiter firms.

#10271. State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Relatively small data breaches in India can turn quite serious, thanks to a sophisticated underground market for trading PII.

An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
