#10242. The Privacy Risks of Browser Extensions: What Developers Should Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The extension a developer installed three years ago can probably read everything they do in the browser today.

General online security advice from VPNpro and similar guides cover the network side of staying safe, but they cannot see what an extension does inside the browser. That layer is more the developer's responsibility. The risk is complicated, but the fix is simple: request fewer permissions, narrower host access, and less data, and review every update. Here is a walkthrough of each.

Think about what a developer has open on a normal day: a cloud console, a staging dashboard, a private repo, maybe webmail. One over-permissioned extension sees all of it.

The most common mistake is asking for broad access early and planning to trim it later. Later rarely arrives.

A manifest like this should raise eyebrows:

A developer who cannot justify a permission in a short sentence likely shouldn't include the permission in the build.

Host permissions deserve their own attention because they define how far the extension can reach. A few habits make a real difference:

This also helps adoption. People hesitate when an extension asks to read every site they visit. A narrow request looks, and is, more trustworthy.

Analytics and error logging are where good intentions leak. A crash report that includes the full page URL may contain a session token in the query string. A “usage event” may capture page titles from internal tools.

The most secure approach is to collect only the data a feature needs and to process the data locally if possible. When data has to be sent, it should be stripped down to the absolute minimum. Avoid sending query strings, and truncate URLs to the domain name where possible. Never send page content if it is not absolutely necessary.

Remote code is another trap. Manifest V3 restricts remotely hosted code for a good reason. A script fetched at runtime can modify its behavior after the fact, and one can’t audit what it will do in the future. Bundle everything and the code that is reviewed will be identical to the code that is run.

A good extension today can become a risky one next year. Two patterns keep repeating.

Ownership changes. Popular extensions get sold, and the new owner ships an update with tracking or worse. The Great Suspender, a widely used tab tool, ended up flagged as malware after a change of hands.

Compromised publisher accounts. If an attacker phishes the developer account, they can push a malicious update to every existing user. Cyberhaven’s extension was hit by a phished administrator account in late December 2024.

The defenses are mostly boring, which is a good sign. Hardware-key two-factor authentication on the publisher account, a short list of people allowed to publish, and a review step before each release stops most of it. Lockfiles, pinned versions and regular dependency audits cover the code side.

Teams that only install extensions can apply the same thinking. Keep an approved list, review updates that change permissions, and remove anything nobody uses. Following security news is worthwhile too, since incidents involving popular extensions tend to be reported publicly.

It is only one layer, though. A VPN protects traffic in transit. It does nothing about an add-on that reads page content inside the browser, so it never replaces a proper permission review.

Simpler habits do more here. A separate browser profile for development keeps test extensions away from personal accounts. Fake or low-privilege accounts for testing avoid exposing real credentials. And installers for any tool, VPN clients included, should come from the official site or store, never from a mirror.

Safe extensions come down to restraint. Ask for less access, collect less data, send less off the device, and explain more to the user. Developers who treat every permission as a liability end up with extensions people can trust, and teams that review what they install avoid the worst surprises.

Critical global infrastructure under threat

China is loitering over undersea cables in “gray-zone” warfare against neighboring countries, as well as the U.S. and its allies, as it seeks to dominate the South China Sea. Several incidents, reported by Nikkei Asia, suggest the PRC is actively mapping the seafloor for vulnerabilities and using civilian research vessels to do so.

A serious incident in September, for instance, saw the Philippine Coast Guard respond to a Chinese research vessel close to an undersea cable. The vessel reportedly ignored radio contact while broadcasting a false ID before manoeuvring to evade capture. The Philippines, in response, sent its largest vessel to respond. That vessel was spotted 37 nautical miles away from the Batanes province, officially part of the Philippines but claimed by China. The incident also saw a Chinese coastguard ship intervene, with Beijing complaining of harassment afterward, according to the South China Morning Post.

There have been no confirmed reports of Chinese attacks on undersea cables, but it isn’t the first report of Chinese attempts to map the region’s undersea infrastructure. A report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a U.S.-based think tank in Washington, DC, found that Chinese research ships were spending more time loitering near cables than any other nation. Their purpose for doing so is unclear, but the report made clear that the efforts were “disproportionate.”

One thing that the U.S. is certain about, however, is that China has the capability. A U.S. congressional report from 2025 highlighted that China is actively developing techniques to cut cables, pointing out that Chinese research teams had already publicly disclosed the details of electric cutting devices that could sever armored cables as deep as 13,000ft underwater.

Ryan Claffey, a research assistant for the Center for a New American Security, a think tank that specializes in U.S. national security, believes that a coordinated response is required to stop Chinese actions in the region. Writing in the report, Claffey warns that “subsea cables are digital lifelines,” arguing that “the U.S. and its allies must protect them in peacetime to stay connected in crisis.”

The People’s Republic of China has maritime disputes with several countries in the region. It continues to hold a claim over Taiwan, which it views as a breakaway province. It also has disputes with the Philippines, as mentioned earlier, along with Vietnam, Malaysia, and Brunei in the South China Sea, as well as Japan in the East China Sea.

Authoritarian nations like Russia, China and Iran have all stepped up operations against undersea infrastructure in Europe, Asia and the Middle East. Russia, for instance, has used fishing trawlers for nearly five years to loiter over communication cables in Europe. Iran, meanwhile, has threatened to attack undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. attacks it again, describing them as legitimate targets during war.

Following the debut of Apple’s first foldable, an unfortunate trend has emerged among early buyers. A number of users found that their display “cracked” with the display panel dying in the center, all in the exact same way, implying there’s a flaw within Apple’s hinge design.

Apple is replacing affected devices, but it is a somewhat harrowing reminder that this is the company’s first attempt at this hardware.

In an ad for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on Instagram, Samsung says that “folding is nothing new to us” and that “we know a thing or eight.” It cuts right to the chase: “Switch to Galaxy Z Fold8.” The attached imagery then depicts the iPhone Duo’s well-known screen “crack.

It's kind of funny that Apple had 8 years to copy the competition, and still failed spectacularly in such a serious way. The hinge section in question either suffers from material failure (metal breaks when it shouldn't) or its a design failure where the hinge simply breaks under a certain pressure (that a foldable should survive).

Either way this doesn't bode well for Apples QA.

That one was posted to Samsung Canada’s account, while another ad from Samsung Malaysia further takes that up a notch:

Feeling a little FOMO seeing all this talk about durability… oops, we’ve just been busy folding and getting on with our day

#10237. Browser Fingerprinting Explained: How Websites Identify You and How Developers Can Reduce It

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most articles on this topic stop at the scary part. This one is written for people who build websites, so we’ll go a bit further: what goes into a fingerprint, what the collection code actually looks like, and what you can change in your own projects.

Think of a fingerprint as a stack of clues rather than a single value. Your time zone is shared by millions of people. So is your screen resolution. Put twenty clues like that together, though, and the crowd shrinks fast.

Here’s roughly where the clues come from.

HTTP headers. Before any JavaScript runs, every request already tells the server a lot. The User-Agent string and the Accept-Language header give away your browser, its version, your OS, and your languages. Chromium browsers also send Client Hints.

JavaScript APIs. Plenty of everyday APIs leak device details. screen.width and screen.height, navigator.hardwareConcurrency (your CPU core count), navigator.deviceMemory (Chromium only), navigator.platform, and your time zone all add something. Plugin lists used to be a goldmine, but modern browsers now return a fixed, generic list, so that one’s mostly dead.

Rendering. This is the clever bit. Ask two computers to draw the exact same text, and the pixels won’t match perfectly. Fonts, graphics drivers, and the GPU itself all nudge the output slightly. Same browser, same version, different hardware, different result.

Network details. Your IP address, connection type, and even the way your browser sets up a TLS connection can help. IPs change, so these clues are less reliable. Trackers mostly use them to back up a match they already suspect.

How unique does this make you? Back in 2010, the EFF’s Panopticlick study tested around 470,000 browsers and found that about 84% of them had a unique fingerprint. (The project still exists, now called Cover Your Tracks.) Later studies with bigger samples found lower numbers, especially on phones, since a lot of phones share near-identical hardware. The percentages move around, but the basic idea hasn’t changed.

Canvas fingerprinting gets talked about the most. Here’s a basic version:

Read through it and you’d never guess it was tracking code. It draws an orange box, writes some text, and exports the image. The catch is that anti-aliasing and subpixel rendering vary from device to device, so that exported string varies too.

The data URL is long and clunky, so trackers usually hash it into something shorter. With the Web Crypto API, that’s a few extra lines:

WebGL fingerprinting follows the same idea with 3D graphics. A script draws a hidden scene and also reads the WEBGL_debug_renderer_info extension, which can reveal your GPU’s make and model. Audio fingerprinting is sneakier. The script generates a sound, runs it through an AudioContext, and hashes the result. Different audio stacks produce slightly different numbers.

It’s worth remembering that the Canvas API, WebGL, and the Web Audio API were built for charts, games, and music apps. Tracking is a side effect of how much they expose. The W3C’s guidance on mitigating fingerprinting in web specifications covers how standards authors try to avoid adding new signals.

You might not write a single line of fingerprinting code yourself and still end up involved. There are three common ways that happens.

Your third-party scripts can do it without asking you. Analytics tags, ad scripts, chat widgets, social buttons. Each of them can call the same APIs your own code can. If your page loads fifteen of them, that’s fifteen possible fingerprinters. Checking what each script does has quietly become part of the job.

Browsers are closing the door. Chrome froze most of the User-Agent string and moved detailed info into Client Hints. Safari has Advanced Fingerprinting Protection. Firefox blocks known fingerprinting scripts, and Brave randomizes values returned by fingerprintable APIs. If your site depends on the old, wide-open APIs, you’re building on ground that’s shrinking every release.

Most of this comes down to one rule: collect less, and know why you’re collecting what’s left.

Search your codebase for the high-entropy stuff: canvas exports, WebGL renderer lookups, font detection, and calls to navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues(). If a feature still works without them, take them out.

In many teams, the biggest win is boring. Someone added a fingerprinting library years ago for one fraud check, nobody reviewed it since, and it’s still loading on every page. Deleting it helps more than any clever fix.

The classic User-Agent string packs browser, exact version, OS, and CPU architecture into one header. Client Hints break that apart so you only get what you ask for.

By default, Chromium browsers already send three basic hints: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. For most sites, that’s plenty, and you don’t need to request anything extra. If a feature really does need more detail, ask for that one hint with Accept-CH:

Skip full version numbers, architecture, and device model unless you have a real reason. Each extra hint makes your visitors a little easier to tell apart.

Keep in mind that only Chromium-based browsers support User-Agent Client Hints. Firefox and Safari won’t send them, so you’ll need a fallback. Where you can, feature detection beats browser detection anyway.

Here’s an uncomfortable truth: once a script runs on your page, it can call canvas, WebGL, and audio APIs, and there’s no header that switches those off. What you can control is which scripts run and how close they get to your page.

None of these is a silver bullet. Together, they cut down how much code gets the chance to fingerprint your users at all.

If your app draws on canvas (dashboards, editors, browser games), that output can be fingerprinted too. Try not to hand raw canvas data to third-party scripts.

Fonts count as well. Load fifteen unusual web fonts and you’ve given every script on the page an easy font fingerprint. A system font stack blends in better, and for interface text, most users won’t notice the difference.

Sometimes you’ll want to keep a fingerprint, for example to flag logins from a device you haven’t seen before. That’s fine, as long as you treat it with care:

Before you ship, open your site in Firefox with Enhanced Tracking Protection set to Strict, and in Brave with fingerprinting protection turned on. If something breaks, it was relying on a signal browsers are trying to get rid of.

Fix the feature. Don’t ask users to turn their protection down. Browsers are only going to get stricter from here.

What works better is a browser with fingerprinting protection built in, such as Brave, Firefox on strict settings, Safari, or Tor Browser. These either add noise to the signals or make everyone look the same. Extensions that block canvas and font reads can help too. So can simply updating your browser, since each release tends to remove a few more leaky details.

No single tool will stop fingerprinting completely. The good news is that it doesn’t have to. Fingerprinting works on probabilities, so making the signals noisier is often enough to break the match.

#10236. Motorola Signature 27 specs detailed in new video, including Tandem OLED display

Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs.

A video hands-on from Danny Winget on YouTube offers a closer look at Motorola’s upcoming flagship, and only makes its arrival all the more enticing.

There are several key specs mentioned in the video, with the most interesting being the “Extreme AMOLED Duo” display which makes use of Tandem OLED technology. Tandem OLED isn’t a new idea, with the tech stacking multiple layers of diodes on top of each other to improve contrast and brightness. Tandem OLED can be found on Apple’s new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, as well as 2024’s Honor Magic 6 RSR. But Motorola’s use of it in the Signature 27 is certainly nice to see, especially given the other spec shared. 12,000 nits of brightness. That rather insane figure is apparently the peak brightness on this new flagship.

Hardware shots of the phone also show the textured backs on the two color variants as well as the curved glass around the display.

I think it’s a interesting phone with a good camera system. But it also depend on the price. Anyway nice to see Motorola compete in the flagship space again.

The battery capacity isn’t revealed, but Winget says that it is “sizable.” Similarly, the vapor chamber is described as “40% larger” but a point of comparison wasn’t given.

It’s all shaping up for a powerful flagship in every sense of the word. Motorola has confirmed that Signature 27 will launch on November 5, and I don’t know about you, but I’m only getting more excited about it.

New power system is already operational in Ulanqab, China, where it will eventually ‘support up to one million AI accelerators.’

Envision Energy says that it has completed the world’s first commercial data center deployment of an integrated 800-volt DC power system. It has been testing the Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model since August this year at its Galaxy AI data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China. Touted as offering simpler, and more efficient power architecture, Envision’s system will also support higher computing density, says a press release. The Galaxy campus will scale to 3GW capacity according to current plans, and eventually “support up to one million AI accelerators.”

Currently, data centers rely on several power-conversion stages to achieve a usable supply from the grid. Envision’s Dubhe tech converts power directly from 10kV medium-voltage AC to an 800V DC bus to boost efficiency and slashes the size of the power conversion apparatus. It is built around three critical capabilities:

The system includes integrated battery support for fast response to AI workload spikes and for short-term backup power. It will also support higher-density AI racks, for more computing power in the same area, says the Chinese tech firm. Moreover, Envision’s system has been designed to work well with renewable energy sources and storage. Key to the efficiency and performance on offer is the AI-driven power management provided by the Envision Dubhe controller, smartly balancing power supply and computing demand. Other benefits include a more compact footprint and a reduced requirement for copper and other cabling.

By the firm’s own accounts the Dubhe tech system is performing well. Thus, it looks set to be instrumental to the expansion of the compute resources at the Galaxy AI data center in Ulanqab. Furthermore, Envision also intends to roll out this 800V DC tech at its Mission Gobi initiative, targetting 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions by 2030.

#10233. Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly

As we near the launch of Motorola’s return to the flagship space, it’s becoming clear that the company is ready to fill a gap left by the departure of OnePlus, though there’s one very obvious difference between the two.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The Motorola Signature 27’s launch is coming up fast and, with it, the first truly exciting flagship the company has launched widely in quite some time. There have been a handful of high-end Moto devices in recent years, but this is the first one in quite a while where it seems Motorola is holding nothing back.

Between a powerful Snapdragon chip, top-tier cameras, and rumors of a massive battery, this is shaping up to be something special. Of course, all-out flagships like this aren’t uncommon in some parts of the world. Oppo, Honor, and other Chinese brands have been building devices like this for years but, especially in the US, they’re just completely lacking, especially now that OnePlus is dead. While OnePlus flagships in more recent years have not quite risen to the same bar as Oppo’s, they’ve been the best equivalent in the States and, now, they’re just gone.

Motorola is stepping up in a big way here, and seems to be the closest many are going to get to a OnePlus replacement.

It’s fitting, really. As much as I’d love to have Google Pixel step up its game here, Motorola’s Lenovo backing and long history in the smartphone space more than earns its spot as a proper flagship smartphone maker. The problem, really, is just going to boil down to pricing.

OnePlus was well known for top-tier specs, of course, but it built its brand on doing so at a lower price point. Even in its final days where prices were creeping higher than ever, a OnePlus flagship was still priced equal to or less than most competitors. Motorola Signature 27 does not seem to be trying to recover that part of OnePlus’ reputation based on early pricing leaks. RAMageddon surely isn’t helping matters, but Motorola’s return to the flagship space is not going to come cheap from the sound of it.

Another sore point for Motorola is in software updates, but it’s not like OnePlus was really doing that well in that regard anyway. Things are moving in a better direction with Motorola moving up to 7-year commitments on certain devices, but there’s still room for improvement and quite the poor track record to make up for.

With the launch of Motorola Signature 27 mere weeks away, I’m personally very excited to see what the company has in store. What do you think?

You’d think that Android foldables effectively doing all of the R&D for Apple’s first foldable would prevent any major issues, but apparently that’s not enough. While the scale of the problem remains unclear, Apple’s iPhone Duo is cracking for many in the same place, suggesting there’s a manufacturing problem in play. It’s not quite an OG Galaxy Fold debacle, but it doesn’t feel far off either.

Google’s latest frontier AI model has been announced in Gemini 4 Carbon. The company says it makes major leaps forward for coding and other purposes and outranks the competition but, like Argon, it’s not immediately available.

After being announced earlier this month, we reviewed the Fitbit Edge this week and the tracker is also now on sale. While it feels like an awkward middle child between the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, owners of prior Charge trackers will likely appreciate the upgrades it brings to the table.

#10231. Google says Googlebook ‘detachables’ are coming soon

At the Android Dev Summit 2026 earlier this week, Google said that Googlebook detachables will be the next form factor after clamshells and convertibles.

This reveal at the Wednesday developer keynote isn’t particularly surprising given leaks earlier this year. On stage, Google highlighted how Googlebook “spans across large screen form factors from clamshells, convertibles, and soon detachables.”

At launch, four of the five devices are clamshells:

The Acer Googlebook 14 at $899 is the sole convertible with a 2-in-1 form factor that allows for laptop, tent, and tablet modes. Notably, day-one limitations suggest Google has some remaining work before launching a pure detachable. While fullscreen apps can open in portrait tablet mode, the Googlebook OS homescreen/desktop, Overview, and app tray are only available in landscape.

The first Googlebook detachable should be from Lenovo. According to a July leak, the tablet has both a detachable keyboard and kickstand. There’s even a Glowbar next to the camera. This device leaked alongside a laptop smaller than the current 15-inch model.

With Googlebook OS coming to tablets, a broader question is what operating system high-end Android tablets will use going forward. There certainly should still be space for tablets running Android, but Googlebook OS in theory allows for a more desktop-like experience as the company keeps iterating.

#10230. 6 Email Tools Developers Can Use to Build, Test, and Monitor Better Email

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A password-reset email can leave your application successfully and still fail the user. It might arrive too late, display an unreadable button, or contain a link pointing to the staging environment.

These failures belong to different parts of the email workflow. Fixing the HTML will not repair authentication, and improving sender reputation will not correct an expired verification token.

For developers and designers, the useful question is therefore: which tool helps us inspect the layer that is failing?

The following six options cover mailbox reputation, local testing, message construction, responsive design, compatibility research, and production monitoring. They serve different purposes; they are not interchangeable alternatives.

For teams managing connected business mailboxes, EmailPond describes a service for automated warmup and reputation monitoring, including connections to Google Workspace and Microsoft 365.

The engineering lesson is to distinguish three outcomes:

A successful submission does not establish that a message reached the inbox.

When evaluating mailbox warmup or reputation services, ask what their measurements actually represent. Are they based on participating test accounts, provider feedback, or a proprietary score? What period and sample size do they cover?

Treat any score as one diagnostic input. A result from a testing network is not evidence that every real recipient will receive the same placement.

Also match the tool to your infrastructure. A connected employee mailbox and an application sending through a transactional email provider may use different delivery paths. Activity on one does not demonstrate the health of the other.

Practical exercise: document the sending path for each message type: visible From address, sending provider, authentication domain, and responsible team. This makes later investigations much more precise.

Mailpit runs an SMTP testing server with a web interface and an API for inspecting captured messages. It is useful when testing registration, receipts, invitations, and password resets without delivering development messages to real customers.

Use local capture to inspect more than appearance:

Point the application at SMTP host 127.0.0.1, port 1025, and open http://127.0.0.1:8025 to inspect messages. This example assumes the application runs on the host; an application in another container needs appropriate container networking.

Binding the ports to localhost keeps this development instance off public interfaces. For a repeatable team environment, pin the image to a reviewed version or digest.

Practical exercise: trigger account verification, capture the message, and confirm that the link works once and fails after reuse. Test token behavior through the application, not just by inspecting the email.

Nodemailer provides email-sending functionality for Node.js, including SMTP transport and HTML/plain-text message construction.

Keeping message construction in a dedicated module makes it easier to review and test. Here is a minimal local example using Mailpit:

Run it with node send-test.mjs. Production configuration needs the authentication and TLS settings required by your provider.

SitePoint’s guide to sending email using Node.js provides additional context for building an email workflow.

Practical exercise: move rendering into a separate function and test missing optional fields, long names, and HTML-sensitive characters. Escape untrusted text when inserting it into HTML.

MJML is a markup language that compiles components into responsive email HTML. Its sections, columns, text blocks, and buttons let teams maintain a readable template source.

Keep source templates in version control and compile them during a reproducible build. Review the final output after personalization and any link rewriting.

A component system reduces repetitive layout work, but it does not establish that every message is accessible or renders correctly in every client.

Practical exercise: test a long translated heading, enlarged text, blocked images, and a narrow viewport. The essential message and primary action should remain understandable in each case.

SitePoint’s HTML email design overview offers background on designing within email-client constraints. Pair its established principles with current compatibility data.

Can I Email publishes support information for HTML and CSS across email clients. It helps developers investigate a specific feature before building a template around it.

Start with the clients that matter to your audience. Then inspect support notes for the features your design depends on, including partial support and the date of testing.

A global support percentage cannot tell you whether a feature works for your particular recipients.

For critical content, design a usable fallback. A button should remain identifiable without a decorative background image. A heading should communicate its meaning even when a custom font is unavailable.

Practical exercise: select three visual features in a proposed template and document what users see when each is unsupported. If losing a feature hides the primary action, revise the design.

Compatibility research narrows the risks. Testing the final message in representative clients checks the actual result. SitePoint’s HTML email testing guide provides further background on that review process.

Google Postmaster Tools provides information about email sent to personal Gmail accounts, including authentication, reputation, spam reports, and delivery errors.

Use it alongside application and sending-provider telemetry. Its data concerns Gmail traffic; it is not a universal view of delivery across every mailbox provider.

For example, if delivery errors increase after a provider change, compare the timing with authentication configuration and sending-volume changes. If users report missing messages while the application shows no failures, inspect later delivery events rather than assuming the original SMTP response proves success.

Google’s email sender guidelines explain authentication and sending requirements. SPF authorizes sending infrastructure for the envelope domain, DKIM provides a verifiable signature, and DMARC evaluates alignment with the visible From domain. Configuring them correctly is foundational, but does not guarantee inbox placement.

Practical exercise: create a release checklist that verifies authentication on real test messages from the production sending path, rather than checking DNS records alone.

Tool selection becomes useful when each tool supports a clear acceptance check.

Production systems also need explicit retry behavior. Queueing email can keep slow sending operations out of an HTTP request, but retries can create duplicate messages.

Use a stable application event identifier to track a notification attempt. Where a provider supports idempotency keys, use them according to its documented limits. Otherwise, record provider message identifiers and handle uncertain outcomes carefully: a timeout can occur after the provider has accepted a message.

Test expired notifications as well. A password-reset message delayed in a queue should not promise that its link is still valid.

For delivery-event webhooks, verify authenticity using the provider’s documented mechanism, deduplicate repeated events, and tolerate out-of-order arrival. Avoid logging message bodies or authentication tokens as routine diagnostics.

A useful email workflow gives the team a clear answer to each question: what did we generate, where did we send it, what happened afterward, and could the recipient complete the intended task?

Start with local capture and reliable message construction. Add template and compatibility checks. Then connect production delivery signals to application events.

The measure of success is whether users can verify an account, retrieve a report, or recover access reliably—not simply whether a send function returned successfully.

#10229. Google reveals new Gemini 4 Carbon AI model, narrowly beating Claude Opus 5.5

Tests now push models to reveal their greater weaknesses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Last week, Google released its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, topping intelligence rankings charts. The model has landed with a grander splash than most. As Artificial Analysis highlights, Gemini 4 Carbon is now the highest-ranked AI model on its latest Intelligence Index V5 benchmark suite, beating Claude Opus 5.5 by one point. It achieves the number one score across four of the nine evaluations, and does so at a lower cost per task than other high-ranking models, like Claude Opus 5.5. Google is offering access to the model for cyber defenders first through its Fairwind program, with wider availability coming sometime after.

Perhaps more crucially, Gemini 4 Carbon stands apart by topping Artificial Analysis' new AA-Omniscience v 1.1 test that tracks hallucinations and knowledgeable recall of information. As governments and institutions look to maximize value and security from their use of AI, being able to claim the lowest hallucination score could prove a significant selling point.

Then again, even the best scored only 54 on the -100 to +100 scale, suggesting even the best frontier models in 2026 are a far cry from being consistently reliable when it comes to accurately recalling information.

AI model rankings change fast and regularly in 2026, and it's no surprise that the latest release from a frontier lab has pushed the envelope, but Google's Gemini 4 Carbon can be seen as a comeback after languishing with irregular releases for much of the year.

Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores a 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index V5 benchmark. That puts it a single point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback), and two points ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra (max). It's also nine points ahead of Meta's Muse Wonder Full (Max), and 10 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback).

But raw, generalized intelligence isn't the whole picture with frontier models in 2026. As developers chase the Pareto frontier— the best-possible confluence of cost and intelligence — Gemini 4 Carbon is also impressively affordable. Its cost per task on the Intelligence Index test is actually slightly cheaper than Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), priced at $7.76 each. That's several dollars cheaper than either Claude Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5, both max with fallback, and not far off half the price of Claude Fable 5.1, which costs $12.99 per task.

Gemini 4 Carbon is still more expensive than OpenAI's GPT 5 Astra and about six times more expensive than GPT 6.1 Sol (max). It's about 13 times as expensive per task as the open-weight DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, too, although that model measures a mere 32 on the Intelligence Index rankings.

Gemini 4 Carbon isn't the best at everything, but it may be the best at most of the high price points. At least for now. Arena.ai has it holding the top spot on its Pareto Frontier chart at the more expensive end of the spectrum, but at lower price points, the Chinese open-weight models like GLM 5.3-Flash and DeepSeek V4 Pro take over.

Artificial Analysis also highlights that Gemini 4 Carbon isn't as good as Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at programming, and it falls behind Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder, and Kimi K3.1 Pro on knowledge work.

But perhaps the most impressive score is Gemini 4's 54 on the AA-Omniscience Index, which tracks knowledge and hallucinations, beating out the competition by often significant margins.

Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index.October 28, 2026

In Google's announcement of the new Gemini 4 model, it talked up its collaboration with the U.S. government for model screening and pre-release testing. In a similar manner to the way Anthropic handled Mythos' release in 2025, Google is rolling out access to Gemini 4 Carbon at a slower pace.

"We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing," Google's launch statement reads.

To that end, it's opening up Carbon to a subset of "cyber defenders," and will gradually make the model more widely available through trusted partners through its Fairwind Program. Before it makes Carbon available to developers, it wants to iterate on its guardrails to make the AI safer and more effective for cybersecurity purposes, making it harder for nefarious actors to use it for exploits and hacking.

Where the idea of slowing the industry and introducing greater oversight for model development has risen and fallen in the estimations of the major tech companies, it does appear to be cementing itself as more of a foundational idea for future model releases. Google talks up its release on the improved safety and security of its model, highlighting that it thwarted all attempts from the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark to have it do something it shouldn't.

Google claims Carbon cuts unsupported claims in its responses twice as much as the Gemini 4 Argon model it debuted just two weeks ago. If it can't complete an action, it will just not do so, rather than fabricating an answer or hedging around missing evidence, Google claims.

It also suggests Carbon will present sources and suggested actions to the user more readily, rather than pursuing its own intentions when there are discrepancies or uncertainties, allegedly cutting model overreach by 26%.

As governments and companies look to make realistic use of AI, tracking usage, managing token budgets, and preventing workers from creating new exploit paths through overuse, a model's safety, security, and reliability will be paramount.

Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on AA-Omniscience, the highest of any model, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48). It answers more questions correctly than Gemini 4 Argon (58% vs 48% accuracy), at the cost of a higher hallucination rate (11% vs 4%). This is still far below Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max), both at 50%October 28, 2026

For the past year, a clear focus from frontier and open-weight model developers has been on efficiency and cost. While raising intelligence and improving capabilities, particularly through agentic workflows, has seen great development alongside pomp and circumstance, many of the major announcements and developments have also considered cost a clear component.

That's not likely to change, with the latest research from Gartner showing that just 3% of companies are actually achieving cost and productivity improvements from AI use. But as organizations push to find the real value in AI, maximize token budgets, and try to empower workers who have found improvements from using AI, they'll want consistency.

Tracking return on investment with AI is notoriously difficult, with hallucinations making that far harder. If Google can sell its latest model(s) as the safest and least likely to hallucinate, and do so with high intelligence at a relatively low cost, that might be the new winning formula.
